case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 12.7.78 passed by the High Court Division in S.M.A. No. 7 of 1973)
full_judgment:
K. M. Subhan, J.—This appeal by special leave is from the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in S.M.A. No. 7 of 1973. The judgment-debtors are the appellants and have raised the following question for determination by this Court.

1. Whether section 14 of the Limitation Act is available in an execution proceeding.

2. In the facts of this case whether it could be said that the second executions petition was within time.

2. The facts giving rise to these questions are that there was a suit for declaration of an easement right over the passing of water through a drain "between the respondents and appellants. The suit was decreed on compromise between the parties concerned on 26th March, 1964. The decree-holder-respondents instituted an Execution case which was dismissed for default on 26th June, 1965. The decree-holder-respondents thereafter filed an application before the Munsif who passed the decree for amendment of the decree under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The amendment sought for was the substitution of the word "uttor parsha" appearing in the second line of paragraph 2 of the compromise petition for the words "uttor purba" on the ground that it was a bonafide mistake. It was stated that the decree would be in executable and meaningless unless the amendment was allowed. This application was filed on 6th April, 1966 and was rejected by the Court on 11th May, 1967. This order of rejection was challenged before the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction but the Rule was discharged on final hearing on 25th June, 1970. The decree holders-respondents, thereafter, filed a second Execution case on 10th November, 1970 which was resisted by the judgment-debtor-appellants under section 47 of the Code, on the ground that it was barred by Limitation having not been filed within three years from the date of the dismissal of the 1st Execution case under Article 182 of the Limitation Act. This objection was negatived by the Executing Court, the Lower Appellate Court and the High Court Division in the Second Miscellaneous Appeal.

The High Court Division dismissed the appeal holding the decree holder is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 14 of the Limitation Act, and as such the second Execution case was not barred by limitation.

<u>3. Mr. A. Salam, the learned Counsel, has firstly pointed that the section 14 of the Limitation Act cannot be invoked in an execution proceeding. The language of section 14 of the Limitation Act does not tend to bar its application to execution proceedings. The provisions of section 14 provide for exclusion of time of proceeding bonafide by a party in a court which has no jurisdiction to entertain the proceeding. This section is available not only to proceeding of the Courts of the first instance but also in the appellate Courts and in execution Courts. Thus the first contention of Mr. Salam fails.</u>

4. In so far as the computing of the period that passed between the dismissal of the first execution case on 26th June, 1965 and the institution of the second execution case on the 10th November, 1970 there is no doubt that more than three years had lapsed thus the execution case becoming barred under Article 182 of the Limitation Act. The learned Single Judge in order to overcome this bar invoked the aid of section 14 subsection (2) of the Limitation Act which is as follows:

"14(2) in computing the period of limitation prescribed for any application, the time during which the applicant has been prosecuting with due diligence another civil proceeding, whether in a Court of first instance or in a Court of appeal against the same party for the same relief shall be excluded, where such proceeding is prosecuted in good faith in a Court which from defect of jurisdiction or other cause of a like nature, is unable to entertain it."

<u>5. Of this sub-section (2) the only words which need interpretation to resolve the question are "same relief" in the background of the application filed under section 151 of the Code by the decree-holder-respondents which was rejected both by the trial Court and the High Court Division. The relief sought in the application under section 151 of the Code was for the substitution of the words "uttor Parsha" in place of word "uttor purba" occurring in the compromise petition. In that application it was maintained that the decree without the substituted words was meaningless and in executable. The relief that was being sought in the Executing Court was for execution of the decree whereas, under Section 151 the relief sought was for substitution of the words in the com-promise petition instead of the words there, in other words an amendment of the decree The question is whether these two reliefs come within the meaning of the expression "same relief" as occurring in section 14(2) of the Limitation Act Mr. Salam has made references to some decisions of the Indian Jurisdiction to show that the reliefs in the Act, should be of similar nature. The decisions are reported in AIR 1935 Allahabad 323, AIR 1918 Lahore 117, AIR 1935 P.C. 85, AIR 1945 Madras 86, AIR 1948 Bombay 185. The general trend of the Indian High Courts in these decisions as cited shows that the relief concerned must be of similar nature. The view appears to be that the words "same relief" could not be construed so as to look not to the primary relief sought in a proceeding but the ultimate object with which the relief was sought. In the Privy Council case a preliminary mortgage decree was obtained which was amended in some respects not material to be particularised. There were a number of mortgagors interested in the mortgage some of whom preferred an appeal before the High Court against the preliminary decree. On the failure of the appeal before the High Court, the decree-holder sought execution under the preliminary decree. In this background their Lordships of the Privy Council were of the opinion that the application to obtain execution under the preliminary decree was not an application for the same relief as the application to the Court for a final mortgage decree for sale in the suit. The Privy Council did not elaborate the reasons for their decision. What appears, however, as embodied in the decision is that the words "same relief" occurring under section 14(2) cannot but be relief of a similar nature. We do not find anything to depart from this view.</u>

6. In the present appeal we find it difficult to bring the prayer for amendment of the decree under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the same relief for execution of unammended decree, within meaning of expression same relief" occurring in section 14(2) of the Limitation Act.

In this view, the appeal is allowed but in the facts of case we make no order as to costs. The decrees of courts below are set aside and the execution petition dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule obtained u/s. 115(old) of the Code of Civil Procedure raises an interesting question of law, namely, whether a decree-holder who has obtained a prohibitory order of permanent injunction can enforce the decree against the judgment-debtor who has wilfully failed to obey it by his detention In the civil prison or by the attachment of his property or by both, in terms of sub-rule (1) of Order 21, role 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure or, is the relief contained in the said provision of the Code limited to mandatory injunction only?

2. The plaintiff-opposite party obtained a decree for permanent injunction against the defendant-petitioners in Title Suit No. 86 of 1972 of the 1st Court of Munsif, Moulvibazar on 16.11.73. They were permanently restrained from creating any disturbance to the peaceful possession of the suit land of the opposite party. On 2nd Poush, 1381 B.S. the petitioners violated the permanent order of Injunction, trespassed into the ease land and cultivated boro paddy thereon The opposite party claimed enforcement of the decree by putting the petitioner into the civil jail and by attaching their properties and filed Misc. Case No. 15 of 1975 in this Court of Munsif, Moulvibazar under Order 21. rule 32 C.P.C.

The learned Munsif by his Judgment and order dated 7.2.77 allowed the Misc. Case and committed the petitioners to the civil prison to suffer imprisonment for a period of 15 days each. Thereafter the petitioners obtained the present Rule.

3. Before 1 advert to the arguments of Mr. M.A. Matin, learned Advocate for the petitioners, I deem it to be convenient to set out sub-rule (1) & (5) of Order 21, rule 32 C.P.C. which are as follows:—

"32. Decree for specific performance for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction.—(1) where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction, has been parsed, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced (in the ease of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for specifics performance of a contract or for an injunction) by his detention in the civil prison, or by the attachment of his property, or by both. …………………………….

(5) Where a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction had not been obeyed, the Court may, in lieu of or in addition to all or any of the processes aforesaid, direct that the act required to be done may be done so far as practicable by the decree-bolder or some other person appointed by the Court, at the cost of the judgment-debtor, and upon the act being done the expenses incurred may be ascertained in such manner as the Court may direct and may be recovered as If they were included in the decree.

Mr. M.A. Matin submits that the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity In the exercise of his jurisdiction In not holding that the Misc. case was not maintainable at all. He submits that when a prohibitory order of Injunction is violated the decree is not executable and the execution case is not maintainable for any of the remedies under Order 21, rule 32 C.P.C. Mr. Matin has cited the case of Burhanuddin Ahmed and ors. vs. Veda Bram Chakraborti and ors; 16 DLR (Dec) 61, in support of his submission.

<u>4. Sub-rule (5) of Order 21, rule 32 C.P.C. as quoted above, may now be noticed. There Is universal unanimity In a series of decisions from various jurisdictions of this sub-continent, including our own, that the remedy provided for in sub-rule (5) Order 21, rule 32 is not alienable when a prohibitory order of injunction Is violated. The prayer of the opposite party in the present case, however, is not for any direction that the act required to be done by the judgment-debtor-petitioners may be done through Court under sub-rule (5) of Order 21, rule 32. The opposite party prayed for enforcement of the decree by detaining the petitioners In the civil prison or by attaching their property or by both, because they have allegedly violated the order. Clearly their case falls under sub-rule (1) of Order 21, rule 32 C.P.C.</u>

5. Mr. M.A. Matin submits that only a decree of mandatory Injunction can be executed by way of detention of the judgment debtors in a civil prison or by attachment of their properties or by both, In case there Is a wilful failure to obey the decree. Sub-rule (1) of Order 21, rule 32 C.P.C. does not apply to a decree of prohibitory injunction.

6. In the case cited by Mr. Matin reported in 16 DLR (Dac) 61, sub-rule (1) of Order 21, rule 32 was held to be inapplicable to an order of prohibitory Injunction. The reasons given by the learned Single Judge are that the words used in sub-rule (1) are "willfully failed to obey". The words are not "willfully disobeyed" or violated the injunction order. Apparently the learned Judge was of the opinion that a blatant violation of a prohibitory order of Injunction Is not the same thing as a willful failure to obey the order. The learned Judge was of further opinion that when there is violation of an injunction order there remains no decree to be enforced. Also there is no provision for evicting a person who violated the prohibitory injunction order. A decree for prohibitory Injunction does not provide how the judgment-debtor who has violated the injunction order can be thrown out of the land. A decree-holder in a case of mandatory injunction may remedy the mischief caused by the judgment-debtor by taking recourse to the provision of sub-rule (5) of Order 21, rule 32 but a decree-holder In case of prohibitory injunction cannot.

With respect, I am frankly unable to accept the reasonings and conclusion of the aforecited decision for reasons more than one.

<u>7. First sub-rule (1) of Order 21, rule 32 appears to me to be a particular manner or method of enforcing an otherwise lamentable decree, if it is violated. The manner and method of "enforcing" the decree have nothing to do with its "execution" is a penalty for the violation of the decree Itself. A prohibitory order of Injunction is as such in-executable, but sub-rule (1) implies that if the prohibitory order is violated then by securing the detention of the judgment debtor in the civil prison or by attaching Ms property or by both such an in-executable decree may be "enforced". In other words, the detention or attachment of property or both is itself the "enforcement" of the decree, lilt is violated. Sub-rule (5) is an alternative or additional remedy. Order 21, rule 32 does not say that a decree-holder cannot avail of the remedy under sub-rule (1) if the remedy under sub-rule (5) is not available to him. A prohibitory order of injunction cannot be executed under sub-rule (5), but Its violation is Independently enforceable under sub-rule (1).</u>

<u>8. Secondly, the use of the words "willfully failed to obey" does not imply that it Is only a negative act of wilful failure that will attract the mischief of sub-rule (1). If a person does exactly the act which he is prohibited from doing then in my opinion it is very much a wilful failure to obey she decree. The words used in sub-rule (1) denote not only a negative state of mind but also a positive act of disobedience.</u>

<u>9. Thirdly, I am also unable to agree, with respect, that when a prohibitory order of injunction is violated, there remains no decree to be enforced. Sub-rule (1) gives a special remedy to the decree-holders for the violation of the decree. It is not a specific method of execution of the decree in terms of the decree itself. A decree for restitution of conjugal rights or for specific performance or for injunction does not in terms provide for the detention of the Judgment-debtor in the civil prison or for attachment of his properly. Sub-rule (1) is a special penalty reserved for the judgment-debtor if ho wilfully disobeys the decree. The enforcement of the decree in terms of the decree itself is not contemplated in sub-rule (1).</u>

<u>10. Fourthly, a wrong will go without remedy if the Code of Civil Procedure is held to be without any provision for punishing a judgment debtor for willfully violating a prohibitory order of injunction. It will then be practically useless to obtain any decree for permanent Injunction. Sub-rule (1) provides a remedy for breach of the prohibitory order itself and however incomplete the remedy may be it is an effective safeguard against wilful violation of a Court's decree.</u>

11. In the case reported in 16 DLR (Dec) 61 some of the earlier decisions which are in accord with my line of thinking have not been noticed. Thus in the case of Prag Dart Vs. Kedar Nadi and ors. AIR 1945 Oudh 81 it has been hold as follows :—

"The judgment-debtor has now come in appeal to this Court where It is argued that neither sub-rule. (5) nor sub-rule. (1) has any application to prohibitory injunctions. It is argued that there must be some definite act to be performed before there can be disobedience to the decree within the meaning of rule 32(1). I cannot accept this argument since it appears to me that if a person is prohibited from doing something and does it, it is just as much disobedience as if he is ordered to do something and fails to do it……………….after all if the decree-holder could never proceed in the execution department to enforce a prohibitory decree, it would seem that such a decree would be completely valueless and he might just as well have no decree at all".

12. The same reasoning has been followed in the ease of Gondila Manjappa Shetty Vs. Manjakke Shedthi and ors., AIR 1961 Mys 268. It has been held therein that a person disobeys an injunction not only if he fails to perform an act which he is directed to do but also when he does an act which he is prohibited from doing. There is as much disobedience in the one casts as In the other. This is how sub rule (1) bee been Interpreted In this decision.

In some other reported decisions, where it has been categorically held that sub rule (5) is only applicable to mandatory injunctions, it has also been observed that sub-rule (I) is available as a relief to the decree-holder in case a prohibitory order of Injunction is violated.

13. Ono such decision is the case of Toon Lal Vs. Sonoo LA AIR 1958 Pal 522. It has been held that where there is an injunction prohibiting the judgment-debtor from doing some act and the judgment-debtor Moo, boys that injunction, the remedy for the decree-holder would be by way of his detention in the civil prison or by way of attachment of his property or by both.

14. Further, in the case of Nari Chinnabba Cherry Vs. E. Chengalraya Cherry and ors., AIR 1950 Madras 237, it has been held that the decree-holder in the case of violation of a prohibitory injunction has not only got a right of suit to get a mandatory injunction for the removal of the obstructions, etc., but has also the easier remedy under Order 21, rule 32(1). He can ask for The detention of the judgment debtor in the civil prison, or the attachment of his property or both, and a Court can order either or both of those things to be done in case the judgment debtor will not remove the obstruction within a time prescribed by the Court. Such an order of the Court will normally be quite effective, and will enable the decree-holder to enjoy the fruits of his decree.

15. In the case of Ajabrao vs. Atmaram, AIR 1954 Nag 245, a Division Bench of the Nagpur High Court also holds that Sub-rule (1) to (4) of Order 21, rule 32 may contemplate both kinds of injunctions, mandatory and prohibitory.

In the case of Muuarl Lal vs. Nawal Kishore, AIR 1961 Par 547, an application was made for enforcemant of a decree of prohibitory injunction under sub-rule (5). It was held that the application does not lie and that the execution of the decree is to be made under sub-rule (1) of rule 32.

16. In the Dacca High Court itself an obiter dicta in the case of Saleh Ahmed vs. Kabir Ahmed, (1961) 13 DLR Dacca 531 remained unnoticed in the case reported in 16 DLR (Dacca) 61. It was argued in the said case that none of the sub-rules (1) to (5) of Order 21, rule 32 applied to a case of prohibitory injunction. The learned Single Judge rejected this contention and observed as follows:—

'I am afraid this amounts to going a little too far. I think sub-rules (1) and (2) of rule 32 of Order XXI, are applicable to cases to prohibitory injunction 1,

<u>17. Though the observations above are in the nature of an obiter these are in conformity with the earlier decisions of the past to various High Courts.</u>

<u>In view of the discussions above I, differ most respectfully with the decision reported in 16 DLR (Dacca) 61 and hold that when a prohibitory injunction is violated the decree-holder's remedy Iies in the enforcement of the decree under Order 21, rule 32 (1) C.P.C. apart from any other remedy that he may have ha&</u>

<u>18. Mr. Matin submits next that the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity in committing the petitioners to the civil prison without discussing the D.Ws'. evidence on record. Mr. Matin does not argue that had their evidence been considered the judgment of the learned Munsif would have been otherwise. It does not appear, therefore, that any illegality or material irregularity has been committed by an omission to discuss their evidence.</u>

<u>I, therefore, find no ground for interference in this Rule.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is discharged bat without any order as to costs. Let the records be sent back immediately.</u>

End.

case_source: (On appeal from the judgment and order dated 31st May passed by the High Court Division in Civil Order 824 of 1976.
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J.-This appeal by special leave arises from the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated May 31st, 1976 in Civil Order No. 824 of 1976.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of the appeal are that the appellant and respondents 11-15 as plaintiff instituted Partition Suit No. 6 of 1940 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Faridpur and preliminary decree was passed on 1st March, 1944. An appeal was preferred by the contesting defendants being First Appeal No. 242 of 1944 which was dismissed on 11th December, 1951. The appellant ultimately applied for final decree on 5th December, 1973 with a prayer for amendment of the preliminary decree by substituting the heirs of the contesting parties who died after the preliminary decree. Objection was filed to the same on 18th April, 1975. The Sub-ordinate Judge allowed the prayer for drawing up final decree, but prayer for amendment of the decree was rejected on the ground that at this stage the Court cannot go beyond the preliminary decree. The appellant moved a revision application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the High Court Division but it was summarily rejected on the ground that the move taken by the appellant was for delaying the proceedings as he is in possession of the properties.

3. Against this order leave was granted to examine the contention raised by the appellant whether the trial Court as well as the High Court Division were correct in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the preliminary decree.

4. Mr. Zinnur Ahmed the learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing for the appellant submitted that although preliminary decree was passed as early as 1st. March, 1944 and the appeal preferred against the decree was dismissed on 11th December, 1951, but as the parties had been possessing their respective shares amicably necessity of final decree did not arise and as such application for drawing up of final decree became necessary because in the meantime the landlordism crests were acquired by the Government and the revisional settlement operation started. As the suit plots were recorded under different plot numbers and khatian numbers, and some of the defendants died in the meantime, the parties felt the necessity of having the final decree with necessary amendments in the preliminary decree. The learned Advocate also explained that unless the heirs of the contesting defendants are brought on record correct allotment of shares would not be possible. He also explained that unless the suit plots with their present numbers are described in the decree, it will again lead to inevitable disputes involving further litigations.

<u>5. From the judgment of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, it appears that completely on an erroneous view that the preliminary decree once passed cannot be amended he rejected the prayer for amendment. The learned Judges of the High Court Division rejected the prayer on a ground which is not at all tenable in the facts and circumstances, that is, that the whole object of the prays for amendment of the decree is to delay the proceeding.</u>

<u>6. The proceedings in a partition suit subsist till passing of the final decree. By the preliminary decree only disputed question of title, if any and extent of share of the parties along with the question of possession, are determined. Once the preliminary decree is passed and rights of the parties determined, the question of abatement of the suit on the death of a party does not arise. However, the heirs are to be brought on record for effecting proper allotment of shares. For substitution of heirs of a deceased defendant in a partition suit after the preliminary decree there is no limitation. It is true that such substitution could be made even after passing of the final decree, that is, at the stage of execution of the decree. In instant case it was adequately explained that in view of the long gap between the preliminary decree and passing of the final decree and death of a number of defendants and their shares having devolved upon their respective heirs, unless the Pleader Commissioner completes his work in their presence, the allotment of shares might be difficult, rather might lead to further litigations.</u>

7. We find there is sufficient force in this submission. The learned Judges of the High Court Division omitted to consider this aspect of the case. So far as the other contention is concerned it appears that it did not get proper consideration either from the learned Subordinate Judge or from the learned Judges of the High Court Division. Change of plot numbers cannot be made a ground for amendment of the preliminary decree but it appears that in view of the long period of time elapsing between passing of the preliminary decree and the final decree, and the wholesale acquisition of the rent-receiving interest of the Zaminders and the raiyats becoming tenants under the Government and the suit plots recorded under different numbers and khatians proper allotment of shares to all the parties including the heirs of the deceased defendants may not be conveniently made by the Pleader Commissioner. But it is a matter for the Pleader Commissioner to note the change while surveying the suit land and reconcile the new plot numbers with the old plot numbers. And on the basis of the report the final decree is to be passed.

In the result the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The order of the High Court Division and that of the Subordinate Judge dated 16th February, 1976 rejecting the prayer for substitution are set aside and the learned Subordinate Judge is directed to dispose of the matter in the light of the observations made above.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule obtained u/s 115 (old) of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order dated 23.5.77 passed in Misc Case No. 25 of 1977 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong.

2. Opposite Party Nos. 1-6 filed Civil Miscellaneous Case No. 35 of 1975 against the petitioner and others in the said Court under Section 14 of the Arbitration, Act for filing an Award with proceedings in Court. On 2.8.75 the said Misc. Case was allowed ex-parte purportedly u/s 17 of the Arbitration Act. The petitioner fried an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. for setting aide the said ex-parte order and decree which gave rise to Misc. Judicial Case No. 92 of 1975. The said Misc. Judicial Case No. 92 of 1975 was also dismissed for default of the petitioner on 18.3.77. Thereafter the petitioner filed an application under Order 9, Rule 9 read with Section 151 C.P.C. for restoration of the Misc. Judicial case No. 92 of 1975 after setting aside the order of dismissal for default dated 18.3.77. This gave rise to Misc. Case No. 25 of 1977.

3. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned order held that the application under Order 9, Rule 9 C.P.C. is not maintainable, but the application u/s. 151 C.P.C. is maintainable. On the merit of the case the learned Subordinate Judge viewing the past conduct of the petitioner held that line petitioner is trying to delay the inaner. Hence ire dismissed the Misc. Case but in the order portion he held that the Misc. Case is not maintainable not only under Order 9 Rule 9 C.P.C. but also u/s 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The petitioner thereafter obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman; learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned Subordinate Judge acted illegally and with materiel irregularity in holding that the application u/s. 151 was not maintainable. Indeed it is difficult to understand why the learned Subordinate Judge found in the order portion of his judgment that the application is not maintainable u/s 151 C.P.C. after having found in the body of the judgment that it is to maintainable.

<u>5. The proceedings, as has been stated before, originate from a spacial statute, namely under section 14 of the Arbitration Act. A decree was passed in terms of section 17 thereof which says that after a judgment it pronounced in terms of section 17 a decree shall follow. An appeal lies against such a decree on limited grounds. An "Order" dismissing an application for restoration of an ex-parte decree passed under suction 17 is not a "decree' but an "Order". Section 39 of the Arbitration Act mentions 5 kinds of "Orders" under the said Act against which appeal shall lie. it specifically says that appeal shall lie from no other "Order". An "Order" dismissing an application for restoration of an ex-parte decree passed under section 17 is not among then. Therefore no appeal lies under the Arbitration Act against an "Order" dismissing an application for restoration of an ex-parte decree passed under Section 17.</u>

<u>6. When an application for setting aside an ex-parte decree preferred under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. is dismissed for default, appeal is provided there from under Order 43, rule 1(d) C.P.C. Order 43, rule 1 C.P.C. contains provisions for appeal from "Order" only. It does not contain provisions for appeal from "decrees". If there was any provision in the Arbitration Act making appealable an "Order" of dismissal of an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. then surely Order 43, rule 1(d) C.P.C. would have applied. The petitioner's application under section 151 C.P.C. would not have been maintainable since a specific remedy of appeal would have been available to him. But since no appeal lies against an order of dismissal of an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. under the Arbitration Act itself the petitioner has no specific and alternative remedy against the dismissal. His application under section 151 C.P.C. therefore was clearly maintainable.</u>

<u>7. Mr. A. K. M. Shafiqur Rahman has cited the case of Belayet Hossein and another vs. Md. Abu Taher and others, 32 DLR (AD) 231, where provision for appeal in a specific, statute, namely the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was considered. It was held that under clause (12) of section 96 of the said Act the appeal was limited to the decree for pre-emption only and the proceeding in respect of which appeal is to be preferred must be a suit. No appeal lies under the Slate Acquisition and Tenancy Act against an order dismissing an application under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. for motoring a proceeding under section 96 of the sail Act decreed ex parte. The reasons given are, firstly, that time order of refusal to set aside the ex pate decree is not a decree and, secondly, that the order was passed in a proceeding which was not a suit. Mr. Shafiqur Rahman submits that following the same reasoning the special statute involved in the instant case, namely, the Arbitration Act should be looked into to see whether any provision for appeal has been provided in the special statute itself against an order dismissing an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. for restoration of an ex parte decree passed under section 17. I am of the opinion that the ratio deaden& of the case just cited applies on all fours in the instant ease.</u>

<u>8. Two other decisions have been cited from the bar. One is the case of Rajashwar Pruned Singh vs. Anaina Prasad Singh A.I.R. 1956 Patna 28 and the other is the case of R.M. Muthukrish-man Chattier and another vs. R. M. Muth-lagiri Chettiar and another A.I.R. 1950 Madras 295 where the words a case open to appeal occurring in Order 43, rule 1 (d) C.P.C. read with section 17 of the Arbitration Act fell fur consideration, but I do not had these two cases to be exactly on the point. Indeed these two cases have proceeded along different lines and have not considered that appeal is a creature of the statute. Order 43, rule 1(d) will apply only in cases of orders arising out of regular suits. If orders passed tinder special statutes are to be made appealable, they must be so made by the special statute itself. The decision of our Appellate Division has dealt with the matter in its correct perspective and the two decisions cited have not touched upon the question of special statute It all.</u>

<u>9. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman next submits that the learned Subordinate Judge acted illegally and with material irregularity in disposing of the application Ms 151 C.P.C. on merits on the date used for hearing on the point of maintainability /alone. He submits That the petitioner has been gravely prejudiced thereby because he got no opportunity to adduce evidence in support of his case.</u>

<u>10. Indeed the very opening words of the impugned judgment shows that the learned Subordinate Judge took up the case for hearing the issue of maintainability only. He should have given an opportunity to the petitioner and the opposite parties to adduce evidence in support of their respective cases. He should not have decided the case on merits without affording both sides an opportunity to present their respective cases on merits. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.</u>

11. The impugned order is set aside and the learned Subordinate Judge is directed to dispose of the petitioner's application u/s 151 C.P.C. after giving both sides an opportunity to adduce evidence in support of their respective cases and after hearing them.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 15 of 1977
lawyer:
M.H. Khandker with Abu Backker—For the Appellant
M. Gholam Rabbani with Ranesh Chandra Maitra—For Respondents 1 & 3
parties:
Md. Wasiq Khan ------- Appellant
Vs.
Md. Sabiq Khan ------- Respondent
case_source: With Appeal from Original Order No. 318 of 1979
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J:-These two appeals arise out of a final decree in a suit for partition.

2. Plaintiff respondent Nos 1-3 filed the suit for partition of paternal properties on 24.11.69 being T.S. No. 344 of 1969 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca, later renumbered as T.S. No 56 of 1972 of the Fourth Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca, and obtained a preliminary decree on contest on 28.2.73. A Pleader Commissioner was appointed by the Court's order dated 18.9.73 to effect partition of the suit properties. By Order No. 77 dated 10.6.75 the learned Sub-ordinate Judge noted that the Pleader Commissioner has submitted his report. He fixed 10.7.75 as the date for filing objection against the report of the Pleader Commissioner. On 10.7.75, the learned Subordinate Judge passed the following order:—

"Plaintiff has filed hajira. Parties have not filed any objection against the report of the Commissioner. So the Commissioner's report is accepted. Therefore, ordered that the preliminary decree is made final. Commissioner's report, map, field book, etc. is made part of the decree."

3. As against the aforesaid final decree dated 10.7.75, the defendant No. 1 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 76 of 1975 on 3.11.75 under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure along with an application for conduction of delay u/s 5 of the Limitation Act, which was opposed by the plaintiff-respondent. By Judgment and order dated 21.5.79 the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the Miscellaneous Case on contest. As against the order of dismissal the defendant No. 1 has preferred F.M.A. Act.318 of 1979.

The defendant No 1 has also preferred F.A. No. 15 of 1977 against the aforesaid final decree dated 10.7.75 in T.S. No. 56 of 1979. Both the two appeals have been heard together and will be disposed of by this Judgment.

Mr. M.H. Khondkar with Mr. Abu Backkar, learned Advocates, appear for the defendant No. 1, appellant in both the two appeals and Mr. M. Golam Rabbani with Mr. Ranesh Chandra Maitra, learned Advocates, appear for the plaintiff-respondents in both the two appeals.

4. Short facts necessary for the disposal of the two appeals are that Late Khan Bahadur Md. Saddiq died in 1965 leaving behind. 4 sons and 2 daughters. Plaintiff No. 1 and defendant Nos 1-3 are the sons of which defendant No. 2 & 3 are the daughters. Partible properties left by the deceased are (1) Schedule A' property, a town property at 62 R. K. Mission Road, Dacca (2) Schedule property also a town property at 61. R.K. Mission Road, Dacca, (3) Schedule 'C' property, also a town property at plot No. 130, Dhanmondi Residential Area and (4) Schedules D and D(i) property, landed property at Mouza Santanapara, P:S. Rupgonj, District Dacca, Plaintiffs claimed 2/5th share in each of Schedules 'A', 93',. 'C', & 'D' properties Defendants. 1-3 filed a joint written statement contesting the suit but at the time of trial defendants 1 & 2 prayed for separate sahams. Defendant No. 1, the appellant, claimed 3/5th share in schedules 'A' and 'B' properties, 1/5th share in schedules 'C' and 'D' properties and 4/15th share in schedule 'D(1)' properties. Defendant No. 2 claimed 1/5th share in ; schedules 'A', 'B', 'C', and .'D' properties and 1/10th share in schedule 'D(1)' properties. He also claimed an enhanced share in the suit properties for loan advanced to his late father. Defendant No. 4 claimed a share of 1/3rd in Schedule 'D (1)' properties. The learned Subordinate Judge apportioned the share of the parties by his Judgment and preliminary decree dated 28.2.73. Plaintiff's share in Schedule 'A', 'B', 'C' & 'D' properties was held to be 2/5th, and in Schedule 'D(1)' properties to be 1/5th. The share of defendant No. 1 in Schedules 'A' and 'B' properties was held to be 3/5th, in Schedules 'C', and 'D' properties to be 1/5th and in Schedule 'D(1)' properties to be 4/15th. The share of defendant No. 2 in Schedules 'C' and 'D' properties was held to be 1/5th and in Schedule 'D(1)' properties to be 1/10th. The share of defendant No. 4 in Schedule 'D(1)' properties was held to be 1/3rd.

5. In the order portion of the Judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge, however the share of the defendant No. 1 appellant in Schedules 'C' and 'D' properties were not mentioned. On an application dated 5-3-74 by the plaintiffs the learned Subordinate Judge by Order No. 76 dated 4-6-74 corrected the order portion of his Judgment. This is the last order that the learned Subordinate Judge passed in the suit before passing order No 77 dated 10-6-75:

6. The preliminary decree drawn up on 27-3-73, however, did not reflect either the original or corrected order portion of the Judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge. It contained some mistakes with regard to the shares of the parties and remains uncorrected even to this day.

7. Mr. M. H. Khondkar, the learned Advocate for the appellant, in assailing the final decree submits that the preliminary decree having not been drawn up in accordance with the order portion of the Judgment there is no valid preliminary decree at all for effecting partition of the suit properties. The Pleader Commissioner could not have worked for effecting a partition of the suit properties in the absence of a validly drawn-up preliminary decree. There was no legal foundation for his work. His entire exercise was a nullity and the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in accepting his report.

8. Mr. Ghulam Rabbani, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents, submits, on the other hand, that notwithstanding some formal defects in the drawing up of the preliminary decree, the Pleader Commissioner while allocating sahams to the parties has not gone beyond the order portion of the judgment dated 28-2-73. The apportionment cannot be taken exception to and no party has received more or less than his or her share prescribed in the Judgment. Even if the decree were correctly drawn up the Pleader. Commissioner would have apportioned sahams to the parties exactly in the same proportion as he has done presently. Mr. Rabbani has submitted an application u/s. 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with sections 151 & 153 thereof for correction of the preliminary decree and has submitted that the acceptance of the report of the Commissioner be upheld ex debito justiciae, in view of the fact that a clerical error of the Court should not be allowed to vitiate the entire proceedings specially when the error has not worked out to the prejudice of any party.

9. It appears that the Pleader Commissioner's report insofar as allocating sahams to the parties is concerned has not gone beyond the order portion of the learned Subordinate Judge's judgment dated 28-2-73. The question is, will the formal defects in the preliminary decree, which are clerical in nature, nullify the entire work of the Pleader Commissioner.

<u>10. We do not see why in such a situation general power of the Court to act ex debito justiciae should not be resorted to. As held by the Privy Council in Jai Behram Keder Nath AIR 1922 (PC) 269, "It is inherent in the general jurisdiction of the Court to act rightly and fairly according to the circumstances towards all parties involved. As was said by Cairns L. C. in Rodger V. The Comptoir d' Escompte de Paris (L.R. 3 P.C. 465 at page 475). 'One of the first and highest duties of all Courts is to take care that the act of the Court does no injury to any of the suitors and when the expression 'the act of the Court' is used, it does not mean merely the act of the primary Court. or of any intermediate Court of appeal, but the act of the Court as a whole from the lowest Court which entertains jurisdiction over the matter up to the highest Court which finally disposes of the case."</u>

<u>11. It will be plainly an act of injustice if for errors of the Court the entire work of the Pleader Commissioner is nullified, more so when in allocating Sahams he has not gone beyond the order portion of the Judgment. It was held in the case of Keshorao v. Yeshwantrao AIR 1957 M B. 17:</u>

<u>"It is settled that no litigant should be allowed to suffer through the mistake of any official of the Court who is connected with the administration of justice. Such mistakes can be corrected under sections 151 to 153, C.P.C. The Court has inherent power to rectify its own errors inadvertently committed and the language of s. 153 is wide enough to cover the correction of mistakes and errors in any proceeding in a suit."</u>

<u>In the case of Ahidhar Ghosh V. Secretary of State for India in Council, 36 CWN 665, a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court with Rankin, C.J. presiding held that where after the judgment of the High Court had been affirmed by the Privy Council the appellant discovered for the first time that in the High Court decree against him, the item of Court-fees paid by the other side on the memorandum of appeal to the High Court had been included twice in the costs, the High Court, on the application of such appellant, permitted the decree to be amended by debiting the costs overcharged.</u>

<u>12. We, therefore, hold that the Pleader Commissioner's report cannot be set aside on the ground that he lacked any jurisdictional basis for his work. His jurisdiction, under the circumstances is unaffected by the formal defects in the preliminary decree which can be corrected ex debito justiciae.</u>

<u>We shall dispose of the application for correction of the preliminary decree later.</u>

13. Mr. M. H. Khondker has submitted next that the date 10.7.75 being fixed for filing of objection against the report of the Pleader Commissioner and not for consideration of the report or for hearing or disposal of the suit, the learned Subordinate Judge acted without jurisdiction in accepting the report of the Commissioner making partition of the property in suit without considering the same, in any manner and passing the final decree for partition.

14. Mr. Ghulam Rabbani submits in reply that the Pleader Commissioner performed his work in accordance with Order 26, rules 14 (1) and 14 (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure Order 26, rule 14 (3) of the Code provides as follows:—

"(3) Where the Court confirms or varies the report or reports it shall pass a decree in accordance with the same as confirmed or varied; but where the Court sets aside the report or reports it' shall either issue a new Commission or make such other order as it shall think fit."

In view of the provisions of Order 26, rule 14 (3) of the Code, Mr. Rabbani submits, no illegality, irregularity or mistake has been committed by the learned Subordinate Judge in passing a final decree on the date fixed for filing objection to the report, when no objection was filed and when there remained nothing for the Court but to proceed with the acceptance of the report and pass a final decree in accordance with the same. Order 26, rule 14 (3) of the Code, he submits, gives the learned Subordinate Judge full authority to act the way he has done in the present case.

<u>15. Technically, Mr Rabbani's submission is unexceptionable, but from the facts and circumstances of the case it appear that there is more than mere technicality involved in it. The preliminary decree was passed on 28.2.7.3 and the Pleader Commissioner was appointed on 18.9.73. Nearly two years there after the Pleader Commissioner submitted his report. By Order No. 77 dated 10.6.75 the trial Court fixed 10.7.75 as the date for filing objection to the report of the Commissioner. The original order-sheet of the trial Court does not show that the recommencement in the Court of the proceedings of the partition suit on 10.6.75 after a lapse of more than one year, the last order of the trial Court being dated 4.6.74, was communicated to the plaintiff or the defendants or their respective lawyers. True, there is nothing in the Code of Civil Procedure or in Civil Rules & Order requiring the trial Court to intimate the parties of the recommencement of the proceedings, as a partition suit continues till the final decree is passed. It is the uniform practice of the Court; however, to inform the lawyers of parties when the Pleader Commissioner submits his report and when a date is fixed for filing objection to the same unless the parties or their respective lawyers are already informed about it. No intimation has been given to the lawyers of any side. Plaintiffs were aware of the recommencement of the proceedings in the trial Court, but the defendant No. 1 appellant says that he was not aware of it. Plaintiffs allege that the appellant watched the Courts cause list and the allegation of lack of knowledge is a deliberate attempt to delay the partition. It appears, however, that, since the Court's proceedings were not continuous and since the Court proceeded to pass the Order No. 77 dated 10.9.75 after an interval of one year without prior or subsequent notice to the lawyers of the, parties, there remains a reasonable possibility of missing the list. Under such circumstances we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that passing of the final decree on 10.7.75 has really been made without the appellant being given an opportunity to present his case against the report of the Pleader Commissioner.</u>

<u>16. As we said before, no Rules and Orders have been violated, but what has been violated her is the principle of natural justice. The appellant ought to have been given an opportunity to file an objection against the report of the Pleader Commissioner. The Order dated 10.6.75 has been passed without his knowledge and although the legislation is silent as to whether the parties are entitled to a notice on the recommencement of the proceedings of a suit in the Court after an interval of some time, yet a practice has developed to intimate the lawyers of both sides, so that no party is prejudicially affected. There was no provision in the Code of Civil Procedure, for example, to serve notice upon the parties under former section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but it has been observed in the case of Fazlur Rahman Vs. Rajah, Ali, 30 DLR (SC) 30. :</u>

<u>"Although section 115 of the Code does not in terms prescribe specifically the service of any notice upon the parties concerned, the practice of issuing a rule upon such parties before the final order made is dictated by the principle of natural justice to which a Court of law is required to adhere before making any judicial order. It is now well settled that whenever a Court or any other body is authorised by law to make an order, which may operate to the prejudice of another, the Court or the said body as the case may be, is bound to observe the principle of natural justice in making the said order or taking the said action, in the absence of any positive legislation dispensing with such observance and must, therefore, give the party affected an opportunity of being beard before the order is made or the action is taken."</u>

<u>17. In this case, too, there is no specific provision of serving notice upon the parties or their respective lawyers after the Pleader Commissioner submits his report. But if considerable time has elapsed between the last occasion when the court had dealt with the proceedings and the submission of the report, it is only fit and proper and, indeed, there is a practice that the lawyers of both sides are to be informed of the recommencement of the Court's proceedings. The decree passed without such intimation will not be a nullity, but in the facts and circumstances of each case the aggrieved party can complain about lack of knowledge of the last leg of proceedings and the Court would be required to examine if the complaint is a reasonable one.</u>

18. Considering, therefore, the facts and circumstance of the case we hold that the acceptance of Commissioner's Report and passing of the final decree dated 10.7.75 cannot be maintained. The application for correction of the preliminary decree should be considered by the trial Court and the preliminary decree should be corrected.

19. Mr. M. H. Khondker has further submitted that the report of the Commissioner is bad for various reasons. We do not propose to go into the merits of those submissions in view of the Order that we promise to pass in this appeal.

20. In the result, P.A . No 15 of 1977 is allowed without any order as to costs. Order No. 78 dated 10.7.75 passed by learned subordinate Judge is set aside in its entirety. The learned subordinate Judge is directed to intimate the lawyers of the parties of the arrival of the records of the case and to fix another date for filing of objection against the report of the Pleader Commissioner and is further directed to complete the proceedings by passing a final decree within 3 (three) months from the arrival of the records of the case.

21. Both Mr. M.H. Khondker & Mr. Gholam Rabbani have advanced elaborate arguments in support of their respective cases in F.M.A. No. 318 of 1979 but Mr. M.H. Khondker has submitted that in case of the appellant's success in F A. No. 15 of 1977 he will not press the appeal in F.M.A. No. 318 of 1979. In view of this submission of Mr. M. H. Khondker F.M.A. No. 318 of 1979 is dismissed for non-prosecution without any order as to costs.

Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, J.—I agree.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 28.4.77 passed by the High Court in Civil Revision Case No. 29 of 1972)
full_judgment:
K. Hossain, C. J:- Decree-holder is the appellant and the matter arises out of an execution proceeding started by one of the judgment debtors for setting aside the auction sale. The facts in brief are that the decree-holder auction purchaser instituted Rent suit No. 496 of 1960 against the Respondent for realization of rent due to him and a decree was passed in the said rent suit in his favour. The decree was put in execution in Rent Execution Case No. 23 of 1962 and in pursuance of the sai I rent execution case land appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 65 of Monza Bara Gopinathpur, P.S. Pirganj, District Rangpur, was sold in auction on 3.1.63. Thereafter, the Respondent 1 one of the judgment-debtors filed an application for setting aside the auction sale held on 3 1.63. The application for setting aside the sale in question was resisted by the appellant decree-holder. The learned Munsif allowed the application and set aside the auction sale. Against the decisions of the Munsif, the decree-holder appellant preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.40 of 1970. The learned Additional District Judge after hearing the parties allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the Munsif and rejected the application for setting aside the auction sale. A revision was taken by the judgment-debtor and it was held by the learned Single Judge that the rent suit itself was not maintainable and all proceedings thereunder and thereafter were illegal and after setting aside the decree and sale, the Munsif was directed to dispose of the rent suit treating it as Money suit. Leave was granted to consider the validity of the decision of the learned Single Judge.

2. The principal view taken by the learned Single Judge is that after the acquisition of rent receiving interest on and from 14th April, 1956, no rent suit could be filed by the rent receiver, only money suits could be filed for realizing the money due as arrear rent and in that regard followed the decision in the case of Abdul Hamid Vs. Ali Baksha Mondal,(1968) 20 D.L.R. 699 a decision of a Single Judge of the Dacca High Court wherein similar view has been taken.

3. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, learned Counsel appearing for the appellant has submitted that another decision of a Single Judge of the Leigh Court in the case of Sultan Ahmed Vs. Hazera Khatoon (C.Rev. Case Nos. 130 and 131 of 1969) which has dissented from the view taken in the case of Abdul Hamid and has held that on and from 14th April, 1956 the relationship of landlord and tenant ceased with the acquisition of rent receiving interest under the Act. Thus with the severance of landlord and tenant relation, the decree-holder ceased to have his right to put the holding to sale under the Bengal Tenancy Act. But his right to proceed against the judgment-debtor remained unaffected and the decree-holder retained his right, title and interest of the judgment-debtor in the property to that extent. The landlord could realize the amount by a suit, which of course wills in substance he a money suit. The view expressed by Sen., J. in this decision, we find, is in accord with law.

<u>4. Details of the history as the right to the rent of the extent receiver on the acquisition of the rent receiving interest need not be set out in detail, excepting that when the rent suit was filed in 1960 the law as to right of extent receiver to recover arrear rent is to be found in section 63C of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which, inter alia, provides that all arrears of rent and cuss together with interest thereon which remained due to any rent receiver in respect of any interest on the date of acquisition, and which have not become barred by limitation shall continue to be recoverable by such rent receiver amicably or through Civil Court, from the persons liable to pay them. We have referred only to the re event part bereft of irrelevant parts. This provision of law no doubt has preserved the right of extent receiver to realize his dues as rent from his ex-tenants and this right is therefore to be construed in the light of the other provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Under section 3 of the Act, with the notification made in the Official Gazette all rent receiving interests of the rent receiver shall vest absolutely in the Government free from all encumbrances. It is not disputed that on and from 14th April, 1956 rent receiving interest of all rent receivers in Bangladesh were acquired under this section, and so the relationship of landlord and tenant so far as the previous rent receivers are concerned ceased to exist. The suit could be filed as money suit and the decree holder in any suit whether described as money suit or rent suit has ceased to have his right treat it as rent suit under the Bengal Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>5. It is now a well-settled principle laid down in the case of Arthur Henry Forbes Vs. Bahadur Singh 41 I.A. 91 and Maharajadhiraj Uday Chand Mahtah Vs. Samarendra Nath Matra 51 C W.N. (F.R.) 9 that in order to have the effect of a rest suit with the right to put the holding to sale, exists only in favors of a person who occupies the position of landlord and so long as the relationship of land-lord and tenant continues. Plainly on the date the rent suit was filed i.e. 1960 the interest of the landlord to receive arrear rent from the judgment debtor remained but the relation of landlord and tenant with the right to put the holding to sale had ceased to exist. What remained is the right as provided under section 63C of the Act to recover the arrear rent either amicably or through Civil Court. Obviously, it is a right to receive the money as arrear rent that was due to ex-landlord. Therefore, whatever be the description of the suit given by the ex-landlord to recover his dues, it cannot be a rent suit having the special right to put the holding to sale in execution of the decree. But then mere misdescription of such a suit as rent suit will not invalidate the decree. The decision in Abdul Hasid's case has missed this aspect of the law. In our opinion the view taken by Sen. J. seems to be in accord with the provision of the law as it stands. The effect of the decree in whatever form it is described, is to be seen and its effect is only one, that of a money decree. For mere misdescription of the suit, the decree passed therein cannot be held to be incompetent. The view taken by the learned Single Judge in the present case therefore cannot be upheld.</u>

6. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel appearing for the respondent finds it difficult to assail the judgment of the Court of appeal below, as there is a concurrent finding of the Courts below that the judgment-debtor himself filed an application under Order 21, rule 90 and the execution proceeding was taken under Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The finding of the learned Subordinate Judge resign that of the trial Court is that the process were deemed to have been served on the judgment-debtor is not in possession of the disputed land. In the face of this finding which is a finding of fact the contention that the unction sale took place in rent execution case, cannot be accepted. Moreover, there is a clear finding by the Court of appeal below that the proceeding was not taken under the Bengal Tenancy Act, but under the Civil Procedure Code and it is to be held that it was disposed of as a money decree and as such there was no scope for interferon with the order of the Court of appeal below by the High Court Division.

In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The judgment of the High Court is set aside and that of the Court of appeal below restored.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3 March, 1987 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 470 of 1984).
full_judgment:
A.T.M. Afzal, J.: In this appeal by leave, at the instance of the defendant, the short point for consideration is whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division was justified in setting aside in revision the order of the Assistant Judge allowing a Miscellaneous Case under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Facts of the case, briefly, are that the respondent-plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 34 of 1982 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Narsingdi for specific performance of contract against his father, Danis Ali Molla. The suit was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 20 of 1984 on transfer to the Court of Assistant Judge, Monohordi. Danis Ali Molla died during pendency of the suit and his heirs including the appellant (a son) were substituted in his place. The suit was decreed ex parte on 31.1.83. The appellant filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 C. P. C. for setting aside the ex parte decree which was registered as Miscellaneous Case No. 23 of 1983. It was alleged that the summons was not served upon the appellant and that he came to know about the ex parte decree for the first time on 10.2.83.

3. Plaintiff-respondent contested the miscellaneous case asserting that the summons was duly served upon all the heirs of Danis Ali Molla including the appellant and that the appellant had full knowledge of the proceeding but even then he did not come to contest the suit. The learned Assistant Judge by order dated 29.5.84 allowed the Miscellaneous Case subject to payment of Tk. 200/- by the appellant to the plaintiff. Plaintiff then went in revision against the said order and a learned Judge of the High Court Division, Dhaka, by the impugned Judgement and order dated 3 March 1987 made the rule absolute and set aside the order of the learned Assistant Judge.

<u>4. Mr. T.H. Khan, learned advocate for the appellant, submitted that having found that the Assistant Judge had not come to any definite finding as to whether summons was served upon the defendant-appellant, the learned Judge of the High Court Division ought to have either remanded the case or examined the record himself for a decision as to alleged non-service of summons. He also submitted that interference in revision being discretionary, the order of the Assistant Judge allowing the Misc. Case upon awarding cost ought not to have been interfered with.</u>

<u>5. The learned Judge of the High Court Division observed in his judgment that the Assistant Judge was required to come to a finding with reference to the evidence on record that there was no service of summons upon the defendant or there was sufficient cause for his non-appearance at the hearing of the suit. In the absence of any such finding the Assistant Judge had erred in law in allowing the Misc. Case only for the ends of justice, he observed further. It will be seen that the learned Assistant Judge evidently did not set aside the ex parte decree on the grounds as are available under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C but he resorted to the inherent power of the Court under section 151 C.P.C. This the Assistant Judge could not lawfully do, because, if he is considering an application under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C he has authority to determine whether the ground for setting aside the ex parte decree as mentioned therein exists or does not exist. He cannot draw upon inherent power while acting under a specific provision of the Act governing the disposal of the case. Therefore, the view taken by the learned Judge of the High Court Division is correct and it could not be said that he was not justified in setting aside the order of the Assistant Judge.</u>

<u>6. Upon a reference to the order of the Assistant Judge it is found that he has considered the evidence of both sides on the question of service of summons but he was not clear about the actual receipt of summons by the defendant. He was, however, absolutely clear that the appellant had knowledge about the suit because his elder brother, another defendant in the suit, had appeared and prayed for time. The suit being among close relations of the same family there could not be any question of the appellant remaining unaware of the same, the learned Assistant Judge observed. It was noticed by the learned Assistant Judge as per record the summons were served upon the defendants. The summons for the appellant was, however, actually served on one Nurul Islam, a cousin of the appellant, living in the same house in the absence of the appellant. Nurul Islam deposed that he had handed over the summons to the appellant. In the copy of the Judgment (Page 35 of the Paper book) is written “যাহাকে উভয় পক্ষের সাক্ষীগনের সাক্ষ অনুযায়ী সুষ্ঠুভা��ে ধারণা করা যায় যে প্রার্থী সমন পৌছানো হয়েছে” Mr. T. H. Khan could not show that the finding as quoted above was wrong. But reading the High Court Division Judgement, it appears that there may be something missing in it. However, taking for argument's sake that the learned Assistant Judge has not come to any finding as to service of summons upon the appellant, we do not think, having regard to all the facts noticed and observation made by the learned Assistant Judge, that there is any necessity for further determination of the question of service of summons upon the appellant. The order of the learned Assistant Judge has been rightly set aside by the High Court Division and there is no force in the submission made by the learned Advocate for the appellant.</u>

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 8-8-79 passed by the High Court Division is S. M. A. No. 28 of 1975)
full_judgment:
K. Hossain, C.J.-The question of law involved in this appeal is whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division correctly held that the executing Court can go behind the decree to see whether the extension of time granted to deposit the balance consideration money for the passing of a decree for specific performance of contract where there was an earlier default order was without jurisdiction.

2. The matter arises out of a suit for specific performance of contract and the facts are that the trial Court passed an ex-parte decree subject to the plaintiff appellant's depositing in Court an amount of Tk. 350/- as balance consideration money by 24.3-70 failing which the suit shall stand dismissed. The plaintiff did not make the payment by the date fixed and the Munsif, by his order dated 6-6-70 dismissed the suit for default in making payment. The plaintiff filed an application on 24-6-70 under section 161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and on 10-2-72 filed another application for setting aside the order dated 6-6-70. He again filed on 17-2-72 an application for converting this application to one under rule 4 of Order 9 of the Code and it was allowed. The Munsif by his order dated 19-5-72 permitted the plaintiff by an ex-parte order to deposit the balance consideration amount by 30.6.72. This was done on 24.6.72 and the ex-parte decree was set aside on 30-6-72 and the decree was sealed and signed on 7-12-72. Thereafter the decree was put into execution and the defendant judgment-debtor took exception to it on the ground that the trial Court had no jurisdiction to pass the order on 19-5-72. The executing court allowed the objection under section 47 of the Code but the lower appellate Court on appeal rejected the objection. Thereafter in Second Miscellaneous Appeal the High Court Division allowed the appeal and dismissed the execution ease. The High Court Division held that the order of 19.5.72, permitting the plaintiff to deposit the balance consideration money was a nullity, inasmuch as the trial Court became functus officio and the suit stood automatically dismissed when the plaintiff failed to deposit the balance amount by 24-3-70.

3. The question for consideration in this appeal has been set out earlier. It is to be seen that the Executing Court which was the trial Court, and which was the successor to the Munsif of the trial Court, held that Munsif in setting aside the ex-parte decree had adopted a wrong procedure for non-compliance of the default order atilt according to the executing Court the suit stood dismissed on the date of default. So, he dismissed the execution case. On appeal the Court of appeal below held that the executing Court was wrong in going behind the decree and the Munsif as executing Court had no right to sit upon the order of the trial Court and to give his own finding on the validity or the correctness of the order. After a lengthy judgment the Additional District Judge allowed the appeal and restored the execution case. On Second Miscellaneous Appeal the learned Single Judge took the view that the order passed on 11- 3-70 by the Munsif was on absolute terms which fixed 24-3-70 as the date of deposit, failing which the suit stood dismissed, and the Court became Anew officio so that the order was without jurisdiction.

<u>4. At the outset, it is to be observed that the jurisdiction of the executing Court to go behind the decree is now well settled and the locus classicus on this point is the case of Gorachand Halder vs. Prafulla Kumar Roy, a Full Bench decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in 20 C W.N. 948, which has been uniformly followed since then. The proposition set out there is that where the decree presented for execution was made by a Court which apparently had no jurisdiction whether pecuniary or territorial or in respect of the judgment-debtor's person to make the decree, the executing Court is entitled to refuse to execute it on the ground that it was made without jurisdiction. It was further held that within these narrow limits the executing Court is authorised to question the validity of the decree.</u>

<u>5. There is no dispute that the proposition that has been laid down in the Calcutta Full Bench's case is well settled. What requires is the application of the principle of the facts of a particular case. It is now well established that the decree be without jurisdiction will be of such a nature as to make it a void decree or a nullity. The distinction between void and voidable decree is to be borne in mind. If the decree is voidable then unless it is avoided by a proper procedure, the decree stands, and is to be executed. In this regard, wrong exercise of jurisdiction and absence of jurisdiction it to be noticed. In Gorachand's case it has been held that if, apparently, the decree is found to be without jurisdiction whether pecuniary or territorial or in respect of judgment-debtor, the executing Court can go into the question of excitability of the decree. In so doing, the Court is to foil ear the principles set out above. It may further be observed that absence of jurisdiction is to be held keeping in view all the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure or other relevant laws.</u>

<u>6. Turning to the facts of the case, it is quite apparent, that the learned Single Judge has gone behind the decree and has considered not the existence or absence of jurisdiction, but the wrong or right exercise of jurisdiction by the trial Court in setting aside his order dated 6.6.70 and in extending time to deposit the money. The error, if at all, is in the exercise of jurisdiction which could have been set aside on appeal. This view is supported by the case of Lula Tripaii Prokash Nandi vs. Bireswar Lai Marwari. 55 C.L J.114. This is not a case of void decree on the ground for absence of jurisdiction of the Court with regard to either the subject matter or pecuniary or territorial, read with the provisions of the Code. On this ground the decision of the learned Single Jude cannot be sustained.</u>

<u>7. There is another substantial ground for allowing the appeal, that the learned Single Judge has misconceived the order of the Munsif setting aside the order dated 6-6-70, inasmuch as the plaintiff on 10th February, 1972 filed an application for setting aside the order dated 6th June, 1970 and prayed for extension of time to deposit the balance consideration money of Rs. 350/- made earlier on 11-3-70. The Plaintiff again made another application on 17th February, 1972 for converting the application to one under Order 9, rule 4 and this prayer was allowed, It is to be remembered that this order in substance is one of review, and that is quite apparent as this application was numbered as Miscellaneous case No. 15 of 1972, and that after hearing and taking evidence on 19th May, 1972 time was extended to 30th June, 1972, and when the deposit was made on 24th June, 1972, the order of 6th June, 1970 was set aside. It is quite apparent that what the Court was doing was reviewing its earlier order and for good reasons.</u>

<u>8. In a case when default order is made, different considerations arise according to the facts and circumstances of the case and the language used in the default order. Crucial test is whether the Court passed a self-executory order operative by its own force, so that with the default after time fixed having occurred, the order became operative of its own motion in that case to Court becomes functus officio. The language employed by the Court for such self-executory order is usually "shall stand dismissed" or "will be treated as dismissed" and so on. But, nonetheless, it will depend on the facts and circumstances of the case whether the Court by employing such language meant it to he a final self-executory order or conditional order so that a final order is called for and the Court passing the conditional default order is the best authority to judge its operation. In this context Shaikh Ayezuddin vs. Priya Sankar 6 D.L.R. 595, and Shah Wali vs. Ghulam Din 19 D.L.R. (S C.) 143 may be referred to.</u>

<u>9. When a default order is passed the party against whom the order is made is, before the default date is over, entitled to pray for extension of time and if that is allowed, it is within jurisdiction of the Court. But if the time is over, and the default has taken place, the question will be whether it was a self-executory default order or a conditional order which required a final order. We have earlier observed the Court passing the order is the best authority to judge its operative effect. If it is conditional default order and not self-executory default order then the second order is necessary for passing the final order. In that event the defaulting party gets an opportunity to pray for extension of time which the Court may grant on sufficient cause shown. Apart from this, there may be a third case which is always overlooked in that, even if the default has taken place by virtue of self-executory order, the Court can review its order on grounds of review set out in the Code of Civil Procedure. Therefore, when a default order is made it depends upon the language used and the facts and circumstances of the case as to its Operation. We have already held in the particular case that the order dated 30th June, 1972 was in substance an order on review and it set aside the earlier order of 6th June, 1970. The Munsif in so doing acted within his jurisdiction and so no question of absence of jurisdiction is invoked. The executing Court and the High Court Division were in error in going behind the decree.</u>

<u>For the reasons, we allow the appeal, set aside the order of the High Court Division and restore that of the first appellate Court but make no order as to costs.</u>

End.
