Vs.
Sree Gopal Chandra Das and others ----- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment & order dated 28/07/1977 passed by the High Court in Civil Revision Case No. 379 of 1977).
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, C. J:- In this appeal facts are not complicated nor they require to be recounted in detail, but a short but important question of law in involved, in that, whether a Court of Small Causes can exercise powers under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Facts are that the plaintiff respondents got an ex-parte decree for ejectment on 27-2-76 against the tenant defendant, and in execution of the decree got delivery of possession through Court on 17-3-76. The defendant appellant filed an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the ex-parte decree which was allowed and then he filed an application under section 144 of the Code for restoration of possession to the suit premises, but it was disallowed on the ground that the Court of Small Causes was not authorised in law to exercise jurisdiction under section 144 of the Code. On revision the learned Single Judge held that the application under section 144 was misconceived and incompetent and so dismissed the revision case.

<u>2. The principal question is whether section 144 of the Code is available to a Court of Small Causes. To appreciate some provisions of the Small Cause Courts Act and Code of Civil Procedure are to be mentioned. First, to turn to some of the provisions of the Small Cause Courts Act We find that section 33 of the Act says that Small Causes Court and Civil Court are distinct and should be always treated as different Courts; section 17 provides that the procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure, save it has been excepted by that Code and this Act, the Small Causes. Court shall follow in all suits cognizable by it, the procedure prescribed in the Code of Civil Procedure, and section 16 says that suits cognizable by a Court of Small Causes shall not be tried by any other Court. To revert back to section 17 again it appears that it contemplates that final order passed by a Small Causes Court will be a decree.</u>

3. Keeping these provisions of the Small Cause Courts Act in view, if we refer to the Code of Civil Procedure. We find, section 7 which has been impliedly referred to by Small Cause Courts Act, says that what has been provided in clauses (a) and (b) to that section shall not be available to a Court of Small Causes and it is to be remembered that section 144 of the Code is not one of the excepted provisions mentioned therein.

<u>4. A combined reading of the aforesaid provisions of the two enactments clearly indicates that the trial provisions of the Civil Procedure Code are available to a Court of Small Causes except to the extent the Small Cause Courts Act or Code of Civil Procedure excludes specifically the provisions of the Code from its application to a proceeding before a Court of Small Causes. It, therefore, follows that the trial procedure prescribed in the Code shall be followed in all suits cognizable by a Court of Small Causes except to the extent excluded. Inevitable conclusion, therefore, is that the provisions of section 144 of the Code which has not been excluded is available to the Court of Small Causes and the power is to be exercised when language of the section is attracted to the facts of the case before it.</u>

<u>5. On turning to section 144 of the Code, we find that it says that the Court of the first instance shall, on an application made to it by a party entitled to the benefit by way of restitution or otherwise consequent upon the variation or reversal of a decree, cause such restitution as to place the parties in a position which they would have occupied but for the decree that has been varied or reversed. In making restitution the Court has been conferred very wide powers including orders for refund of costs, payment of interest, damages, compensation and mesne profits consequent on such variation or reversal. It is also to be remembered that the benefit under this section cannot be had by suit since sub-section (2) clearly bars it.</u>

6. It is now to be seen, whether there is anything in section 144 of the Code which bars a Court of Small Causes from exercising the powers conferred under the section. One such view is that the variation and reversal of the decree must be by a superior Court, and so if the decree is varied or reversed by the trial Court, which is mentioned in the section as the Court of the first instance, then this power is not available. This view gets support from the case of Gopal Pario vs. Searna Bewa 34 C.W.N. 707 of the Calcutta Nigh Court. As against this view, there are decisions of other High Courts of the sub-continent which have taken a contrary view. We may mention the decisions of three High Courts namely, that of Bombay, Madras and Allahabad.

7. The Bombay High Court in Swamirao Vs. Valentine, A.I.R. 1920 Bombay 12, has held that where in execution of an ex-parte decree property is recovered from the judgment-debtor, the latter is entitled to restitution of the property on the ex-parte decree being set aside.

8. In the Madras decision, Balarama Reddi Vs. Govinda Reddi A.I.R. 1947 Mad. 54, it has been held that a judgment-debtors entitled to restitution of property sold in execution of ex-parte decree on its reversal under certain conditions laid down in the judgment.

9. The decision of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Allahabad Theatres vs. Ram Sajiwan A.l.R. 1949 All 736, is that words, varied or reversed would cover a case in which a decree  has been varied or reversed by the same Court. Where an ex-parte decree is passed and possession delivered to the plaintiff in pursuance of the decree and the decree is set aside and the defendant applies for restitution under section 144 of the Code, he can get the relief under the said section.

<u>10. It therefore, appears the preponderant view is that the variation and reversal does not convey the idea of superior Court making such order, and we think that is in accord with the language of the Code where no such qualifying word has been used. We do not find any cogent reason to restrict the language and limit of its scope and operation.</u>

<u>11. Another contention raised by Mr. Rafiqur Rahman in support of exclusion of jurisdiction under this section of a Court of Small Causes is that under section 2 of the Code, an order passed under section 144 of the Code is a decree which is appealable and whereas the decree passed by the Small Causes Court is not appealable the order passed under the section will not acquire the character of a decree. The argument can be answered, if we look at the character of the proceeding before a Court of Small Causes. Reference has already been made to the provisions of the Small Cause Courts Act to show that a proceeding before the Small Causes Court is known as a suit and it ends with a decree. Therefore, we do not find any bar in treating the order passed by the Court of Small Causes by referring to section 2 of the Code, as a decree. The question of appeal is a separate question. The right of appeal is to be specifically conferred by law. No doubt the Civil Procedure Code provides that when there is a decree, an appeal lie to the next higher Court but then the right of appeal has been expressly taken away from a decree passed by a Court of Small Causes, So, the order passed by a Court of Small Causes no doubt will be a decree but will not be appealable. Bar to appeal cannot be an Impediment of treating an order made under section 144 of the Code as a decree or its application to a Court of Small Causes. It is to be observed that no separate execution proceeding is required to enforce the order made under section 144 of the Code, On a consideration of the various provisions discussed above and the contention of the learned Counsel for the respondents, we are of the opinion that the power conferred to the Court of first instance under section 144 of the Code is available to a Court of Small Causes and in that view of the matter, we set aside the orders of the Courts below and allow the appeal without any order as to costs and remit the case to the Court of first instance to dispose of the matter in accordance with law.</u>

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 201 of 1962.
lawyer:
Moinul Huq, Miah Abdul Gafur ----- For the Appellants.
S.F. Ahsan ----- For Appellants No. 2 & 3.
B.N. Chowdhury, B.B. Roy Chowdhury ----- For the Respondents.
A.S.M. Nurul Islam ----- For D.R.
parties:
Administrator of Waqfs and another ----- Appellants.
Vs.
Musammat Sahera Begum Chowdhurani and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.-This appeal Was filed by the then Administrator of Wakfs, who was defendant No. 3 as Commissioner of Wakfs in the suit, against a decree for specific performance of a contract for sale of two residential premises in the City of Dacca, which are admittedly Wakf properties.

2. The plaintiff's case, in brief, is that the premises in suit which were originally Debtor properties were acquired by Defendants Nos. land 2 as the Mutwallis of Osman Gani Wakf by a registered deed of purchase dated 20-9-47 on a consideration of Tk. 35,000/- paid out of the fund of the said Wakf estate. There was a business belonging to Osman Gani Wakf estate at 26 Patuatully, Dacca, which required additional capital investment for its continuance and development and with the sanction of the Wakf Commissioner, defendants Nos. 1 and 2 the Mutwallis, entered into a written contract with the plaintiff for the sale of the said premises on 13-12-1959 for a consideration of Rs: 3.5, 000/- out of which Rs. 10,000/- was paid in cash as earnest money. It was agreed between the parties that defendants Nos. 1 and 2 would take Income Tax Clearance Certificate from the Department concerned and that they would Inform the plaintiff on receipt of the said certificate, whereupon the sale was to be completed within a month from that date. On 3-11-59 defendant Nos. 1 and 2 informed the plaintiff that the Income Tax Clearance Certificate had been obtained whereupon the plaintiff purchased the necessary stamps and there- after on 30-11-59 sent a notice to defendants Nos. 1 and 2, tendering the balance of the consideration money and requesting them to execute and register the necessary deed of sale. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 did not. However come forward in response to the said notice to execute the deed but, on the other hand sent a notice dated 10-3-60 intimating that the Commissioner of Wakfs had withdrawn the sanction for sale of the premises in suit on the complaint of certain beneficiaries of the said Osman Gani Wakf Estate.

3. It has been asserted in the plaint that the Wakf Commissioner was not competent to revoke the earlier order or the Wakf Commissioner granting sanction and defendants Nos. 1 and 2 are bound to execute and register the deed in terms of the agreement for sale.

4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2, the Mutwallis, filed a written statement substantially admitting the plaintiffs case but pleading that the said defendants were unable to execute the deed of transfer in view of the subsequent order of the Wakf Commissioner withdrawing the sanction which was previously given for the sale of the suit properties.

5. The main contest, however, was by defendant No. 3, the Commissioner of Wakf, who has subsequently been renamed as the Administrator of Wakf. In a written statement filed by him it has been contended that it is not correct that the Commissioner of Wakfs was incompetent to withdraw the sanction which was previously given by him, that the order of the Commissioner dated 4-1-56 according sanction for the sale was subject to certain conditions for safeguarding the interest or the beneficiaries and that the said conditions having not been complied with by the Mutwallis, defendants Nos. 1 and 2, the Commissioner of Wakfs has rescinded the former sanction, that, the purpose for which the sanction was granted has been frustrated by the efflux of time as the business, for replenishing the fund of which the sanction for sale was accorded, came to a very decadent state so much so that the capital dwindled to almost Rs. 4,000/- from Rs, 57,000/- and that in the circumstances the very purpose of the sale of the suit property viz, the improvement of the Patuatully business was no longer in existence.

6. The suit was contested also by defendants Nos. 4 to 13, who, claiming themselves to be beneficiaries of the Wakf, were added as defendants. They also filed a joint written statement contending, inter alia, that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 sold away most of the valuable properties of the Wakf in Assam and the major portion of the money have been misappropriated and some portion of the money was invested in the Patuatully business but the said business also has been lost, that the Mutwalli having colluded with the plaintiffs husband had entered into an illegal and fraudulent Contract for transfer of the suit properties, that actually the properties worth Rs. 85,000/- have been contracted for sale for an inadequate price of Rs, 35,000/- only, that the sanction of the Commissioner or Wakfs for sale of the suit properties have been withdrawn on the petition or these defendants and that the suit premises being the only source of income for fulfilling the wishes of the Wakf it was not at all proper and reasonable to transfer the same.

7. The only substantial issue which was pressed at the hearing was framed in very general terms, namely, whether there should be a decree for specific performance of the contract as alleged.

8. The learned Subordinate Judge in Course of his judgment has come to the finding that the Mutwallis, defendants Nos. 1 and 2, had entered into a valid contract for transfer of the suit properties on the basis of the sanction granted by the Wakf Commissioner dated 4-1-56 and that the specific performance of the said contract cannot be refused on the ground that it would lead to the liquidation of the Wakf. As regards the question of fulfillment of the conditions attaching to the sanction for the sale, namely, that the suit properties should be sold to the person making the highest offer and that the transaction should be made in presence of the lawyers of the par- ties, the learned Subordinate Judge has held that the said conditions were of advisory nature and that the said conditions have, as a matter of fact, been fulfilled. The learned Subordinate Judge has also come to the finding that there is no evidence of collusion or fraud, that it is in evidence that the Patuatully business required money at the time when the agreement in dispute was entered into and that the fact that the Patuatully business does not now exist should not prevent the court from giving effect to the said contract as there was a valid purpose for the agreement at the time Which it was entered into, The learned Subordinate Judge appears to have decided the case on the view that the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree for specific performance of a contract simply because his contract was duly entered into against a consideration in respect of the suit properties, that it is not necessary to go. into the question whether by the sale the plaintiff is going to acquire perfect title or not, that the plaintiff is not bound by the subsequent order of the Wakf Commissioner made in absence of the plaintiff and that the plaintiff having Stated in good faith in entering into the contract for sale and paid money for the same is entitled to get a decree for the specific performance of the contract.

The suit has been ultimately decreed on the basis of the aforesaid findings and consideration and the present appeal was preferred against the Said decree by the then Administrator of Wakfs, who was formerly the Wakf Commissioner and is now being prosecuted by the Administrator of Wakfs, Bangladesh.

9. The learned Advocate appearing in support of the appeal has contended that section 53(1) or the Bengal Wakf Act, 1934 clearly provided that there could not be any transfer by a Mutwalli of any immovable property of a Wakf without the previous sanction of the Commissioner and the Commissioner having rescinded his earlier sanction by his subsequent order dated 13-2-60, the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in decreeing the suit on the view that it was not the business of the Court to see whether the decree passed by the Court will confer any title on the holder of the decree in view of the absence of the necessary sanction required under section 53(1) of the Wakf Act at the time of the passing of the decree. The learned Advocate has submitted that there having been no sanction by the Wakf Commissioner at the time the decree for specific performance of the contract is passed, the deed of sale which would be executed by the Court in pursuance of the decree for specific performance of the contract would not confer any title upon the decree holder and as such the decree passed by the Court would be infructuous. According to the learned Advocate, it is an established principle of law that no court shall pass an infructuous decree. It has been urged on behalf of the appellant that the learned Subordinate Judge was not correct in holding that the question of title of the decree holder would be settled in a future suit. The learned Advocate for the appellant has also contended that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in failing to notice that the conditions which were attached by the Wakf Commissioner to the sanction granted on the 4th January, 1956 were not complied with and as such there was no valid sanction for the transaction. It has been urged by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the sanction which was granted by the Wakf Commissioner by his order Ext. E dated 4-1-56 was for the purpose of the protect ion and improvement of the Wakf business and that the said business having been non-existent by the time the matter came up before the court for a decision, the Court below was wrong in not exercising his discretion under section 122 of the Specific Relief Act by refusing to enforce the disputed agreement for sale.

Mr. Moinul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf or the added respondents, who are some of the beneficiaries of the Wakf has generally supported the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant.

10. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff respondent has tried to justify the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge and has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge was right in holding that in a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of a certain immovable property, the Court is merely to see whether there was a valid contract at the time it was made and not to consider the question whether any valid title will be conferred upon the holder of the decree as a result of the passing of the decree. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent has also contended that the sanction having been lawfully given under section 54 of the Bengal Wakf Act by the Wakf Commissioner by his order dated 4-1-56 and a valid agreement for sale having, been entered into on the basis of the said sanction, the Wakf Commissioner was not within his power to revoke the sanction to affect the right which has been created as a result of the agreement for sale, Ext. 1, executed in pursuance of the aforesaid sanction. On the question as to whether the Court could have exercised his discretion under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act in the instant case by refusing to enforce the agreement for sale Ext. 1 on the ground that the reason for which the sanction was granted by the Wakf Commissioner in his order dated 4-1-56 was no longer in existence, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent has submitted that the exercise of the discretion on the ground of hardship as has been mentioned in clause 11 of section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, has reference to the state of, things as were in existence at the date of the contract and this question of hardship cannot, be judged with reference to the change of circumstances which might have taken place as a result of lapse of time.

<u>11. Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, on which reliance has been placed on behalf of the appellant in support of his contention that the discretion of the Court, which the Court Undoubtedly has in regard to a suit for specific performance of a contract, should not be exercised in passing a decree for specific performance of contract in the present case, does no doubt, provide that the jurisdiction of the Court to pass a decree for specific performance of a contract is discretionary but this discretionary power is not arbitrary. In order to appreciate the contentions of the parties the provision of the said section may be usefully quoted:</u>

<u>"22. The jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, and the Court is not bound to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so but the discretion of the Court is not arbitrary but sound and reasonable, guided by judicial principles and capable of correction by a Court of appeal.</u>

<u>The following are cases in which the Court may properly exercise discretion not to decree specific performance:</u>

<u>I. Where the circumstances under which the contract is made are such as to give the plaintiff an unfair advantage over the defendant, though there may be no fraud of misrepresentation on the plaintiff's part.</u>

<u>II. Where the performance of the contract would involve, some hardship on the defendant which he did not foresee, whereas its non-performance would involve no such hardship on the plaintiff.</u>

<u>The following is a case in which the Court may properly exercise a discretion to decree specific performance:</u>

<u>III. Where the plaintiff has done substantial acts or suffered losses in consequence of a contract capable of specific performance.</u>

<u>It has been urged that the purpose for which sale of the disputed properties was sanctioned having failed in view of complete closure of the Wakf business, and the disputed premises being the only tangible properness left for carrying out the desire of the Wakf, it would involve a great hardship to the beneficiaries of the Wakf.</u>

12. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff respondent has cited before us a number of decisions in which it has been laid down that the question hardship or oppressiveness of a contract should be judged with reference to the conditions as were in existence at the date of the contract and not with reference to the change of circumstances which has occurred as a result of passage of time. Mr. Chowdhury has placed his reliance on the Privy Council decision in the case of Davis Vs. Maung Shwe Gon, reported in 38 Calcutta 805 same case 15 C.W.N. 935 same case 14 C.L.J. 250. The following observation of Mr. Ameer Ali who delivered the judgment of the Judicial Committee may be quoted.

......it has been strongly urged by Counsel on behalf of the defendant that as a decree for specific performance is discretionary their Lordships, having regard to the onerous character of the bargain, should not affirm the decision of the Chief Court. In the absence of any evidence of fraud or misrepresentation on the part of the plaintiff which induced the defendant to enter into the contract, their Lordships see no reason to accede to the argument. The bargain is onerous, but there is nothing to show that it is unconscionable".

This Privy Council decision did not apparently deal with the case of hardship which a contracting party did not foresee at the time of the contract, as is contemplated in clause II of section 22 of the Act.

13. Out of the other decisions cited by the learned Advocate mention may be made of the following: Immadi Mahalakshmamma Vs. Immadi Venkatachalamaya and another, reported in A.I.R. 1954 Madras 870, A.C. Kunju Mohammad Vs. Goverdhan Hathlbai Co. and others, reported in A.I.R. 1956 T.C. 93, Mt. Bibi Moliman Nissa and another Vs. Tafazul Kari, reported in A.I.R.1959 Patna 132, Ram Suudar Saha and others Vs. Kali Narain Sen Choudhury and others reported in A.I.R. 1927 Cal. 889 and Baijnath Vs. Kshetrahari Sarkar and others, reported in A.I.R. 1955 Cal. 210. It has been laid down in these cases that hardship should be co-lateral to the contract and be arising out of the terms of the contract should not be judged in the light of the Subsequent event.

14. The law of specific performance of contract as embodied in the Specific Relief Act has been enacted in the light of the well established principles of English law. Reference may be made to paragraphs 419 and 430 at pages 301 and 302 of Vol. 36 of Halsbury's Laws of England (3rd Ed.) where the rule as to hardship being a ground for refusing specific performance of a contract as has been deduced from the various case laws of English courts has been stated in the following words:

"TIME AT WHICH HARDSHIP MUST ARISE: As a general rule hardship, to operate as a ground of defence, must be such as existed at the time of the contract, and not such as has arisen subsequently from a change of circumstances; thus the court may refuse to enforce an award on a submission to arbitration if the submission involves hardship but not on the ground of mere hardship and unreasonableness In the award itself, so a covenant to renew a sub-lease without fine may be enforced though the terms of the renewal of the sub lease are changed and made more onerous. In some cases, however, hardship subsequently arising may be treated as a ground for refusing specific performance. The result generally follows if the change of condition involving hardship to the defendant, has resulted from the act of the plaintiff especially if the plaintiff's conduct operated as something in the nature of a trap.

430. HARDSHIP FLOWING FROM CONDUCT OF DEFENDANT; Hardship which flows from the conduct of the defendants, or a hardship which simply results to the defendant because the purpose he had in view has failed or be cause his speculation has proved unfortunate to him cannot be set up by way of defence. Where the defendant is a company the court cannot consider that performance may involve hardship to individual members as distinguished from the company."

15. The English law on this question has also been stated very succinctly by Edward Fry in Chapter VI of his Treatise on the Specific Performance of contracts (1861) at pages 181-191. The relevant passages from this chapter may be usefully quoted as follows:

"250. It is a well established doctrine, that the Court will not enforce the specific performance of a contract, the result of which would be to impose great hardship on either of the parties to it. 251. The question of hardship of a contract is generally to be judged of at the time at which it is entered into: if it be then fair and just, it will be immaterial that it may, by the force of subsequent circumstances of change of events, have become less beneficial to one party except where subsequent events have been in some way due to the party who seeks the performance of the contract. For whatever contingencies may attach to a contract or be involved in the performance of the either part, have been taken upon themselves by the parties to it. And so at law, the reasonableness of a. contract is to be judged of at the time, it is entered into, and not by the light of the subsequent events; and we have already seen that the same principle applies in considering the fairness of a contract."

The learned author however states in paragraph 255 at page 184:

"It cannot however be denied that there are cases in which the court has refused its interference, by reason of events subsequent to the contract."

and recites two instances in which the Court refused specific performance of contract because of hardship arising out of events which happened subsequently, although in paragraph 256 at the same page he proceeds to add:

"Notwithstanding these cases, the general rule seems to be that events subsequent to the contract and not so involved in it as to render it unequal at the time it is entered into, cannot be brought forward to show the hardship of enforcing it."

16. On an examination of these statements of English law which seem to be the basis of the interpretation given by various courts in the Indian sub-continent to the relevant provision of the Specific Relief Act, it appears that according to the said statements, the court is to generally confine itself, for the purpose of determining hardship as a ground for relieving a contracting party of his liability to per form the contract, to the consideration of the kind of hardship which might arise from the facts and circumstances existing at the time of the contract but through mistake or inadvertence was not taken notice of and not of that kind of hardship caused by the development of future events, because a contracting party, as a man of ordinary prudence, while entering into a solemn agreement, is expected to take into consideration the lapse of time which may intervene the date of the contract and its performance and any possible change of circumstances which may arise during this interval and he should not be allowed to deviate from his assurance to the detriment of the other party on the ground that the contract has become less beneficial to him due to the lapse of time, for which the other party is in no way responsible. There is no doubt that this rule, should generally be regarded to be based on sound and reasonable judicial principle, but it is not, as will appear from the above quoted statements, a rigid and inflexible rule and there had been occasions where even the English Courts exercised their discretion to refuse specific performance on the ground of hardship which arose out of future events. Every case is to be judged by the light of its own facts, and a court of law is not to be hamstrung by some rigid formulation in the exercise of its discretion granted under a positive provision of the law which does not prescribe any such restrictive condition.

17. The substantive provision of section 22 of the Act is very general and wide and there is no restrictive condition excepting that it should not be arbitrary but should be sound and reasonable, guided by judicial principles and capable of correction by a superior Court. The cases, as stated in clauses 1 and II of the section, where the court may properly exercise its discretion to refuse specific performance of the contract are obviously illustrative.

18. Pollock and Mulla, in their commentary on the Contract and specific Relief Acts (Eighth Edition, 1957) have made the following interesting comment at page 798 of their book:

"Our section 22 with its subdivisions and illustrations is really more like an elementary lecture than legislation. We are far from saying that an exposition of this kind was not required or at least useful in 1877. It must not be supposed to be exhaustive.

19. It should be noticed that the manner in which Clause 11 has been worded does not in any way indicate that the exercise of its discretion under this clause should be confined to the consideration of the hardship arising out of the state of events existing at the date of the contract. The hardship contemplated in this clause is the one which would arise out of the performance of the contract—a future event, and which was not foreseen by the defendant—also indicative of a future eventuality and in describing the nature of hardship in this clause, no limiting words of the kind, "not arising out of the events subsequent to the contract" or "arising out of the events existing at the date of the contract" have been used. If we compare the language used in this clause with that in clause 1 the difference will be obvious. The unfair advantage contemplated in clause 1 is such as given rise to by "the circumstances under which the contract is made". According to this clause the fairness of a contract is to be judged of at the time when the contract is entered into and not by subsequent events, but the frame of clause II does not lead to such a conclusion as to the hardship dealt in the said clause.

20. The Judicial authorities in the Indian sub-continent appear to have tried to confine the application of this clause to the case of hardship arising out of the circumstances existing at the date of the contract more or less on the authority of the decisions of t he English courts of equity which were undoubtedly regarded as laying down sound and reasonable judicial principle But we have seen that this was considered to be a general rule, but there were exceptions to it depending upon the peculiar facts or special features of a case.

21. This question as to whether the cases mentioned in section 22 of the Act are exhaustive was considered by a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court in Nowab Meah Chowdhury Vs. Syed Ezazuddin Ahmed and others, reported in 13 D.L.R. 554 same case D.L.R. 1962 Dacca 655 in which specific performance of contract was refused on the ground that the decree if passed, would lead to multiplicity of litigation. In delivering the judgment of the Bench Hasan, J (with whom M.R. Khan, J concurred) made the following observations:

"As to the true import of section 22 of the Act the facts, in our opinion does not show that it is exhaustive but the instances that have been given in sub-section (1)(2) of section 22 of the Act are nothing but illustrative. To grant specific performance of contract is absolutely within the discretion of the Court and no rigid rule can be laid down when and where and this discretion can be exercised by the Court. The discretion that shall have to be exercised by the Court will depend on the circumstances of each case but that discretion must be a judicial one."

22. In another case, namely, Mir Hasmat Ali Vs. Dhirendra Kumar Ghose and others, reported in 16 D.L.R. Dacca 239 same case P.L.D. 1965 Dacca 56, Murshed J (as he then was) in delivering the judgment of the Bench (A. Subhan Chowdhury, J concurring) quoted with approval the following observation of Night Bruce, L.J. In die case of Rede Vs. Caxes 34 L.J CH. 145: 42 Digest 465, para 326:

"The doctrines and principles applicable to this case are opposed to granting specific performance in the present instance; and if it is not clear that the breach of contract was a breach of trust, it must be held at least to be extremely doubtful whether it is not so."

The learned Judge proceeded to make the following observation thereafter:

"Specific performance was refused in the case on the ground that it was not unlikely that the enforcement of the contract might lead to a breach of trust even when such breach of trust was not proved. We have cited the above case in order to illustrate the point that Courts have exercised a very wide discretion to refuse specific performance and to emphasize a well established principle that a Court of Equity is a forum or conscience and that it would refuse to lend Its helping hand in regard to matters where the Court will feel that it will be unconscionable to do so having regard to the interest of the public. As to what would constitute unconscionable transaction will of necessity depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case and no specific from can be enunciated which will be of universal application."

23. The instant case has, in our opinion, certain special features of its own which cannot be overlooked. The promissors whose agreement for sale is the basis of the present suit were not the owners of the property in their personal capacity. They were mere Mutawalli of a wakf-al-awlad whose primary duty was to preserve the wakf and to effect its improvement. Their position was analogous to that of trustees although they might not be trustees in the strict sense of law.

<u>24. The properties in dispute are two residential houses in the city of Dacca, constituting the only tangible assets of the wakf. The only other property was a cloth shop at Patuatully. The sanction required under the Wakf Act was sought on the basis that the cloth business. the income of which would be sufficient to carry out the objectives of the wakf, was to be preserved and improved and for the said purpose, some capital investment was necessary. In spite of opposition on behalf of the female beneficiaries of the wakf sanction was granted by the then Wakf Commissioner, subject to certain conditions. The object of the proposed transfer was such as required immediate account on the part of the Mutwallis for infusion of additional capital in the decaying business so that the business could be set on its feet and be operated as the source of necessary fund for the implementation of the will of the Wakf. Unfortunately, no immediate step appears to have been taken by the Mutwallis for the collection of the necessary fund for providing support to the sagging business. A period of 3 years 9 months 9 days had elapsed before the disputed agreement for sale of the properties could be executed. In the meantime, the cloth business being on the wane, the wakf commissioner with drew the sanction and revoked his earlier order, before the agreement for sale could be implemented. By the time the suit which was instituted to enforce the agreement was heard, the cloth business has come to a complete step with the result that the money which could be collected by the sale of the properties could not be invested in a running business nor could be utilised by purchasing any new property of comparable worth, the price of which had soared up in the meantime to a great extent. The possibility which stared the beneficiaries of the Wakf including the Mutwallis in their face was the complete extinction of the Wakf and the office of Mutwalli.</u>

<u>25. It can hardly be disputed that it is a case of extreme hardship which is likely to result from the performance of the contract and, as the preamble of the Agreement, Ext. 1 will show, the Mutwalli defendants did not foresee it. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, we have no manner of doubt that this is a fit case in which the discretionary power of the court to refuse specific performance of contract should be exercised, even though it may be argued that this hardship arises out of events subsequent to the date of contract.</u>

26. The exercise of the discretionary power of the Court may be tested from another stand point. It has been regarded. as a sound and reasonable judicial principle by the Courts of Equity in England that the Court should exercise its discretion to refuse specific performance in a case where the performance of the Contract, will, in the opinion of the Court, lead to unfairness to third parties or involves a breach of trust or compel the defendant to do an act which he is not lawfully competent to do.

27. We may refer, in this connection, to paragraph 426 at pages 300-301 of Vol. 36 of Halsbury's laws of England (3rd Edition), which is as follows:

"Another species of unfairness which may stay the hand of court is that the contract; if enforced, would be injurious

to third parties, or would involve a breach of trust, or a breach of a prior contact with a third party, or would compel the defendant to do an act which he is not lawful competent to do or would involve a breach gross of duty as between principal and agent."

28. Edward Fry in his Treatise on the Specific Performance of Contracts already referred to has made the following statement on this point in paragraph 245 of his book at page 179.

"One kind of that unfairness which stays the interference of the Court arises where the enforcement of the contract would be injurious to third parties. Therefore, where an estate was settled in strict settlement, giving to the settlor a life estate and an ultimate remainder, and the tenant for life entered into a contract for the sale of the fee, the Court refused to allow the purchaser to take the interest of the tenant for life with compensation, on the ground that a father and a stranger would be likely to use an estate without impeachment of waste in a different way, and that therefore the sale might prejudice the interest, of the persons in the remainder.

The Court will never exercise its extraordinary power in compelling a specific performance, where to do so would necessitate a breach of trust, or compel a person to do what he was not lawfully competent to do, partly, as it seems, on the ground of the unfairness and illegal taint of such a contract in itself, and partly of the hardship to which it would expose the person forced to execute it."

We shall have to examine the facts of this case in order to see if the discretionary power of the Court can be invoked in this suit on any of the grounds referred to above.

29. The evidence on record does not give a good account of the conduct of defendant’s No. 1 and 2 as the Mutwallis of the Wakf in question. The evidence which was adduced to show that efforts were made by the Mutwallis to find out acceptable purchases was by defendant No. 1, one of the Mutwallis examined as D.W. 1, the plaintiff's husband, P.W. 1 and a broker, P.W. 2, D.W. 1 has stated that he contacted brokers but did not advertise the sale.P.W. 1 has merely stated that the talk of purchase took place two months before the Bainapatra and P.W. 1 a broker who was examined to prove that the Mutwalli defendants made efforts to obtain high price for the suit premises has stated that he worked for a year to get purchasers for the disputed premises. The evidence on record does not show that the defendant Mutwallis took any prompt action for collection of the necessary fund for the purpose of the Wakf business in pursuance of the sanction given by the Wakf Commissioner.

30. It appears from the order of the Wakf Commissioner dated 13-2-60 Ext. E (1), that immediately after the partition of the country the business had a capital stock of Rs. 57,000/- which dwindled to only Rs. 4,000/- at the time when the said order was made. It is the evidence of D.W. 1, one of the Mutwallis, that the capital of Patuatully business which was a cloth business was Rs. 40,000/- and that has ceased to exist. The said witness has also stated that the building in which the business was carried on has also passed away from their hands. It seems to be the admitted position that the disputed premises is the only Wakf property left.

31. The claim of the plaintiff is being seriously contested by the beneficiaries who have been added as defendants. Defendant No. 12 on being examined as D.W. 3 on behalf of the beneficiaries has stated that the rental income of the properties is Rs. 5401/- and the Wakf Estate has no property other than the disputed premises and that the beneficiaries are objecting to the sale as the said premises were the only properties.

32. The contract which is being sought to be enforced was by the persons in exercise of their powers, more or less, as trustees of the Wakf Estate. It has been contended that the Wakf business having ceased to exist the consideration money which would be available as a result of a decree for specific performance of contract cannot now be invested in the said business and that the said money may now be kept in the Bank, the future of a new business being very uncertain. It has therefore been submitted that the effect of the enforcement of the contract will be the extinction of the only tangible properties of the Wakf resulting, in all probability, hardship to a number of the beneficiaries in the facts and circumstances of the case there is no doubt in our opinion, that this contract if enforced would be injurious to a number of third parties viz. the beneficiaries.It scams to us also that the performance of this contract is likely to involve a breach of trust and would compel the defendants to do an act which they are not lawfully competent to do.

<u>33. Due to the dilatoriness the Mutwallis, no immediate action was taken by them to find out a suitable buyer, pursuant to the order of the Wakf Commissioner, so that sufficient money could be put into the decaying business without any delay so as to restore it to its old vigor. Because of this unwarranted delay, the object for which the proposed transfer was sanctioned by the appropriate authority has become illusory.</u>

34. The alienation of the only house properties of the Wakf estate in the city of Dacca at this stage by the Mutwallis would be without any comparable benefit in return and would amount to virtual destruction of the Wakf, The withdrawal of the sanction by the Wakf Commissioner has removed the protective cover from the Mutwallis act of transfer of the disputed properties and by the execution of the impugned kabala the defendants would be doing an act which is not lawful for them to do.

Section 21(e) of the Specific Relief Act may also be pertinently referred to in this connection, which provides that a contract made by trustees either in excess of their powers or in breach of their trust cannot be specifically enforced.

35. The Wakf Commissioner by his order dated 4-1-56 Ext. E accorded sanction for sale of the Wakf premises and added the following conditions:

"The joint Mutwallis are to see that the house is sold to the person making the highest offer and transaction is made in the presence of the two pleaders viz. Mvi. A. Mannan Faquir and Mvi. Shah Azizur Rahman who represent the two contending parties the proportionate share money of the daughters of the Wakf in sale proceeds shall be paid to the daughters immediately after the transaction. The daughters of the Wakf shall be paid their allowance of Rs.16/- per month from the profit of the business as usual."

36. The deed of agreement which has been executed by defendant’s No. 1 and 2 for selves and as Mutwallis on the one hand and the plaintiff on the other contains tile following passages as a preamble to the deed which are relevant for our present purpose:

"Whereas the properties referred to ill the schedule hereunder written were purchased by the Vendors in their personal name but with the money out of fund of the Osman Gani Wakf Estate of which they are the Mutwallis and the same has been included in the statement filed for enrollment of said wakf and the said property has been so treated so long.

And whereas the business of the aforesaid Wakf Estate is short of fund to replenish which the Commissioner of Wakf has granted permission to sell the under motioned property on the application of the Vendors Mutwallis."

And the last paragraph of the deed, which is one of the terms of the transaction is to the following effect:

"Defect in title, that is failure of warrantly of title or any bar that may be imposed by the authorities against completion of such transaction shall be a legitimate ground for repudiation of the contract.

It has been contended on behalf of the appellant and the beneficiary respondents that the aforesaid condition having not been fulfilled the sanction of the Wakf Commissioner ceased to be operative and the agreement, Ext.1 is not liable to be enforced.

37. In regard to the question of fulfillment of the two conditions embodied in the order granting sanction, the learned Subordinate Judge has firstly held that the highest bid was of the plaintiff and that the requirement of the presence of the two lawyers of the contending parties at the time of the transaction has reference the payment of the consideration and that as such there was no breach of any of those conditions. It has been further held by the learned Subordinate Judge that, in any view of the matter, those conditions were of merely advisory nature and are not conditions precedent to the validity the sale.

38. In order to determine the real import of the conditions imposed by the Wakf Commissioner, at the time of granting the sanction, we shall have to judge the said conditions in the perspective of the wakf character of the disputed properties. Section 53 (1) of the Wakf Act declared the incompetence of a Mutwalli to make an absolute transfer except with the previous sanction of the Wake Commissioner and section 54 of the Act provides for grant of sanction by the Wakf Commissioner "on such terms and conditions as he may in his discretion impose". Properties being in the nature of trust properties, the Legislature imposed restrictions on the transferring power of a Mutwalli for the good of the object of such a wakf estate. The Statutory provision makes it abundantly clear that the terms and conditions as may be imposed by the Wakf Commissioner are part of the order granting sanction and the sanction can be operative subject to the said terms and conditions. Non-compliance with the said terms and conditions will naturally make the order of sanction inoperative and ineffective. We do not agree with the learned Subordinate Judge that such conditions were merely of advisory nature.

39. On the question of fulfillment of the said conditions it may be pointed out that the learned Subordinate Judge was not correct .n interpreting the word "transaction" as mentioned in the last paragraph of the order of the Wakf Commissioner dated 4-1-56, Ext. E, as an act of payment of the consideration. To ensure settlement of the highest price and the payment thereof the Wakf Commissioner imposed those conditions. Let us examine this question in further details.

40. It appears from the order of the Wakf Commissioner dated 8-12-53, as contained in Ext. E that the Mutwallis applied for permission to sell certain wake property on 16-5-55, that it was opposed by some of the female beneficiaries and that the permission was refused as the application of the Mutwallis did not disclose any particulars of the property to be sold, the amount of money required for running their business or the highest offer, if any, received for such a sale. On the subsequent date i.e. 4-1-56 permission was granted in the teeth of the opposition by the female beneficiaries, who seriously disputed the bona fides of the Mutwallis, who are their brothers, in regard to the proposed transaction. Form a perusal of the order, it appears to be clear to us that in order to safeguard the interest of the beneficiaries and put a check against any possible malafide action on the part of the Mutwallis, the condition was attached that it must be to the highest bidder and that the transaction, meaning thereby the transaction of sale including settlement of the terms and conditions of the sale, was to be made in presence of the lawyers of the two contending parties, namely, the Mutwallis and the female beneficiaries. In this premises, we have no hesitation t6 hold that those conditions were an essential part of the order granting sanction and were not of merely advisory nature.

<u>41. Another important fact may be mentioned here. Both the parties clearly visualised that there might be a bar imposed by the appropriate authority in future against the transaction and it was therefore specifically provided in the agreement itself that such a bar would be a valid ground for repudiation of the contract.</u>

<u>42. The subsequent order of the Wakf Commissioner by which the sanction granted previously was revoked can be well construed as a bar imposed by the authorities as Contemplated in that term of the agreement. The sanction having been withdrawn the general prohibition as provided in section 53(1) of the Wakf Act was brought back in operation. Having regard to the facts of the case, the defendants may very well plead such withdrawal of the sanction as legitimate ground for repudiation of the contract as incorporated in term No. 9 of the agreement. Ext. 1.</u>

<u>43. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, it appears to us that the execution of a deed of sale of the disputed premises by the defendant Mutwallis in pursuance of the deed of agreement Ext. 1 in this case would involve a breach of duty on their part and that to pass a decree for specific performance of contract in this case would compel the Mutwallis to do a thing which they are not lawfully competent to do. It is doubtful if the deed of sale which may be executed in pursuance of the decree made in this suit will confer any clear title upon the plaintiff. It is no doubt true that ordinarily the objection to enforcement of an agreement for sale is the concern of the purchaser, but we cannot shut our eyes to the distinct possibility that, in consequence of a decree passed in this suit, the parties may be involved in further litigation on the question as to whether the Mutwallis did lawfully transfer the properties. The discretionary power of the court to refuse specific performance of a contract should be exercised in our opinion, in this case on these grounds also.</u>

<u>In that view of the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the opinion this is a fit case where specific performance of the contract should not be granted.</u>

<u>44. The next question which requires to be considered is the refund of the earnest money to the plaintiff. The plaintiff having entered into the contract paid the earnest money to the defendants in 1959 and immediately there after called for the execution of the deed on tendering the balance of the consideration. It is no doubt true that on the objection raised by some of the beneficiaries, defendant Mutwallis in the meantime did not come forward to execute the deed and ultimately the sanction granted by the Wakf Commissioner was withdrawn. The plaintiff had parted with the sum of Tk. 10,000/- as back as 1959 and having regard to the principle of section 38 of the Specific Relief Act the plaintiff is entitled to compensation in this regard. The earnest money was lying with the defendants and evidence has been adduced to the effect that the said amount of money has not been spent by the Mutwallis but has been kept in deposit in a Bank. We think that the ends of justice will be met if he said amount of money namely, Tk. 10,000/- plus another amount of Tk. 10,000/- towards the profits or interest are paid to the plaintiff. We therefore allow this appeal, set aside the Judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismiss the suit for specific performance of contract and at the same time we direct that defendant Nos. 1 and 2 shall pay the sum of Tk. 20,000/- to the plaintiffs in course of a month from the date. In default, the said amount shall bear 9% interest until payment.</u>

<u>In the circumstances of the case we direct that the parties shall bear their respective costs throughout.</u>

A.S. Faizul Islam Chowdhury, J.-I agree.

End.

ABM Khairul Huq, Advocate, instructed by Mvi Md Wahidullah Advocate-on-Record — For the Appellant. 
Dr Rafiqur Rahman, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record — For the Respondents.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 1-4-90 passed by the High Court Division in FA No. 91 of 1987).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J: The question raised in this appeal by leave by the plaintiff-appellant Sonali Bank is, whether in the instant mortgage suit for sale the plaintiff is also entitled as of law to a decree for interest both pendente lite and till realisation of the decretal amount.

2. The Appellant-Bank instituted Title Suit No. 31 of 1983 (later re-numbered as Title Suit No. 131 of 1984) originally in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, later transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 2, Dhaka which was a suit for recovery of money by sale of mortgaged property for a preliminary decree for Taka 14,00,000.00 with interest at 20% till realisation with a direction that the Schedule property be sold on failure to pay the decretal amount and to make the preliminary decree final on failure to pay as aforesaid and also praying for a personal decree against the defendants for the said amount. The Commercial Court decreed that suit for an amount of Taka 8,85,485.39 payable in quarterly instalments of Taka 50,000.00 but allowed no interest as prayed for, by judgment and decree dated 24-12-86. The appellant-Bank took an appeal to the High Court Division, FA No. 91 of 1987, against the said decree on the ground that interest on the decretal amount pendente lite and till realisation was wrongly refused by the trial Court. By the impugned judgment dated 1-4-90 a Division Bench of the High Court Division dismissed the said appeal holding that the Commercial Court had exercised its discretion in refusing interest to the plaintiff on the decretal amount on valid ground.

3. Leave was granted to consider the submission of the appellant that award of interest on the decretal amount pendente lite is mandatorily available to the plaintiff under Order 34, rules 2, 4 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a suit for sale of mortgaged property. Interest should also have been allowed on the said sum from the date of the decree till realisation of the same. The High Court Division has failed to properly construe Order 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure and has failed to properly construe the facts of the present case as also the decisions in the case of Dawoodbhai Kassamji Matiwalla vs. Shaikhali Alibhoy, AIR 1953 (Born) 445 and Kishen Raj vs. Radhalal, AIR 1958 (Rajasthan) 145, cited at the Bar.

4. Defendant No.1 (respondent No. 1 herein) is a company carrying on the business of export and buying and selling of jute. Defendant Nos. 2-9 are its Managing Director and Directors who guaranteed the loan sanctioned by the appellant-Bank. Defendant No. 1 was given accommodation by the plaintiff-Bank to the extent of Taka 5 lakh repayable with interest at 2¼% above Bank rate minimum 10½% on 7-4-76 and against pledge of jute goods. The limit was enhanced to Taka 40 lakh in 1976-77 against the pledge of jute goods and equitable mortgage of property at Gulshan. The limit was renewed for 1977-78 and 1978-79. In 1979-80 the cash credit limit was reduced to Taka 20 lakh with a blocked loan amounting to Taka 7,36,000.00. As securities of the loan the defendants furnished various DP notes, letters of undertaking, guarantees, etc. Upto 20-1-83 there was an outstanding of Taka 3,69,485.39 in the pledge account and an outstanding sum of Taka 7,36,000.00 in the blocked loan account, in total an outstanding sum of Taka 11,05.485.39. The plaintiff claimed interest pendente lite, tentatively calculated at Taka 2,94,514.61 and filed the suit on 24-1-83 for a preliminary decree for Taka 14 lakh along with other prayers as already noticed.

5. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3-8 merely stated in their joint written statement that they are willing to negotiate a settlement and after mutual accounting repay the plaintiff's just and actual dues.

6. During the pendency of the suit the defendants paid a sum of Taka 2,20,000.00 and deducting this amount from the outstanding due of Taka 11,05,485.39 the trial Court passed a preliminary decree under Order 34 rule 4(1) CPC for a sum of Taka 8,85,485.39. Interest was refused on the ground that the block loan will not bear any interest as per terms and conditions and the plaintiff-Bank did not file any proper account of sale of the pledged goods. Besides, the Bangladesh Bank by a Circular dated 19-3-84 waived penal interest charged against the borrower and also it is well-settled that the Court is not bound by the interest awarded in the contract itself.

7. The High Court Division on appeal held that the instant suit was not a suit for foreclosure or redemption of mortgage. It was not a case of award of interest on mortgage money. Hence it was not compulsory to award payment of interest on the decretal amount. The award of interest on the decretal amount pendente lite and from the date of decree till realisation is purely a matter of discretion of the Court and the Commercial Court has exercised its discretion on valid ground in refusing interest to the plaintiff.

8. Mr ABM Khairul Huq, learned Counsel for the appellant-Bank has submitted, first, that section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure gives the Court a discretion to award interest pendente life and from the date of the decree till realisation, but section 34 CPC is a general provision which governs only money decrees. Order 34 is a specific provision of the Code of Civil Procedure governing suits relating to mortgages of immovable property. The High Court Division failed to notice rule 4(1) of Order 34 which provides as follows:

“In a suit for sale, if the plaintiff succeeds, the Court shall pass a preliminary decree to the effect mentioned in clauses (a), (b) and (c) (i) of sub-rule (1) of rule 2 together with such amount as may have been adjudged due in respect of subsequent costs, charges, expenses and interest, "

9. Mr Khairul Huq then refers to rule 2 (1) of Order 34 which is as follows:

"2.-(1) In a suit for foreclosure, if the plaintiff succeeds, the Court shall pass a preliminary decree—

(a) ordering that an account be taken of what was due to the plaintiff at the date of such decree for—

(i) principal and interest on the mortgage,

(ii) the costs of suit, if any, awarded to him, and

(iii) other costs, charges and expenses properly incurred by him up to that date in respect of his mortgage-security, together with interest thereon; or

(b) declaring the amount so due at that date; and ……………….”

10. Mr. Khairul Huq then submits that whether the suit for sale is passed in terms of rule 2(1)(a) or (b) the amount due to the plaintiff will consist of the principal and interest on the mortgage "at the date of such decree", in other words, from the date of the institution of the suit till the passing of the decree and the trial Court has no option but to award interest pendente lite in a suit for sale.

11. Dr Rafiqur Rahman, learned Counsel for the respondents, has made a feeble attempt to show that the suit was in fact for a personal decree against the Managing Director and other Directors and that it does not fulfill the characteristics of a mortgage suit. Having gone through the plaint and decree passed in the suit under Order 34 rule 4(1) CPC we have no manner of doubt whatsoever that this is a mortgage suit for sale and a preliminary decree has to be drawn up in terms of rule 4(1), read with rule 2(1) in the manner mentioned in clauses (a), (b) and (c)(i) thereof. The plaintiff-Bank obtained a mortgage by deposit of title deeds. A mortgage by deposit of title deeds being placed on the same footing as a simple mortgage (section 96 of the Transfer of Property Act) the only remedy is a suit for sale which the plaintiff-bank availed of in the instant case.

12. By Act 21 of 1929 Order 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure was amended and a new rule 11 was inserted which deals specially with interest. When rule 11 remained unamended, the Privy Council held in the case of Jagannath Prosad Singh Chowdhury vs. Surajmul Jalal, AIR 1927 (PC) 1:

"Really this matter is determined beyond question by Order 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This may, for this particular case of mortgages, differ from the general provision of section 34 of the Code; but if so, the particular avoids the general."

13. In other words, what the Privy Council held is that section 34 CPC is a general provision with regard to award of interest but Order 34 is a specific provision in respect of suits relating to mortgages of immovable property and therefore the particular will exclude the general. In relation to mortgages Order 34 CPC will exclude the provisions of section 34 CPC

14. After a new rule 11 was inserted by Act 21 of 1929 the Federal Court had the occasion to deal with the question of award of interest pendente lite and interest till realisation. It was held by Sulaiman, J. in the case of Jaigobind Singh vs. Lachmi Narain Ram, AIR 1940 (FC) 20 as follows:

"It follows that this special provision, which removes any conflict that there might have been between section 34 and Order. 34, Rr. 2 and 4, gives a certain amount of discretion to the Court, so far as interest pendente lite and subsequent interest are concerned. It is no longer absolutely obligatory on the Courts to decree interest at the contractual rate up to the date of redemption in all circumstances, if there be no question of the rate being penal, excessive or substantially unfair within the meaning of the Usurious Loans Act, 1918."

15. Before the aforesaid observation of the Federal Court is appreciated it will be useful to quote rule 11 of Order 34 CPC in full, as inserted by Act 21 of 1929.

"11. In any decree passed in a suit for foreclosure, sale or redemption, where interest is legally recoverable, the Court may order payment of interest to the mortgagee as follows, namely:

(a) interest up to the date on or before which payment of the amount found or declared due is under the preliminary decree to be made by the mortgagor or other person redeeming the mortgage-

(i) on the principal amount found or declared due on the mortgage, at the rate payable on the principal, or, where no such rate is fixed, at such rate as the Court deems reasonable,

(ii) on the amount of the costs of the suit awarded to the mortgage, at such rate as the Court deems reasonable from the date of the preliminary decree, and

(iii) on the amount adjudged due to the mortgagee for costs, charges and expenses properly incurred by the mortgagee in respect of the mortgage- security up to the date of the preliminary decree and added to the mortgage money,- at the rate agreed between the parties, or, failing such rate, at the same rate as is payable on the principal, or failing both such rates at nine percent per annum; and

(b) subsequent interest upto the date of realisation or actual payment at such rate as the Court deems reasonable—

(i) on the aggregate of the principal sums specified in clause (a) and of the interest thereon as calculated in accordance with that clause; and

(ii) on the amount adjudged due to the mortgagee in respect of such further costs, charges and expenses as may be payable under rule 10."

16. It was argued in subsequent case that as rule 11 uses the word "the Court may order payment or interest" the award of interest was also discretionary under rule 11. Reliance was also placed on the afore quoted observation of the Federal Court. But in a series of subsequent cases cited by Mr AB Khairul Huq we find that it has been held that the real import of rule 11 is that the Court is bound to grant interest up to the decree. Thus in the case of Sukhraj Rai vs. Ratinath Panjiara, AIR 1942 (Patna) 102, it was clearly held that rule 11 does not affect the Court's power to allow pendente lite interest under Order 34 rule 2. The Federal Court did not intend to lay down in the afore-cited case that under rule 11 the Court can refuse pendente lite interest altogether. All that the Federal Court stated is that the Court has a discretion under rule 11 in the matter of awarding pendente lite interest, i.e. a discretion in the rate of interest to be given to the mortgagee.

17. Next, in the case of Dawoodbhai Kassamji Matiwalla vs. Shaikhali Alibhoy, AIR 1953 (Born) 445 it was held that the position of law prior to 1929 was that the Court could not deprive the mortgagee of the interest agreed upon till the date fixed for redemption. This decision was based on the principle propounded by the Privy Council in the case previously cited at AIR 1927 (PC)1, namely, that upto the date of the preliminary mortgage decree and also upto the further period of grace which the Court gave to the mortgagor for redeeming the mortgage, interest was in the domain of contract and not in the domain of judgment and the Court had no discretion to vary the rate of interest and award to the mortgagee interest less than what the mortgagor had agreed to pay. But after the amendment in 1929 rule 11 did not make it obligatory upon the Court to order payment of interest at the rate agreed upon up to the date fixed for redemption. It gave discretion to the Court to award a reasonable rate of interest. Impliedly it also gave discretion to the Court to award a lesser rate of interest than agreed upon between the mortgagor and the mortgagee. As such rule 11, after it was inserted by Act 21 of 1929, merely conferred upon the Court a discretion to vary the rate of interest but not to do away with interest pendente lite altogether while decreeing a mortgage suit.

18. In the case of Nilmoni Sarkar vs. Baidyanath Das Manna, AIR 1957 (Cal) 140 the same view was followed, namely, that the Court is bound to decree pendente lite interest, it being left to the discretion of the Court at what rate it is to be allowed. The circumstances of each particular case is to be taken into consideration.

19. In the case of Kishen Raj vs. Radhalal, AIR 1958 (Rajasthan) 145 the position of law has been summarised in paragraphs 19 and 21 of the report substantially along the lines indicated above.

20. In the case of Patel Narharilal Kuberdas vs. Partners of the Firm of Pari Bhogilal Amratlal, AIR 1963 (Guj) 253, it is again reiterated that in a case of a suit for the sale of property mortgaged or charged, an account has to be taken of what was due to the plaintiff at the date of such decree as provided in Order 34 rule 2 and Order 34 rule 4. The Court has to take an account of the principal and interest on the mortgage and the amount due to the plaintiff on the date of the decree. The Court has, therefore, no discretion in the matter of taking accounts of the mortgage. It was, however, contended that section 34 overweighed Order 34 and that where section 34 gives a discretion to the Court that discretion cannot be taken away by Order 34. It was rightly held that there was no inconsistency between the two. Section 34 gives a discretion to the Court in cases where the Court passes a pure money decree. Order 34 leaves no discretion to the Court where the Court is dealing with suits under Order 34.

21. Finally, in the case of Laxmi Chand Gangaram vs. Brijbhushan Das, AIR 1970 (Madhya Pradesh) 34, more or less the same views with regard to the award of interest and the rate at which interest is to be awarded has been reiterated.

<u>22. It thus appears that the preponderance of judicial decisions in the sub-continent is that whether it is a suit for foreclosure or for sale the Court has to pass a preliminary decree in terms of rule (2)1) of Order 34 and that the Court has no option but to award interest pendente lite to the mortgagee. In a suit for redemption the principle is not very different because the preliminary decree therein has to be passed under Order 34 rule 7 CPC which is substantially in the same terms as in rule 2. The High Court Division was not well-founded in law in not being persuaded with the decisions cited in AIR 1953 (Born) 445 and AIR 1958 (Rajasthan) 145 on the ground that as those were suits for foreclosure and redemption, the principles stated therein are inapplicable in the instant suit. In a suit for sale the preliminary decree is drawn up in the same manner as in a suit for foreclosure.</u>

<u>23. We therefore hold that the High Court Division acted illegally in not holding that the plaintiff-appellant was entitled to interest pendente lite, ie, from the date of the institution of the suit upto the date of the passing of the decree.</u>

24. Now as for the rate of interest we have already noticed that the Court is not obliged under rule 11 to award the contractual rate of interest while awarding interest pendente lite. Contractual rate of interest was payable according to the Privy Council in the case reported in AIR 1927 (PC) 1 but after the enactment of Act 21 of 1929 the newly inserted rule 11 of Order 34 gives the Court a discretion in the matter of fixing the rate of interest to be awarded pendente lite. That is the purport of the decision reported in AIR 1940 (FC) 20 and the other decisions already noticed.

25. The original agreement between the parties is that the defendants will pay interest at 2¼% above Bank rate, the minimum being 10½%. Subsequently on an extension of the cash credit facilities the rate of interest was increased to 13½%. In the plaint the plaintiff has asked for interest at the rate of 20% pendente lite.

<u>26. At the close of the argument Mr ABM Khairul Huq has submitted a signed statement of accounts on behalf of the appellant-Bank which shows that by November, 1990 the respondents have paid off the entire decretal dues by instalments. So there remains nothing due from them except the interest pendente lite. It also appears that the Managing Director of the defendant-company died on 3-5-83 and after his death the company failed to run their business and were thus unable to pay any interest. Even then the decretal amount remains fully paid in 1990. After a passage of 7 years from the satisfaction of the decree we are not inclined to impose the contractual rate of interest upon the judgment-debtor. We are of the opinion that the interest of justice will be served if the defendants are directed to pay interest at the rate of 6% on the decretal sum with yearly rests from the date of institution of the suit till the date of decree in two equal yearly instalments.</u>

<u>27. With regard to interest from the date of decree till realisation we find that the discretion of the Court is even wider in this area and considering the facts and circumstances of this particular case as already noticed we think that no interest should be paid on this score.</u>

The appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. The trial Court is directed to draw up a fresh decree in terms of this judgment.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Fazlul Karim ----- for the Petitioner.
D. M. Rahman for Shah Hurmutullah ----- for the opposite part.
parties:
Darogali SK. & ors ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Melatan Nessa Bibi &ors ------ Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
<u>1. This rule has been obtained by the defendant against the order dated 30.7.69 passed in Misc. Case No. 9 of 1960 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court Sirajgonj and has arisen in the following circumstances Opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 2 of 1966 for declaration of title and khas possession of the suit land on partition against the defendant petitioner and on 17.2.69 the suit was decreed exparte in preliminary form. This exparte decree was, however set aside on an application of the defendant petitioner on 11.7.69 under Order 9 Rule 13 which was registered as Misc Case No. 9 of 1969 and the Court recorded the following order:</u>

<u>"That the Misc Case be allowed on contest and the exparte decree passed in Title Suit No. 125 of 1967 on 17.2.69 be set aside and the suit be restored to its file and original number subject to payment of costs of Rs. 100/- to the opposite parties by 30.7.69 and in default the Misc Case will stand dismissed."</u>

<u>2. It appears that on 30.7.69 the petitioner filed an application praying for time stating that as they were very poor and were unable to collect money to pay the costs of Rs, 100/- but the learned Munsif rejected his prayer as the order dated 11.7.69, as quoted above as according to him it is final and time allowed by that order cannot be enlarged. Thereafter on 31.7.69 the petitioner again filed an application under section 151 C.P.C. praying for re-consideration of his prayer for extension of time stating further that the sherista of his lawyer having learnt of the order much later, the same could not be communicated to the petitioner in time and as such, it was not possible for the petitioner to procure the amount of costs and pay it within time, and since their petition for extension of time has been rejected it has caused irreparable loss to them The learned Munsif also rejected this prayer on the ground that the order No. 56, dated 11.7.69 allowing Misc. Case subject to payment of Rs. 100/- as costs to the contesting opposite party by 30.7.69 achieved its finality on the lapse of time beyond 30.7.69 inasmuch as the said order allowing the Misc. Case was subject to the condition that in case of default of payment of the costs either by depositing in Court or otherwise the Misc. Case would stand dismissed. The dismissal in default was automatic and needed no death stroke in that behalf. The petition under section 151 C.P.C., according to him does not therefore in the circumstances of the case lie. Present Rule has been obtained by the petitioner challenging the order passed by the learned Munsif on 30.7.69 rejecting his application for extension of time.</u>

3. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners has contended that the learned Munsif failed to exercise his jurisdiction in not extending the time to deposit the costs treating the order to deposit the costs as to be final inasmuch as in law, he had power till the expiry on 30.7.69 to extend time as prayed for. In this connection the learned Advocate has further submitted that under section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court has ample power in the facts and circumstances of the case to enlarge such period because, according to him, the order of payment of costs by the learned Munsif by 30.7.69 has been made in compliance with the provisions of  Rule 13 Order 9, C.P.C. which provides amongst other that the Court shall make an order setting aside the decree as against him (the defendant) upon such terms as to costs, payment into Court or otherwise as it thinks fit and shall appoint the day for proceeding with the suit. This according to the learned Advocate comes under section 148 as the order of payment of cost by 30.7.69 by the Court is an Act prescribed or allowed by the Code within the meaning of section 148, C.P.C. and the Court may in its discretion, from time to time enlarge such period though the period originally fixed or granted might have expired.

4. In support of his argument the learned Advocate has referred to some rulings, namely, 6 D.L.R. 595 in the case of Sheikh Ayezuddin Vs. Priya Shankar Chowdhury, A.I.R. 1961 (S.C.) 882 in the case of Mahanth Ram Das Vs. Ganna Das, and 62 C. W. N. 588 in the case of Jyotish Chandra Sen Vs. Rukshini Ballav Sen and ors.

5. In 6 D.L.R. 595 an application under section 174 of the Bengal Tenancy Act was allowed by the learned Munsif with costs on petitioners depositing the decretal amount together with statutory compensation by 11th August, 1951 in default the Misc. Case shall stand dismissed. On 11th August, 1951 the learned Munsif allowed the prayer of the petitioner for further extension of time upto 29th August, 1951 but on that date as well, the judgment debtor petitioner failed to deposit the amount and the case was dismissed. Subsequently the judgment debtor deposited the decretal amount on 8th September, 1951 which was not accepted by the Court. His lordship Akbar, J. as he then was held sitting singly:

"That as it was very clear that the court directed that the Misc. Case shall stand dismissed if the decretal amount was not paid by 11th August, 1951.
