On 11th August 1951, the date of payment was extended till 29th August, 1951. As the amount was not paid by the said date, the suit was dismissed. In the circumstances, there is no room for doubt that the proceeding terminated on that date and in the words of Kekewich, J. the action was dead. Thereafter the Munsif being functus officio had no jurisdiction to extend the time".

6. In this case the learned Munsif finally passed the order dismissing the suit for default but it may be noted that he did it after extending the time once on 11.8.59 although there was default order and his lordship did not express any disapproval regarding that order.

7. In A.I.R. 1961 (S.C.) 882 in the case of Mohanth Ram Das Vs. Gonga Das where a Bench of the High Court while deciding the appeal in favour of the appellant, Mohanth Ram Das, passed the pre-emptory order fixing period for payment of deficit court fee and the appellant made an application for extension of time before the time fixed had run out but the application came on for hearing before a Division Bench after the period had run out and the Division Bench dismissed the application for extension of time. On appeal the Supreme Court of India made the following observation:

"The case is an unfortunate and unusual one. The application for extension of time was made before the time fixed by the High Court for payment of deficit court fee had actually run out. That application appears not to have been considered at all in view of the preemptory order which had been passed earlier by the Division Bench hearing the appeal, mainly because on the date of the hearing of the petition for extension of time, the period had expired. The short question is whether the High Court, in the circumstances of the case, was powerless to enlarge the time, even though it had peremtorily fixed the period for payment. If the Court had considered the application and rejected it on merits, other considerations might have arisen; but the High Court in the order quoted went by the letter of the original order under which time for payment had been fixed. Section 148 of the Code, in terms allows extension of time, even if the original period fixed has expired, and Section 149 is equally liberal. A fortiori, those sections could be invoked by the applicant when the time had not actually expired. That the application was filed in the vacation when a Division Bench was not sitting should have been considered in dealing with it even on July 18.1954, when it was actually heard. The order though passed after the expiry of the time fixed by the original judgment would have operated from July 8, 1954. How undesirable it is to fix time peremptorily for a future happening which leaves the Court powerless to deal with events that might arise in between, it is not necessary to decide in this appeal. These orders turn out, often enough to be inexpedient. Such procedural orders, though peremptory (conditional decrees apart) are in essence in terrerem, so that dilatory litigants might put themselves in order and avoid delay. They do not, however, completely stop a court from taking note of events and circumstances which happen within the time fixed. For example, it cannot be said that if the appellant had started with the full money ordered to be paid and came well in time but was set upon and robbed by thieves the day previous, he could not ask for extension of time, or that the courts was powerless to extend it. Such orders by not like the law of the Medes and the Persians. Cases are known in which courts have moulded their practice to meet a situation such as this and to have restored a suit or proceeding even though a final order had been passed".

8. In 62 C. W. N. 588, same case in A.I.R. 1959 Cal. 35, A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Jyotish Chandra Sen Vs. Rukmini Ballav Sen, it appear that on 22nd April, 1957 the Court ordered that the additional written state me to be accepted provided the defendant pays a cost of Rs. 16/- to the plaintiff by the 16th May, 1957, in default of payment of cost the additional written statement will stand rejected. It was held by the Division Bench as follows:

"Order VIII, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that an additional written statement may be accepted by the leave of the court on such terms as the court may think fit. Where one of the terms is that certain amount should be paid within a fixed time that in our opinion is an act allowed by the Code and when a period is fixed by the Court for doing that act section 148 of the Code in terms applies".

9. Mr. D. M. Rahman, the learned Advocate on behalf of the opposite party on the other hand in support of the order of the learned Munsif has submitted that the words namely, the Misc. Case will stand dismissed denote a finality to the order of the learned Munsif and as such, he does not retain any jurisdiction to deal with the matter and has referred to 3 D.L.R. 313; 11 D.L.R. 23 and 27 D.L.R. 232.

10. In 3 D.L.R. 313 in the case of Mahendra Chandra De and other Vs Govinda Prashad, a Division Bench of the High Court in Lowazema allowed time for one month to put in the additional copy of paper book in default the appeal will stand dismissed. It was held that:

"There is a difference between the order "the appeal will stand dismissed" and the order "the appeal will be dismissed". The former order contemplates a final order to be passed in future and therefore, the case has not been finally disposed of and the court can extend time under section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

11. In 11 D.L. R. 23 in the case of Afazuddin Molla and others Vs. Abdur Rahman Sk. and another, an application under Order 9 rule 13, C.P.C., for setting aside a decree, was allowed on condition of payment of Rs. 12/- by 30.5.55 as costs and in case of default it was ordered that the Misc. Case shall he treated as dismissed.The money being not deposited on 30.5.55, the Court on that date ordered that the Misc Case be dismissed. It was held that the Court having passed the order before expiry of the date granted to the petitioners the order was void and without jurisdiction. In that connection it was also observed that the expression shall be treated as dismissed shows that the order passed by the court was not a final order and the court is not functus officio to entertain the application under section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure and to extend time.

12. In 27 D.L.R. 232 in the case of Rajendra Shirali and others Vs. Mahadev Shirali, a suit for specific performance of contract for sale of certain land was decreed exparte and it was ordered that the plaintiff will deposit Rs. 75/- to the credit of the defendant within 15 days, in default the suit will stand dismissed. No deposit having been made by the plaintiff within the time allowed, the court passed the order on 19-4-69 dismissing the suit Subsequently on an application under section 151 read with section 148 of the C.P.C. filed by the plaintiff it restored the suit vacating the order of dismissal and extended time for the deposit of sum of Rs. 75/- The learned Munsif rejected the application that there was nothing for the court to do. On revision before this Court his lordship Bhattacharya, I. relying on the case of Shah Wall Vs Ghulam Din alias Gaman and Muhammad Din, reported in 19 DLR (SC) 143 held as follows:

"There is a specific provision in the Code in section 148 for extension of time, where any time is granted by the Court for doing any act prescribed or allowed by the Code. This provision has obviously no application to a case where time is fixed by the Court in a decree for performing an obligation which arises out of a contract between the parties. Moreover, if we consider that the power under the aforesaid provision can be invoked even in a case where time is fixed by the Court in its final order, there is no question of exercise of such power in this case in view of the fact that the conditional order has become operative, and the court has become functus officio".

It was further held while considering the applicability of section 151 to extend time:

"In the first place, we have to remember that if the Court has lost seisin of the case altogether, there is no scope for the application of section 151 C.P.C. It is only if the Court has retained jurisdiction in the litigation that jurisdiction arises. If jurisdiction had already ceased to exist the scope of making order in the inherent jurisdiction of the court totally disappears. The real question, therefore, is whether in a case like this, where an order has been made for the payment of certain money within a certain time for the purpose of getting specific performance and at the same time an order has also been made that if the money is not paid the suit will stand dismissed the Court retains jurisdiction. Though not without hesitation I have reached the conclusion that in such a case it will be unrealistic and unjust to say that the Court has retained jurisdiction Whether the Court has retained jurisdiction or not will in my view depend very much on the substance of the directions given. In granting a decree for a specific performance the Court makes it conditional on the payment being made within a certain time and it appears that the time specified was intended by the Court to be the essence of the order, it would be unreasonable in my opinion to held that the Court has still retained jurisdiction. Where a decree for specific performance is made and at the same time a direction is given to the plaintiff to put in the money within a certain time and there is no indication that time is the essence of the order it might be possible and ordinarily reasonable to say that though a time has been specified for the performance of the act, the Court has not finally dealt with the matter and retains jurisdiction to pass such other orders as may appear to it to be reasonable. Where, however, the Court makes also an order that if the amount is not deposited within the time specified the suit will stand dismissed, I find it difficult to agree that the Court retains any jurisdiction whatsoever".

13. In the above case time was fixed by the Court in a decree for specific performance an obligation which arose out of the contract between the parties. Moreover, the conditional order of dismissal, because of non-compliance, was followed by a final order dismissing the suit which has become operative, the case is plainly distinguishable. It may be observed that his lordship Bhattacharya, J. had reached the conclusion, though not without hesitation, that in such a case it will be unrealistic and unjust to say that the Court retains its jurisdiction. The question according to the learned Judge depends very much on the substance of direction given and that time specified was intended by the Court to be an essence of the order, so it was thought unreasonable to hold that the court has retained its jurisdiction. Several decisions including 62 C.W.N. 588 and A.I.R. 1961 (SC) 882 Supra, have been referred to in this case and it has been pointed out that the Court retained the season over the principal action, even though the interlocutory proceeding has come to an end and has jurisdiction in such cases to given an extension of time.

<u>14. In the present case, as it will be seen, that the conditional order passed on 30-7-69 was not followed by a final order of dismissal which can only be passed on the expiry of 30-7-69 and, as such, the Court did not become functus officio on the date, namely, 30-7-69, when the prayer for extension of time was refused because it was fried before the default order became operative. Moreover, the conditional order of default was not a matter of controversy for the purpose of setting aside an exparte decree. It is in my opinion was a "procedural order though peremptory" and "in essence, in terrerem, so that the dilatory litigants might put themselves in order and avoid delay and does not however completely stop a Court from taking note of events and circumstances which happen within the time fixed" as expressed by their lordships of Supreme Court of India in A.I.R. 1961 (S.C.) 882 Mohanth Ram Das Vs. Ganga Das (Supra). I am in respectful agreement with that view and hold that the court retained its jurisdiction to extend time beyond 30-7-69 on an application to that effect filed and that date.</u>

15. The result is that this Rule is made absolute and the order passed by the learned Munsif disallowing the extension of time is set aside and it is directed that the costs of Rs. 100/- for payment to the plaintiff be deposited in the Court below within one month of the intimation of arrival of the record. On the deposit of the said costs the suit will be restored to its file and original number failing which the Misc. Case will stand dismissed and the exparte decree will be restored.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 539 of 1965.
lawyer:
Md. Abdur Rashid for B.B. Roy Chowdhury ------ For the Appellants. 
B.N. Chowdhury ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Jagar Chandra Das & ors  ------ Appellants.
Vs.
Dherendra Mohan Pramanik  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
The plaintiffs appellant's case, in brief, is that Sarada Prosad Roy, Jnanada Prosad Roy, Prornoda Prosad Roy and Kornada Prosad Roy gifted the suit lands to Sankar Prosad Roy in 1337 B.S. Sankar Prosad Roy possessed the suit lands exclusively and in 1366 B.S. he leased out the same to the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs possessed the suit land under their own plough from 1353 to 1366 B.S. In 1366 B.S. they cultivated plot Nos. 449, 450 and 451 by hired plough and plot No. 447 through bargadars. The defendants cut away the plaintiffs jute from the suit land under the cover of an order under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

2. The defendant's case is that he purchased at a certificate sale C.S. Plot Nos. 449, 450 and 451 and 4 annas share of plot No. 447 and in another sale he purchased 6 annas share of plot No. 477 and took possession through court. One Bimala Charan Roy and others filed a preemption case against him which was compromised and the defendant obtained C.S. plot No. 447. He denied that there was any absolute gift in favor of Sankar Roy who was in Calcutta from long before 1353 B.S.

3. The suit was once decreed and, on appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge, after holding that an absolute right had been transferred to Sankar Prosad  Roy, remanded the case for rehearing with an opportunity to the plaintiffs to amend their plaint. The suit was again decreed. The learned Munsiffound that Sankar Prosad  Roy did not lease out the suit plots to the plaintiff's and the plaintiffs did not acquire any title by adverse possession, but as there was some reliable evidence for the plaintiffs possession for 3 years, 1366 to 1368 B.S., the suit was decreed for khas possession after evicting the defendant from the suit land. It was also held that the defendant did not get any title in the suit land by auction purchase and he had no right, title and interest in the suit land and that there was no evidence how Bimala became co-sharer in the suit plots., and the defense case of Bimala's possession prior to 1368 B.S. was a surprise as it was not mentioned either in the written statement or in the additional written statement.

4. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court after finding that there was no evidence to hold that the defendants were in possession of the suit land from 1366 B.S. He held that as no cross objection was filed by the plaintiffs they were estopped from agitating any point with regard to title or adverse possession. From the defendant's documents Ext. C-CCD, the sale certificate, Exts. D and D(l), writs of delivery of possession and Exts. E.E. (I), F.F.(1), G.G.(1), and H.H.(I) of the pre-emption proceedings the learned Subordinate Judge held that the defendant came upon the suit land earlier than 1368 B.S.

5. Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid, the learned Advocate for the appellants, has submitted that having regard to the provision of Order 41, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Court of Appeal below erred in law in not allowing the plaintiffs to show that the finding of the trial court on the question of title and adverse possession was erroneous. He has contended that without reversing the finding of the trial court that the defendant had no right, title and interest in the suit plots and without adverting to the oral evidence of the P.Ws. as to the plaintiffs possession in the suit land the court of appeal below erred in law in reversing the decision of the trial court. He has also complained that the lower appellate court's finding, based only on the defendant's documents, that the defendants came upon the suit land earlier than 1368 B.S. is rather vague as it has not pointed out a definite time when the defendant came upon the suit land.

6. Mr. Md. Abdur Rashid in support of his first contention has referred to the case of Sm. Jobeda Khatun and another Vs. Hazi Mohammad Ibrahim and others reported in AIR 1957 Cal 360 and that of Probodh Chandra Barman, Managing Director, Tripura Modern Bank, Chittagong Vs. Messrs Abdul Rahman, Abdul Gani and others (1960) 12 DLR 459.

7. In the AIR 1957 Cal. 360 the plaintiffs suit was decreed in part and it was held on appeal that the plaintiff as respondent in the appeal was entitled to support the decree in his favor on grounds found against him and the respondent was allowed to challenge, but without any success, the trial court's adverse finding against him with regard to a kabala. In the 12 DLR 458 it was held that the plaintiffs were entitled to challenge as respondents the trial court's adverse finding against him on the question of admissibility of a renewed bond.

<u>8. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondents, has vigorously resisted the first contention of Mr. Rashid. He has drawn my attention to the following observation of Srinivass Aiyangar, J. who deliver d the judgment in Sri Ranga Thathachariar Vs. SrinivasaThathachariar AIR 1927 Mqdras, 801. Though the word 'decree' has been used in r. 22 it is clear that what the rule contemplates really is the decision by the court below and merely enables the decision arrived at by the lower court to be supported on grounds other than those on which the lower court proceeded. We are satisfied that under that rule it is not open to a respondent to have adjudicated by the appellate court rights or causes of action which have been decided against him in the court below and in respect of which he has filed no appeal or memorandum of objection." This view was followed in a number of decisions Mr. Chowdhury has cited some of them, particularly, Namadao Shankar Patil Vs. Ramrao Maroti PatiI reported in AIR 1933 Nagpur, 310.</u>

9. Thathachariar's case was dissented by a Full Bench of the Madras High Court in Venkata Roy Vs. Satyanarayan Murthi, AIR 1943, 698 where in the following question referred to the Full Bench was answered in the affirmed: "Whether under Order 41 rule 22, Civil Procedure Code it is open to a defendant respondent who has not taken any cross-objection to the partial decree passed against him, to urge in opposition to the appeal of the plaintiff a contention which, if accepted by the trial court, would have necessitated the total dismissal of the suit."

10. The cases reported in AIR 1927 Madras 801 and A.I.R.1943. Madras 698 were cited before the Indian Supreme Court in Itakhoolie Tea Estate Vs. Its Workmen AIR 1960 SC 1949 but the Supreme Court found it not necessary to expresstheir preference for any of the two views and, instead, held:

"Under Order XLI, Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure any respondent may support the decree of any of the grounds decided against him in the Court below. But this does not and cannot, confer on him a right higher than that he would have had if he had preferred an appeal against the ground decided against him. To put it differently, he cannot support the decree on a ground which would not have been available to him if he were all appellant."

11. Later, in Sri C. P. J. Temple Vs. Harikrishna A.I.R. 1973 SC 2565 the Indian Supreme Court upheld the view expressed in A.I.R. 1943 Madras 698 (F.B.) and observed:

"The decree of the High Court here in so far as it held that the mortgage money can be recovered only from the half share in the properties was also a decree in favor of the respondents as it did not allow the claim of the appellants to recover it from the entire interest in the properties. To that extent, the respondents had a decree in their favor. That decree they could support on any of the grounds decided against them by the court which passed the decree. And when they do this, they are only supporting and not attacking that decree. We think that the rule laid down by the Madras High Court in the above decision is sound. And there is no reason why the respondents should be barred from urging the plea."

12. Mr. Chowdhury has also cited Roshan and others Vs. Mst. Abedur Nessa and others reported in P. L. D. 1963 Dacca 712 where the learned Single Judge refused to take exception to the lower appellate courts observation that the defendant-respondents, by not filing any cross-objection, impliedly accepted the trial court's finding for the plaintiff as to a settlement of a tank. The learned single Judge of the High Court, however found that the lower appellate did not base his decision solely on this but on examination of the evidence on the record found independently thereof that the plaintiff took her alleged settlement ad had been in actual possession on that basis.

<u>13. In an appeal the appellant challenges a decision, adverse to him, but favorable to the respondents. The decision passed in favor of the respondent might be based on all or some of the grounds urged by the respondent before the court below. On hearing of the appeal it may come of on examination that the grounds accepted by the court below are without any substance and the grounds which did not find favor with the court below may be found to be substantial. In such a situation the respondent may be left high and dry but for rule 22 of Order 41 which gives him liberty to urge the grounds decided against him in the court below in support of his decree. Where a suit is wholly decreed or dismissed the application of rule 22 does not create any difficulty. It is only when a suit is decreed in part, confusion may arise as to the extent of its application. A partial decree is, in effect, a decree for the plaintiff, so far as the plaintiff's case is accepted, as well as a decree for the defendant, so far as the plaintiff's case is dismissed. Whether an appeal is preferred by the plaintiff or defendant the respondent has a decree in his favor and he can invoke rule 22 in his aid and by doing so he merely supports the decree and does not, and in fact, cannot attack the decree without filing a cross objection. When the respondent agitates the grounds rejected by the court below he merely demonstrates that en proper application of evidence the impugned decree cannot be disturbed and the appellant is not entitled to challenge the same. The legal provision in question is a defensive mechanism to protect the decree and it can only be used to thwart the appellant's attack on the decree in question and not for attacking the decree itself.</u>

14. In the instant case the trial court rejected the plaintiff's claim based on the grounds of title and adverse possession, and only decreed the suit for khas possession in the suit land on the evidence of possession. In appeal as the plaintiffs-respondents did not file any cross-objection the lower court held that the findings of the trial court regarding title and adverse possession were conclusive and the plaintiffs would be estopped from agitating the question of title and adverse possession any longer. The lower appellate court clearly erred in law in not allowing the plaintiffs-respondents tourge the grounds rejected by the trial court. The plaintiff-respondents were entitled under rule 22 in support of the decree to urge the grounds of title and adverse possession not for getting a decree for declaration of title on the suit land but for demonstrating that the defendants- appellants were not entitled on proper appreciation of the evidence on the record to challenge the decree at all.

15. The lower appellate court has not only shut out the plaintiffs from agitating the grounds of title and adverse possession but also did not discuss the oral evidence adduced by the plaintiffs as to their possession in the suit land. I think the matter should be remanded to the lower appellate court for rehearing of the appeal in accordance with law.

16. In the result the appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge are set aside and the case is remanded to the lower appellate court for re-hearing of the appeal in accordance with law. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Dr. Kamal Hossain with SR Karmakar, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner Nos. 1-4. 
Miah Abdul Gafur with Shafiqul Islam, Advocates ----- For the Opposite-Party No.1.
parties:
Moynul Hasan an ors ----- Petitioners
Vs. 
Nazmul Haq @ Nazmul Hasan and ors ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
AKM Sadeq J: This Rule obtained by the plaintiff-petitioners, is directed against order No. 30 dated 31.12.86 passed by Mr. AKM Fazul Karim, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 756 of 1985 allowing an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The parties herein are heirs and descendants of late Shamsul Huq who died leaving a substantive amount of immovable property.

2. The petitioners and the opposite party No. 1 are full brothers born of the womb of the opposite party No.2 Jamila Khatoon.

3. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a suit for partition of their paternal ejmali properties being Title Suit No. 278 of 1983 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against all his co-sharers including opposite party No.1, who was shown as defendant No.8. The defendant No. 8 (opposite party No. 1) did not enter appearance. On 10.11.1983 the defendant Nos. 1-6 namely the mother and sisters of the petitioner and the opposite party No.1, the brother of the petitioners entered appearance. They effected a compromise and filed a solenama on 27.2.84. The final decree was drawn according to the solenama dated 1.4.84. On 4.5.84 opposite party No. 1 Nazmul Hassan filed a seperate suit being Title Suit No. 163 of 1984 for partition of ejmali properties impleading all the heirs of his father late Shamsul Haque and prayed for appointment of a Receiver. On 20.6.1984 the petitioner along with other defendants entered appearance. They filed a written objection on 25.4.1985 against the prayer of appointment of a Receiver stating, inter alia, that the earlier Title Suit No. 287 of 1983 between the parties had ended in compromise. A copy of the said petition was served upon the learned Advocate of the opposite party No.1 on 25.4.85. On 17.8.85 the opposite party No.1 filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 read with section 151 of the CPC being Miscellaneous Case No. 756 of 1985 for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 27.2.84 as against him in Title Suit No. 278 of 1983 on the ground that he did not receive any summons and he came to leam about the ex parte decree on 27.9.84 on receipt of notice in FMA Case No. 174 of 1984 preferred by the petitioners against the order dated 16.3.85 of appointment of a Receiver in Title Suit No. 163 of 1984. The opposite party Nos. 1-10 of this Miscellaneous Case resisted the application by filing written objection denying the allegation of non-service of summons upon the petitioners and pleading bar of limitation.

4. Both the parties led evidence and on consideration of the evidence the learned Subordinate judge by his impugned judgment and order dated 31.12.86 allowed the application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC, set aside the ex parte decree dated 27.2.84 in Title Suit No. 278 of 1983 and restored the suit to its original file and number.

5. Being aggrieved the plaintiff-petitioners have obtained the Rule.

6. The learned Counsel for the petitioner Dr. Kamal Hossain has urged that the application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC in question was barred by limitation and the learned Subordinate judge did not advert to this aspect of the case : this has constituted non-consideration of an essential law point. He has elaborated his argument by stating that the petitioner has admitted that his advocate had received the copy of the objection petition to the prayer for appointment of receiver in Title Suit No. 163 of 1984 wherein it was clearly stated that the earlier Title Suit No. 178 of 1983 had ended in compromise on 27.2.84. Therefore, the petitioner is bound by definite knowledge of the date of ex parte decree against him in Title Suit No. 278 of 1983; the present application under Order 9 rule 13 of the CPC was brought on 17.5.85. Therefore, the application was clearly barred by limitation.

<u>7. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, on the other hand, submitted that the order sheet would show that no summons was at all issued for service upon the petitioner who was defendant No. 8 in the suit and the evidence on record also would show that there was no service of summons upon the petitioners. A compromise decree without service of summons upon a party to the suit amounts to fraud and if fraud is proved, there is no question of limitation. Again he submitted that under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code if summons is not duly served on the defendant, that is a good ground for setting aside an ex parte decree without any reference to limitation. He submits that a perusal of the provision of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes it apparent that due service of summons is an essential condition which must be satisfied before the Court can proceed to give a judgment. In a proceeding under Order 9 rule 13, CPC if a party satisfies a court that summons were not duly served upon him, the Court shall be bound to set aside such an ex pane decree. In such a case question of knowledge is not at all relevant and decree will be set aside even if the defendant had knowledge of institution of a suit. In support of the submission the learned Advocate had placed before us the decisions in the case of Abul Khair Mia Vs. Abdul Latif Sarder, 32 DLR 167 (AD) and Abdur Rashid & another Vs. Abul Barik and another 35 DLR 163 (AD). The learned Advocate has further urged that in the instant case there was an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act and although the learned Subordinate Judge did not refer to it in his judgment, it is clear to see that he in consideration of such an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act had condoned limitation. By an amendment of the Order 9 rule 13 of the Cede of Civil Procedure section 5 of the Limitation Act has been made applicable.</u>

<u>8. We have gone through order-sheet of the Tittle Suit No. 278 of 1983. We have noticed with concern that even without issuing summons for service upon the Opposite Party No. 1 who is defendant No. 8 in the suit, not to speak of service of summonst upon him, the compromise decree in question was passed on 27.2.84 dividing the entire properties in the suit amongst the compromising parties, to the exclusion of the opposite party No. 1 (defendant No. 8). This speaks of suppression, even fraud. Studied in the light of the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, we are inclined to hold, in the facts and circumstances of the present case, that limitation was not a material point for decision of the Miscellaneous Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Since the opposite party No. 1 (defendant No. 8) had made a prayer for condonation of delay in bringing his case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, supporting the same by an affidavit, stating his definite date of knowledge (29.7.85), it is obvious that the learned Subordinate Judge had condoned the delay in consideration of the application under section 5 of the Limitation Act in exercise of his discretion.</u>

<u>9. This Court has repeatedly pointed out unless the discretion exercised by a subordinate Court is whimsically and arbitrarily exercised, the discretion is not to be interfered with. Even if the discretion exercised by the subordinate Court is not in strict conformance with law and rules, the discretion would not be interfered with if it does not occasion failure of justice. In the instant case restoration of the partition suit for decision in presence of all the co-sharers including the present petitioners occasions no failure of justice. Therefore, we are not inclined to interfere with the impugned order of the learned Subordinate Judge.</u>

In the result, the Rule is discharged without, however, any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Nizamuddin Haider ------- For the Petitioner. 
M. A. Sattar ------- For Opposite Party.
parties:
Zauz Ali Molla ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Fatema Bibi and others ----- Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of one of the heirs of the deceased plaintiffs is directed against an order of the learned Munsif refusing, to make the preliminary decree final on the ground that the application was made after a long lapse of 43 years. The learned Munsif, however, noticed an order dated 16.4.31 striking off the suit for non-compliance of certain order of the Court.

2. At this stage there is no dispute that one Mariam Bibi instituted Title Suit No. 788 of 1929 in the 2nd Court of Munsif at Bagerhat for partition and the said suit was decreed in preliminary form on contest on 31.7.30 granting the plaintiff 6 minas 15 gondas share in the property in suit. There is nothing on record to indicate that the said preliminary decree was varied or altered on appeal or review, Meanwhile, Title Suit No. 41 of 1973 has been instituted by the ooposite party Nos. 3 to 6 for declaration of their title to some land of the aforesaid partition Suit No. 788 of 1929. During the pendency of the said suit, the heirs of Mariam Bibi filed a petition for final decree in terms of the preliminary decree. The learned Munsif however, rejected the petition mainly on the ground that the order dated 16.4.31 was not challenged by the persons effected thereby and that it was filed after a long lapse of 43 years by the heirs of the original plaintiff Who cannot maintain the petition for final decree.

<u>3. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the Rule contends that the suit was decreed in preliminary form granting certain shares in favour of the plaintiff and as such the suit was not liable to be dismissed unless the said preliminary decree was reversed on appeal. In support of this proposition, Mr. Haider has referred to the case of Laehmi Narain Marwary and others Vs. Balmakund Marwary and another 29 C.W.N. 391. In this case their Lordships of the Privy Council held that an order dismissing the suit after the preliminary decree was passed was without jurisdiction. In the instant case the order dated 16.4.31 is an order by which the said suit was struck of for non-compliance of the Court's order relating to commissioner's fee, etc. An order of this type has been described by their Lordships of the Privy Council as "unfortunate" order. This appears to consonance with the principle that decree passed by the Court in preliminary form remains pending until the final decree is passed. Evidently, the said partition suit did not reach up to the stage of the final decree because of non-compliance of certain order. Their Lore ships of the Privy Council did not approve ail order of the type of the instant case. Although it was noticed that negligence or dilatoriness on the part of the parties might create some obstruction, nevertheless it was not intended that such a suit could be struck off during the stage of the final decree.</u>

<u>Similar view is available in the case of Kambala Sundararajamma Vs. P. S. Ramuln Chetty and others A.I.R. 1932 Madras 519. In this case it has been held that "after a preliminary decree in a partition suit has been Passed it is not competent to the Court to dismiss the suit subsequently. The preliminary decree can only be reversed on appeal and whatever default there may be in the subsequent stages of the suit, that preliminary decree itself cannot be vacated." Similar view is also available in the case of Lachmi Narayan Tewari and others Vs. Ramsaran Tewary and another A.I.R. 1925 Patna 433. In this case it has been held that "the Court has no jurisdiction to dismiss the suit after a preliminary decree has been passed in a partition suit merely because, there has been delay in producing the commissioner's fee. Keeping the above principles in view, it is evident that the learned Munsif failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in him in not allowing further proceeding of the said partition suit, the object whereof is attainment of final decree through Court. The grounds as to the lapse of time and the order dated 16.4.31 do not appear to stand on sound footing. Evidently the order dated 16.4.31 was without jurisdiction. The lapse of 43 years is of no consequence in a suit for partition where a preliminary decree was lawfully granted by a Court.</u>

4. Mr. M. A. Sattar, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties has pressed his contention that long lapse of time and absence of any action on the part of the person effected by the order dated 16.4.31 rendered the preliminary decree incapable of further proceeding towards the final decree. Mr. Sattar is not supported by any authority in respect of his contention.

For the reasons stated above, the Rule succeeds and is made absolute without any order as to costs.

The learned Munsif is directed to proceed with the partition suit according to law.

Send down the records expeditiously.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.599 of 1995.
lawyer:
Sultan Ahmed, Advocate, instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record — For the Petitioner 
Not represented — Respondents.
parties:
Shamsul Islam (Md.) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Dhirendra Nath Paul and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated August, 1995 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No.957 of 1992)
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: Plaintiff-respondents' suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession, OC Suit No. 371 of 1980 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Natore in which the defendant-petitioner filed a joint written statement with other defendants was decreed ex-parte on 30-8-1988 and on an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the ex parte decree was set aside and the suit restored by order dated 16-2-1992 in Miscellaneous Case No.72 of 1988 on terms of payment of cost of Taka 600.00 not on the finding that the defendant was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing but “ন্যায় বিচারের খাতিরে”|

<u>2. By the impugned judgment and order dated 16 August 1995, a Single Judge of the High Court Division set aside the aforesaid order of restoration in revision, Civil Revision No. 957 of 1992, relying, among others, on Reazul Hoque Molla vs. Afizullah Molla 42 DLR (AD) 74, which has laid down that Court cannot act in exercise of inherent power where relief is provided and claimed under a specific provision of the Code, such as Order 9 rule 13.</u>

3. Seeking leave to appeal from the aforesaid judgment and order, Mr, Sultan Ahmed, learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner, variously tried to justify the order of the learned Assistant Judge but the fact remained that the petitioner did not adduce any evidence as to his alleged illness preventing him from appearing in court while the suit was called on for hearing. So, the miscellaneous case was decided on mere assertion which was denied. There is thus no substance in any argument.

The petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate — For the Petitioner 
Nazrul Islam for Korban Ali, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Sirajuddin Mondal -----  Petitioner
Vs.
Amena Khatun and others  ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued against the opposite parties calling upon them to show cause as to why the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge Rajbari in Title Appeal No. 25 of 1988 setting aside and reversing the judgment and decree passed by the court of Subordinate Judge, Rajbari in Title Suit No. 21 of 1985 should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. It appears that the opposite parties filed the Title Suit for a decree for declaration that they are the sole heirs of Yasin Mondal. They also prayed for a further declaration that the order dated 29.9.84 passed by the Upazila Revenue Officer, Pangsha in Miscellaneous Case No. XIII-64/83-84 is illegal, null and void, etc. The plaintiffs claimed that they were the sole heirs of Yasin Mondal, son of Jadu Mondal. They also claimed that Bishu Mondal was father of Jadu Mondal and he had no other son except Jadu Mondal. But recently the defendant No. 1 claiming himself to be chachata brother of Yasin Mondal filed a Mutation case and fraudulently obtained an order dated 29.2.84 from the Upazila Revenue Officer allowing mutation in respect of the share claimed by him in the suit property. In fact, the defendant No. 1 Serajuddin Mondal is not a chachata brother of Yasin Mondal and never possessed any property of Yasin Mondal. As he falsely claimed himself to be a chachata brother of Yasin Mondal and as he obtained fraudulently an order of mutation, the plaintiffs filed the suit for getting the relief mentioned above.

3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations contained in the plaint. He claimed that Shariatullah had two sons named Gopal Mondal and Bishu Mondal, Gopal Mondal died leaving behind two sons in Taju and Baju. Taju died leaving behind two sons in this defendant and his brother Daimuddin. Baju died unmarried and this defendant and his brother Daimuddin inherited the share of Baju Mondal. This defendant further claims that Bishu Mondal died leaving behind two sons in Adu Mondal and Jadu Mondal Adu died leaving behind one son in Ismail and Jadu died leaving behind one son in Yasin and widow Matijan. Ismail died leaving behind two daughters Khudiram and Kiran and chachata brother Yasin Mondal. Yasin died leaving behind 5 daughters in the plaintiffs and chachata brother in this defendant. In this way, this defendant inherited 3 annas 6 gandas 2 karas 2 kranties share in the property left by Yasin and he has been possessing his share of the property and got his name mutated in respect of his share by filing a mutation case before Upazila Revenue Officer.

4. Further case of the defendant is that Bahadur Mondal, one of the co-sharers of the suit property, died leaving behind daughter in Putiran Bibi, wife in Sundari Bibi and two sons of two chachata bothers in this defendant and Yasin Mondal respectively Putiran sold her share to this defendant by registered kabala dated 8.4.70. In that kabala it is stated that Yasin Mondal and Serajuddin Mondal were chachata brothers. The defendant also claimed that the plaintiffs in order to deprive his legal share in the suit property filed the present false suit.

5. The learned lower Court, on consideration of the evidence on record came to a finding that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit property and, as such, the suit was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned lower Court also believed the case of the defendant and found him to be chachata brother of Yasin Mondal. On such findings, the learned lower Court dismissed the suit. Against that judgment and decree, the plaintiffs preferred an appeal before the court of the District Judge, Rajbari. The appeal was numbered as Title Appeal No. 25 of 1988 and was heard and disposed of by the learned District Judge himself. The learned District Judge found that the defendant No. 1 has lineal connection with Yasin Mondal and also found that the plaintiffs acquired 16 annas interest in the suit property including the two annas share of the widow of Yasin Mondal which they acquired by way of gift. The learned appellate Court also found that the determination of the question of possession is redundant because the plaintiffs prayed for declaration of their heirship to the extent of 16 annas in the suit property. After arriving at such finding, the learned appellate Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of the lower Court and decreed the suit.

6. The defendant by filing this revisional application challenged the validity of the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. It is stated in the revisional application that the learned appellate Court committed an error of law in holding that the question of possession was redundant, though the learned trial Court found that the plaintiffs were not in possession and, as such, the suit was hit by the provisions of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. It has also been stated that when the plaintiffs did not make any prayer for declaration of their title, the appellate Court committed an error of law in declaring title of the plaintiffs in the suit property.

7. The plaintiffs/opposite parties entered appearance and filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein they supported the judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate Court.

8. At the time of hearing, on perusal of the record and the judgments passed by the courts below, it appeared that both the courts were under a misconception that the suit was filed for a decree for declaration of title of the plaintiffs in the suit property. From the prayer portion of the plaint, it appears that the plaintiffs prayed for two declarations-(1) that the plaintiffs are the sole heirs of Yasin Mondal, (ii) that the order dated 22.9.84 passed by the Upazila Revenue Officer of Pangsha in Miscellaneous Case No. XIII-64/83-84 is illegal, null and void, etc. It further appears that the plaint was not amended with regard to the prayer originally made by the plaintiffs. So, it is clear that in this suit the plaintiffs did not pray for declaration of their title in the suit property but unfortunately, both the courts below treated it as a suit for declaration of title. The learned trial Court in its judgment observed as follows:-" As it is a case for declaration of plaintiff's title I think it is necessary to adjudicate the possession". After making such observation the court discussed about the evidence on the question of possession and after referring to the statements of the witnesses of both sides, the court came to a conclusion that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit property and after arriving at such a conclusion, the court held that the suit was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Thus, from the above it is quite clear that the learned trial Court treated the suit to be a suit for declaration of title of the plaintiffs in the suit property. The learned appellate Court though considered that the question as to who were the heirs of Yasin Mondal was the pertinent question to be decided, yet the operative portion of the judgment shows that the appellate Court also treated the suit to be a suit for declaration of title. The relevant portion is reproduced here:- " It is declared that the plaintiffs acquired 16 annas share upon the suit property as heirs of Yasin Mondal and also under a deed of gift from defendant No. 3 Halimunnessa." It is interesting to note that the plaintiffs themselves did not make such a prayer for declaration in the plaint. The relevant prayer of the plaintiffs as made at prayer (a5) is as follows:

(ক) আরজীর কথিত মতে বাদীগন ইয়াসীন মন্ডলের একমাত্র ও ওয়ারেশ থাকা ঘোষনা মূলক ডিক্রি দিতে।”

So, in view of prayer (ক), I do not understand how the appellate Court made such a declaration as quoted above. Thus I am of the opinion that the courts below failed to consider properly the nature of the suit and relief sought for in the suit.

9. It further appears that the plaintiffs have also prayed for a declaration that an order dated 22.9.84 passed by the Upazila Revenue Officer in a mutation case is illegal, null and void, etc. The order has not been marked exhibit either by the trial Court or by the appellate Court but curiously enough the appellate Court declared the order as illegal, null and void, etc. without admitting that order into evidence. It is not understood how an order can be declared to be illegal unless the same is before the court. The District Judge declared the order illegal when the order was not admitted into evidence and marked as an exhibit. The learned appellate Court committed an error of law in declaring the order illegal without admitting the order into evidence and marking it an exhibit.

10. From the record it further appears that the plaintiffs though prayed for declaring them as sole heirs of Yasin Mondal, they admitted in the plaint itself that the defendant No. 3 was the widow of Yasin Mondal. From the evidence it transpires that the defendant No. 3 Halimunnessa is the second wife of Yasin Mondal. She is obviously an heir of Yasin Mondal. When it is admitted that defendant No. 3 is wife of Yasin Mondal, the question of declaring the plaintiffs as sole heirs of Yasin Mondal does not arise at all. At the time of hearing, when it was pointed out to the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party/ plaintiffs he frankly conceded that the prayer (ক) of the plaint was a wrong prayer. There cannot be any doubt the prayer (ক) is wrong. Even according to the case of the plaintiffs, the plaintiffs cannot be considered as sole heirs of Yasin Mondal. So, they cannot get a declaration as prayed for in the plaint at prayer (ক). The learned appellate Court without properly appreciating the prayer declared that the plaintiffs acquired 16 annas share in the suit property as heirs of Yasin Mondal. It appears that the defendant No. 3 gifted her share to the plaintiffs. It is also mentioned in the plaint that the plaintiffs got the share of defendant No. 3 on the basis of a deed of gift dated 13.8.84 but in spite of such gift it cannot be said that the defendant No. 3 is not an heir of Yasin Mondal. The learned Advocate for the opposite party/plaintiff frankly admitted that the frame of the suit was defective and the prayer was also defective and so he prayed for sending back the suit on remand for fresh trial after giving an opportunity to the plaintiffs to make necessary amendments of the plaint.

<u>11. From the above, it is clear to me that both the courts below could not appreciate the question of law involved in the suit and the courts disposed of the suit and appeal under some misconception. It further appears that the plaintiffs were also under some misconception as a result of which they made a wrong prayer at prayer (ক). In this suit, the main question is, who the heirs of Yasin Mondal Admittedly are, the plaintiffs are five daughters of Yasin Mondal and defendant No. 3 is widow of Yasin Mondal. The defendant's case is that one Shariatullah died leaving behind two sons Bishu and Gopal. He further claims that Yasin Mondal is a descendant of Bishu Mondal and he is descendant of Gopal Mondal The courts below came to contradictory decision as reads the genealogy given by both sides. As this court found some defects in the frame of the suit and also found that the courts below were under some misconception while deciding the suit and the appeal, it appears to me that at this stage no decision should be given on this disputed question of genealogy by this court. It also appears to me that for ends of justice, the suit should be sent back on remand as prayed for by the learned Advocate for the opposite party/ plaintiff.</u>

<u>12. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree of both the courts below be set aside and the suit be sent back on remand to the trial Court for fresh trial in the light of the observations made in the body of the judgment. The plaintiffs may file an application for necessary amendment of the plaint and the learned trial Court be at liberty to decide the matter of amendment in accordance with law. The trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously.</u>

13. Send back the LC records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Wahab Miah, Advocate instructed by Md Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record — For the Appellant. 
Md. Ozair Farooq, Advocate instructed by Md Nowab Ali, Advocate-on-Record— For the Respondent No.1. 
Not represented—Respondent Nos. 2-8.
parties:
Danish Ali and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
Sakina Bai and others Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 27-7-1997 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Order No 2929 of 1997).
full_judgment:
Md. Abdur Rouf J: This appeal, following leave, by the plaintiffs is from the judgment and order dated 27-7-97 passed by the High Court Division, in Civil Order No 2929 of 1997 summarily disposing of an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, setting aside the order dated 6-4-97 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No 89 of 1987, directing defendant-respondent No. 1 Mrs Sakina Bai to appear in court personally at the time of hearing of the said case for her examination in court.

2. The relevant facts are that, the plaintiff-appellants on 31-12-86 got an ex parte decree in Title Suit No 203 of 1984 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka for declaration of their title to the suit property, comprising of land and buildings within Dhaka City, on adverse possession. Defendant-respondent No. 1 through her son Samsuddin Soleman as her constituted attorney instituted the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case, under Order IX rule 13 CPC, for setting aside the said ex parte decree on the ground of fraud and non-service of summons. In the said Miscellaneous Case the plaintiffs on 28-1-94 filed an application seeking for a direction upon defendant No. 1 Sakina Bai Soleman to make her personal appearance in court for her examination. It was, inter alia, stated in the petition that the alleged attorney of defendant No 1 after creating a forged amukternama had falsely instituted the case and that they have received information that the said Sakina Bai is a dead person and that she died 2/3 years back. By filing a written objection on behalf of defendant No.1 the prayer of the plaintiffs was opposed stating, inter alia, that she is very much alive and has been residing abroad at present and that her son as her legally constituted attorney has been conducting the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case.

3. Hearing both the parties the trial judge by an order dated 6-4-97 allowed the plaintiffs'' prayer for personal appearance of defendant No. 1 in court. Whereupon defendant No. 1 through her aforesaid attorney moved the High Court Division in revision as already noted. A Division Bench of the High Court Division without issuing any Rule in the matter and in the absence of the plaintiffs disposed of that revisional application by the impugned judgment and order, setting aside the order of the trial Court holding, inter alia, that the trial Judge upon taking an absolutely erroneous view on the Ward Commissioner's Certificate to be a death certificate of defendant No 1 wrongly directed her to appear in person before the court.

4. Leave was granted to consider whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the High Court Division committed an error of law in granting full relief to the defendant-respondent without issuing any Rule upon the plaintiffs and without hearing them. Secondly, whether the learned Judges of the High Court Division misunderstood and misconstrued the intent and purport of the order of the trial Court which had passed the order for personal appearance of defendant No. 1 in Court in consideration of the conflicting claims of both sides as to the existence or non-existence of Sakina Bai.

5. It appears that the plaintiffs in support of their application produced before the trial Court a certificate from a Ward Commissioner of Dhaka Municipal Corporation to the effect that no person named Sakina Bai Soleman, wife of late Soleman had ever resided in Flat No 3/B or in any other flat of Aminabad Colony situated at 56/57 Siddeswari Road, Ramna, Dhaka.

6. Mr Md Wahab Miah, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-appellants, submits that the learned Judges of the High Court Division acted illegally and arbitrarily in setting aside the impugned order of the trial Court without giving any opportunity to the plaintiffs to defend the impugned order. Mr Wahab Miah further submits that in view of the provisions of Order V rule 3, CPC the trial Court upon assigning proper reasons had passed the impugned order on contest, but the learned Judges of the High Court Division upon taking an erroneous view wrongly set aside the impugned order of the trial Court without even issuing any Rule or hearing the plaintiffs.

<u>7. The learned Advocate citing the cases of Abdul Wahhab vs Ali Ahmed, 44 DLR (AD) 55, Abu Ahmed Abdul Hafiz vs MA Haque Sariji 1983 BLD (AD) 532 and Sukumar Sen vs Gouranga Bijoy Das, BLD 1989 (AD) 162 has rightly submitted that the granting of full relief by way of disposing a revisional application summarily without issuing any Rule and behind the back of the affected opposite party is neither legal nor fair. The learned Judges of the High Court Division appear to have committed a serious error of law in passing the impugned order giving the defendant-respondent the full relief in a summary manner without giving any opportunity to the plaintiffs to place their case in support of the trial Court's order.</u>

<u>8. On consideration of the disputed question raised by both the parties the trial Court in the interest of a fair settlement of the issue whether defendant No. 1 Sakina Bai is dead or alive directed her attorney, who happens to be her son, to produce her in court for examination. The learned Judges of the High Court Division appear to have taken an erroneous view that the trial Court in passing the impugned order misconstrued the Ward Commissioner's certificate as a death certificate although nothing has been mentioned therein as to the death of Sakina Bai. Rule 3 Order V, CPC provides that where the Court sees reason to require the personal attendance either of the defendant or of the plaintiff it may so direct. The trial Court upon taking into consideration the plaintiffs' application for personal appearance of defendant No 1 and the objection raised on her behalf and the alleged certificate produced by the plaintiffs from a Ward Commissioner of City Corporation, Dhaka passed the impugned order in exercise of the authority vested in it under rule 3 Order V, CPC. As such, the learned Judges of the High Court Division are not at all justified in setting aside the said order of the trial Court. Simply because the trial Court made a wrong observation in the impugned order that the plaintiffs had submitted the ward commissioner's certificate dated 19-9-95 in support of the death of defendant No 1. The High Court Division was wrong in setting aside the impugned order of the trial Court.</u>

9. Mr. Ozair Farooq, learned Advocate appearing for respondent No. 1, also finds it difficult to support the judgment of the High Court Division.

Thus we find substance in this appeal. It is allowed without, however, any order as to cost. The impugned Judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the trial Court is restored.

End.

lawyer:
CQMH Md. Ayub vs. Bangladesh, 47 DLR (AD) 71; relied. 
Md. Serajul Islam Khan with ASM Lutful Karim, Advocates — For the Petitioners

parties:
Jahanara Begum Dead her Chowdhury Mahfuzul Islam and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Chairman, Court of Settlement and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: This Rule was issued at the instance of the petitioner calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why impugned judgment and order dated 12-4-89 (Annexure B) passed by the Court of Settlement in Case No.100 of 1988 should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. Petitioner having died her heirs was substituted on 21-1-91. One Kamruddin filed an application for being added as respondent in this Rule and by order dated 31-3-93 he was added as respondent No. 3 in this Rule. Thereafter on 14-12-95 petitioner filed an application for striking out the name of aforesaid added respondent No. 3. By order dated 14-12-95 that application of the petitioner was kept with the record to be considered at the time of hearing of the Rule. This Rule was taken up for hearing on 27-8-96. At that time learned filing Advocate did not appear and Mr. ASM Lutful Karim appeared on his behalf and was allowed to plead for the petitioner after accepting the power and on his prayer the matter was adjourned to 28-8-86 after hearing the matter in part. Yesterday learned filing Advocate filed an application praying for hearing his earlier application for striking out the name of respondent No. 3. Today he filed another application praying for expunging the order of hearing the Rule today as part heard and for deleting the name and signature of Mr. ASM Lutful Karim Advocate from record.

3. Today when the matter was called learned filing Advocate prayed for hearing his earlier application for expunging the name of respondent No. 3. We allowed him to place his earlier application for expunging the name of respondent No. 3. But the learned Advocate insisted for passing an order upon that application. Since by earlier order dated 14-12-95 that application is to be considered along with writ petition we could not agree with the submission of the learned Advocate. In the other application filed by the learned Advocate today it has been stated that on 27-8-96 he came to Court and had to go back to his residence due to his personal difficulties and engaged and requested Mr. Lutful Karim for acting for him to appear in this Court and to pray for two days adjournment and the said Advocate prayed for two days adjournment on that date and accepted the power under direction of the Court and the said Advocate not being engaged in this case by the petitioners his name and signature should be deleted and order listing the Rule as part heard should be expunged.

4. When this Rule was taken up for hearing an 27-8-96 Mr. ASM Lutful Karim prayed for adjournment of the matter after but his verbal prayer having been refused he sought time for seeking instruction from the learned filing Advocate during the recess period and requested to pass over the matter till 2-00 PM. At 2-00 PM the said learned Advocate informed the Court that he has instruction from the learned filing Advocate to accept the power and to proceed with the hearing provided Court keeps the matter part heard till 29-8-96. Accordingly the matter was heard in part and adjourned to 29-8-96. In such circumstances we find no reason to allow the prayer for expunging the order of listing the Rule today as part heard and deleting the name and signature of the said Advocate and hence the said application is rejected. It appears from the impugned judgment that the case of the petitioners before the Court of Settlement was as follows:

5. House No. 27 Banga Bandhu Avenue, Dhaka originally belonged to Sufia Musa Salejhee on the basis of decree passed in TS No.153 of 1960 in her favour on 21-6-60 and she sold the said property to respondent No. 3 Kamruddin on 15-3-63 and since then said Kamruddin was in possession of the property partly through monthly tenants partly in Khas. While in such title and possession he entered into an agreement on 28-12-70 with Abdullah Bhuiyan to sell the house to him at a consideration of Taka 1,52,000.00 and on receipt of the sum of Taka 1,20,000.00 as advance delivered part possession of the house to the said buyer and promised to deliver possession of the rest on or before registration of the kabala. The said Abdullah Bhuiyan having died during the war of liberation his father Abul Hossain Bhuiyan and mother Safurun Nessa inherited her interest. After liberation Abul Hossain Bhuiyan father of Abdullah Bhuiyan asked the respondent No. 3 to execute and register kabala in terms of the aforesaid agreement but he having refused to do so said Abul Hossain Bhuiyan and Safurun Nessa filed TS No. 211 of 1977 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge Dhaka for specific performance of contract and the suit was decreed ex parte on 3-3-78 and they got kabala executed and registered through Court in 1979. While the said Abul Hossain Bhuiyan was in part possession of the property through his employees carrying on restaurant business his employees inducted some women and others in different portions of the building as monthly tenants towards the end of 1979. These tenants formed an association named Jatiya Mohila Samity and trying to get an allotment of the building in their favour treating the house as an abandoned property. Abul Hossain Bhuiyan died an 16-1-85 and as such, he could not take steps against the trespassers and unauthorised persons before his death. Thereafter the said women managed to get an order of allotment in their favour treating the property as abandoned property. The tenanted portion was in possession of Mr. Abdul Majid Khan who died leaving sons and they started Misc. Case No. 42 of 1982. Thereafter Govt. started Misc. Case No. 50 of 1982 but the same was dismissed and subsequently revieved and other case was pending and that order of restoration was challenged in CR Case No. 72 of 1986. Heirs of Abul Hossain Bhuiyan were substituted in the Title Execution Case No. 39 of 1978 and Misc. Case No. 50 of 1982 and those cases are still pending and, as such the building cannot be treated as abandoned property and inclusion of the same in the 'Ka' list was illegal.

6. The case was contested by the Government in the Court of Settlement stating that Kamruddin was a non-local and left the house in question and went to Pakistan during the war of liberation in 1971 and his where abouts was not known when President's Order 16 of 1972 came into force on 28-2-72 and the house was rightly included in the list of abandoned houses and under the direct control of the Government through allottees : (1) Bangladesh Jatiya Women's Co-operative Societies (2) Friends Traders and (3) Gini Exchange. There was no representation to the Govt. either by the petitioners or by their predecessor-in-interest to release the holding asserting their right of possession and ownership in the house. Alleged bainapatra dated 28-12-70 was a get up and antedated document. Alleged sale an 9-7-79 was in contravention of Articles 6 and 14 of President's Order 16 of 1972 and section 6 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and, as such, void and inoperative.

7. On consideration of the materials on record Court of Settlement observed that petitioners could not show any basis of possession of the case holding and in fact, they are out of possession from the very inception of President's Order 16 of 1972. Moreover there was no iota of evidence either documentary or oral on the side of the petitioners to establish that Kamruddin was present at the time of liberation when President's Order 16 of 1972 came into force and that he was in possession of the case holding at the relevant time and the petitioners on the other hand has not proved that they possessed the same at any point of time either directly or through any tenant. So the property became abandoned and vested with the Govt. Court of Settlement further observed that petitioner's vendor Kamruddin being absent and his whereabouts having been not found the property became abandoned with effect from 28-2-72 and his absence in the proceeding of the civil Court lent support to the same. There was no evidence or justification why the suit was filed in 1977 for specific performance of contract when the alleged contract was made in 1970. So the Court of Settlement held that the property became abandoned on and from 28-2-72 and petitioners failed to establish their title, interest and possession and as such, they are not entitled to any relief as prayed for.

8. It appears from the impugned judgment as well as averments made in paragraph 17 of the Writ Petition that the petitioners did not adduce any witness in support of their case and relied on documentary evidence such as decree passed in TS No. 211 of 1977, Kabala executed in pursuance of the said decree, Misc. Case Nos. 588 and 50 of 1982 and CR Case Nos. 72 of 1984 and 805 of 1986. So the Court of Settlement decided the case on the basis of documents produced before it.

9. Grounds taken in this Rule is that petitioners are in possession of the title deeds and the kabala on the basis of agreement dated 28-12-70 and as such disputed property did not come within the purview of President's Order 16 of 1972. Court of Settlement acted illegally ignoring the decree and kabala in favour of the petitioners and others and part possession of the case property. In view of the pendency of CR No. 72 of 1984, 806 of 1986 in the High Court Division arising out of said TS No. 211 of 1977, case property could not be enlisted as an abandoned property.

10. Petitioners own case is that they filed the aforesaid TS No. 211 of 1977 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract for sale on the basis of agreement dated 28-12-70. There is no averment that in that suit petitioners challenged treating of the house as an abandoned property. Petitioners also admitted in the Writ Petition that their employees of the restaurant business inducted some women and others in different portions of the building in 1979 and they formed Jatiya Mohila Samity and were trying to get an allotment in their favour treating the house as an abandoned property. But in their application before the Court of Settlement they admitted that the said women managed to get an order, of allotment in their favour treating the house in question as abandoned.

11. From the above it is clear that according to their own version petitioners are no longer in possession of the house in question since 1979 and Jatiya Mahila Samity was in possession since 1979 in the portion of the house which they claimed were in their possession before that. But in support of their claim that they possessed part of the house upto 1979 they produced no evidence before the Court of Settlement either oral or documentary. Hence the finding of the Court of Settlement that petitioners have not proved possession of the house at any point of time either direct or through any tenant cannot be found fault with.

<u>12. As to the other ground that inclusion of the house in the 'ka' list of abandoned houses during pendency of CR No. 72 of 1984 and 806 of 1986 was illegal it appears from clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 5 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance 1985, that if a suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings is pending before any court, before the date of publication of the list in the official Gazette in which vesting in or possession of the Govt. of the building as abandoned property has been called in question in any manner, such property is to be excluded from such list. We have already noticed that petitioner filed suit only for specific performance of contract without challenging the abandoned character of the property or taking over of the same by the Govt. as abandoned property. So there was no illegality in the inclusion of the house in the 'ka' list of the abandoned houses. In the case of CQMH Md. Ayub vs. Bangladesh reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71 our above view finds support. In view of the same Court of Settlement rightly found that petitioners failed to discharge the presumption under section 5(2) of the said Ordinance.</u>

13. By order dated 31-3-93 this Court allowed the prayer of Kamruddin to be added as a respondent No.3 in this Rule. It appears from the said order that the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr. Sirajul Islam Khan refused to accept copy of the said application filed by the respondent No.3 to be added as a respondent. So the copy of the said application was sent to the said Advocate by registered post with A/D on 21-3-93. From the order of the Court of Settlement dated 5-3-88 it appears that the said Kamruddin was added as a party in that case No.100 of 1988. Thereafter petitioner filed an application for striking out the name of respondent No. 3 and the said application came up for hearing on 14-12-95 and the Court directed to keep the said application in the report to be considered at the time of hearing of the Rule. On consideration of the fact that respondent No. 3 was party before the Court of Settlement and he is a necessary party in this Rule we find no ground to strike out his name. Therefore, petitioner's application for striking out the name of respondent No. 3 is rejected.

14. In the above facts and circumstances and discussions made above we find no illegality in interfering with the impugned judgment. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. Order of stay stands vacated.

End.

lawyer:
