parties:
Jobeda Khatun ----- Petitioner
Vs.
M A Mannan and others ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree passed in Title Appeal No. 32 of 1982 by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka affirming the judgment and ex parte decree made in Title Suit No. 874 of 1979 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka.

2. The opposite party 1 instituted Title Suit No. 263 of 1976 for specific performance of contract against the petitioner and the opposite parties 2 and 3 on the allegations, inter alia, that the property described in the Schedule-'B' to the plaint belonged to him and the property described in the schedule-A' belonged to the petitioner. For exchange of their property they entered into an agreement dated June 16, 1975. According to the terms of the said agreement, the liabilities and debts of the petitioner in respect of the Schedule-A' property was to be paid by the opposite party 1 and in addition to that he was to pay Taka 5,000.00 to the petitioner and the opposite party was to obtain clearance certificate from the Income-tax Department and permission from the Ministry of Urban Development for the transfer of the properties. It was further stipulated that unless the deed is registered they will remain in possession of their restrictive property. The opposite party 1 was to complete all the formalities and to execute and register the deed of exchange within one year. The petitioner received Taka 1,000.00 on the date of agreement and Taka 5,065 only was received under a separate receipt. But as she failed to perform her part and refused to execute and register the deed of exchange although opposite party 1 was ready to perform his part of duty the suit was filed.

3. The petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement on 19.7.1976 stating that she was not aware about the ownership and possession of the opposite party of "B' schedule property and 'A' schedule property is a two-storeyed building of the value of not less than Taka 2 lakh and the value of the 'B' schedule property would not be more than Taka 30,000. As she was a pardanishin lady the opposite party 1 approached her through one Muslim and created confidence in her saying that he would give protection to her property who was married to an old Urdu-speaking man and at the time of execution of the agreement her husband was away from Dhaka and the opposite party 1 on different pretexts took the necessary papers and documents of her property and after having had received those threatened her with dire consequence if she refused to execute the deed of exchange. She alleged that under the threat held out by the opposite party 1 she had to sign the so-called agreement for exchange which was obtained under duress, coercion and undue influence. It was further alleged that neither she nor her husband understand English language and the contents of agreement were not disclosed to them and the agreement was signed without understanding the import of the same. It was further alleged that most of the attesting witnesses are the men of opposite party l. It further stated that the suit should be dismissed for non-fulfillment on the part of the opposite party 1 of his part of contract within the stipulated period in terms of the agreement.

4. The defendant 2, the Chief Manager of the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation, also filed a written statement on 12.11.1976.

5. The trial Court framed issue on the valuation of the suit and an Advocate Commissioner was appointed to investigate who submitted his report about the valuation of the property and on the basis of which the total valuation of the suit was fixed at Taka 55,000.00 and the court directed opposite party 1 to pay deficit court-fee by 30.11.1977. For non-payment of deficit court-fee on 6.6.1978 he was asked to show cause within 3 days as to why the plaint 'should not be rejected. As the opposite party 1 did not comply with the said order the plaint was rejected on 9.6.1978. The said order was followed by an application under section 151 CPC for review and to allow opposite party 1 to file the deficit court-fees unsuccessfully leading to filing of Civil Revision No. 1042 of 1978 in the High Court Division. The opposite party obtained a Rule on 17.7.1978. The petitioner herein opposed the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. But when the matter was, in the seisin of the High Court Division the plaintiff suppressing the fact about the pendency of the Rule instituted the present suit on 7.12.1979 in the court of Subordinate Judge. Dhaka for specific performance of contract in respect of the same property against the petitioner without impleading the House Building Finance Corporation valuing the suit at Taka 15,000.00.

6. It is alleged that the subsequent suit was barred by limitation under Article 113 of the Limitation Act as the cause of action arose on 16.5.1976 as disclosed in paragraphs 13 and 6 of the plaint to Title Suit No. 263 of 1976 and the Title Suit No. 874 of 1979 respectively. It was further stated that as in the subsequent suit Schedule-'A' property of the petitioner was mortgaged with the House Building Finance Corporation in a Loan Case No. HB-D-5376 of 1970 the suit suffers from defect of parties as the Corporation was not impleaded in the suit which contested the earlier suit by filing written statement. It is further alleged that the suit was instituted on 7.12.1979 and the court fixed on 20.12.1979 for service return unusually within a short period and within 3 days a fraudulent appearance of the defendant 1 was recorded on 11.12.1979 on the filing of a fictitious vakalatnama followed by an application praying for time to file written statement although the date for appearance on 20.12.1979 was fixed. On that date the plain tiff got another application filed in the' name of petitioner praying for time for 7 days to file written statement and both the application and the power are forged and fraudulent. It was further alleged that the order No. 2 to order No, 6 were not written by an official of the Court but the plaintiff got the same written in collusion which some outsiders which is against the provisions of Article 874 of the CRO(Vol-1). It is further alleged that all service returns from Civil Revision No. 1042 of 1978 down to Title Execution Case No. 24 of 1980 will show that on all occasions the plaintiff procured the services of the same process server, Fariduddin, who particularly submitted on 8.12.1979 service return of the later suit which was contrary to Order 5 rule 18 CPC and Article 70(1) of the CRO (Vol-1) as no name of any person witnessing service of summons was noted in the service return. The trial Court on 15.2.1980 passed the ex parte decree on the basis of such service or summons. It is further alleged that after obtaining the ex parte decree the opposite party 1 with evil design moved this Division on IS.4.1980 to discharge the Rule without disclosing about anything regarding institution of Title Suit No. 874 of 1979 and obtained an order of discharge on 15.,4.1980, After the discharge of the aforesaid Rule on 15.4.1980 heput the said illegal decree in execution on 2.5.1980 in Title execution Case No. 24 of 1980 behind the back of the petitioner suppressing the process and gaining over the said process server Fariduddin and ultimately got the deed of exchange registered through court without getting permission from the House Building Finance Corporation. It is further alleged that the registration of the document was null and void according to Article 21 (5) of the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Order, 1973 and after obtaining this void document the plaintiff got the writ of khas possession although in the application under Order 21 rule 11 (2) CPC he did not pray so. The petitioner in execution of the said writ was evicted from the property on 3.10.80 during the vacation of the civil Court on which date she came to know about the institution of this suit. Till 1.11.1980 the civil Court was on vacation and on that date she applied for certified copies of ex parte judgment and decree dated 15.2.1980 and 17.3.1980 respectively which were made ready on 20.1.1981 and was obtained on 16.2.1981 and on that very date the petitioner filed the Title Appeal No. 32 of 1981. The memorandum of the appeal was accompanied by an application under section S of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay in filing the appeal stating that the appellant was kept out of knowledge about the ex-pane decree due to fraud practised by the opposite party 1. The appeal was registered on 16.2.1981 and the application for condonation of delay was taken up for hearing on 18.2.1981 but the learned District Judge ordered to decide the condonation application at the time of hearing of the appeal and called for a report from the civil Court as to whether the orders of the Title Suit No. 874 of 1979 from order Nos. 2 to 6 were written by the outsider as alleged and the learned court was informed on 11.3.1981 about the same that the order-sheet was written by the outsiders. .

7. The appeal of the petitioner and the condonation. application, in filing the appeal, however, came up for hearing on 25.8.1983 but the hearing was adjourned at the instance of the opposite party 1 on several occasions and all on a sudden the court fixed 12.4.1984 for arguments and after hearing the argument of the petitioner en 16.5.1984 and again the appeal was adjourned to 21.5.1984 for hearing of the argument of the opposite party 1. The court heard him more than 3 months thereafter and before leaving the station the judgment was delivered on 30.8.1984 dismissing the appeal. It is alleged that the judgment was in contravention of the provision of Order 20, rule 1 CPC.

<u>8. Mr. MI Farooqui first, submits that as the petitioner in his petition for condonation of delay alleged fraud and forgery in obtaining ex parte decree from the very beginning of the institution of Title Suit No. 263 of 1976 for suppressing summons and for filing of a forged power the question of limitation for institution of the appeal is to run from the date of knowledge when the petitioner on 3.10.1980 was evicted through police force. He placed reliance upon Article 18 of the Limitation Act Mr. Farooqui secondly, submits that where the whole appeal was before the lower appellate Court for hearing the appeal on merit and for hearing the application for condonation the appellate Court only dismissed the appeal on the ground of limitation erroneously without deciding the appeal on merit and the judgment has led to occasioning failure of justice in that the Court by earlier order said that hearing of both the application for condonation of delay and the appeal would be taken up at a time and such order manifestly makes it clear that the appeal as a whole on merit and on the ground of limitation was to be disposed of. He submits that this has not been done here. Mr. Farooqui placing reliance upon the decision in the case of Abul Khair Mia Vs. Abdul Latif Sardar, 32 DLR (AD) 167, the case of Aftabuddin Fakir Vs. Sowdagar Rabi Das and others, 43 DLR 42, contends that where a party pleads fraud the court is required to reach a finding as to whether the fraud alleged is practised for determination of the question of limitation. On reference to the judgment I do not see such finding regarding fraud although the petitioner seriously alleged fraud practised upon the trial Court in obtaining ex parte decree and in evicting the petitioner from her house from the very filing of the power in the trial Court down to the date of eviction arid the appeal was dismissed merely holding that the appeal is barred by limitation. From the facts and the attending circumstances of the ease I am of the opinion that the court of appeal below committed illegality in dismissing the appeal merely on the ground that the appeal is barred by limitation.</u>

<u>9. Mr. Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed vigorously canvassed before me that from the very beginning of the first suit upto the satisfaction of the decree in Title Execution Case No. 24 of 1980 the petitioner had knowledge as she took steps on different dates in the suit and was posted with all the subsequent developments of the case. He referred me to the report of process server on submission of which the court fixed the date of ex parte hearing. Mr. Khandaker, however, makes an argument that when the petitioner filed the application for setting aside the decree under Order 9 rule 13 CPC she had also the opportunity to prove the same by adducing the evidence and also had opportunity to prove the alleged signature on the power. But that has not been done at the trial stage and the petitioner at the appellate stage is estopped to plead fraud for obtaining an ex parte decree by the opposite party 1. There are 3 alternative remedies provided in the Code against ex parte decree. Therefore, I am not convinced that in an appeal from an ex parte decree fraud cannot be pleaded as contended by Mr. Khandaker. I do hold that appellant in an appeal from ex parte decree which has been obtained by the plaintiff can plead fraud practised upon the court in obtaining such decree independent of filing an application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC. Mr. Khandaker further addressing on limitation from 3.10.1980 to 16.2.198I, the time when the petitioner had knowledge about the ex parte decree and the time when she filed the appeal, pointed out to me that on 1.11.1980 application for certified copies was filed which were made ready on 20.1.1981 but the petitioner took delivery of the same on 16.2.1981 and thereafter the appeal was filed out of time by 27 days. Mr. Khandaker further submits that the law enjoins upon the appellant to explain each day's delay in filing the appeal and in the present case that not having been done by the appellant the court of appeal below dismissed the suit on the ground of limitation legally. I am unable to agree with the contention of Mr. Khandaker. Till 1.11.1980 the civil Court was on vacation. The limitation shall run against the petitioner from when she came to know about the ex parte decree. The appeal was to be filed on 2.11.1980 but it was filed on 16.2.1981 on re-opening of the civil Court after long vacation. The calculation from the date of knowledge to the date of institution of the appeal taking into consideration the date on which the certified copies of the judgment and decree was prepared and delivery of the same was taken leads me to hold that the appeal was filed not only within time but before 3 days of the expiry of the period of limitation. Therefore, in my opinion, the appeal was not barred by limitation as held by the lower appellate Court without expressing its opinion on the fraud as alleged in that where fraud is pleaded the court must take into consideration the question of fraud and decide the same as the question of limitation is founded on the allegation of fraud. The court ought to have disposed of the appeal on merit after arriving at a conclusion as to whether fraud was practised in obtaining the ex parte decree or not. Where fraud is alleged to have been practised and it is so found the question of limitation will start from the date of knowledge of fraud practised.</u>

10. From what have been stated above, I set aside the judgment and decree impugned and I remit the appeal to the court of appeal below for re-hearing. As the petitioner has been thrown out of the house through police force I direct the court of appeal to commence re-hearing of the appeal within 1(one) month from arrival of the records of the courts below.

11. In the result, the rule is made absolute.

12. No order as to costs.

13. Send down the lower court records at once. Mr. M I Farooqui prays for taking back the certified copies annexed with the application under section 115(1) CPC. He is permitted to take back the certified copies after supplying the true copy of each of them. The office shall take due caution in returning the same.

End.

full_judgment:
This rule arises out of an order dated 23. 8. 67 passed by the learned Munsif, North Roazan, Chittagong rejecting an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the judgment-debtor-petitioner for restoring the Misc. Case No. 53 of 1967 filed by him under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the execution proceeding started by the decree holder opposite party.

2. Circumstances leading to this rule are as follows: Opposite party decree holder instituted other suit No. 45 of 1965 in the Court of Munsif, Roazan for specific performance of contract for sale and ultimately obtained a decree for Rs. 1000/- for money that was advanced by him with costs On 31.1.66, the opposite party decree holder also obtained a decree for Rs. 287.50 in the Court of No. 1 Haldia Union Council which he put into execution as well in other execution case No. 48 of 1967 in the aforesaid Court of the learned Munsif. Thereafter he put his decree for Rs. 1000/- obtained in other suit No. 45 of 1965, being execution case No. 8 of 1967, and attached some of the property of the petitioner-judgment debtor. Subsequently the decree holder agreed to accept Rs. 1000/- as full satisfaction of the debt in both the aforesaid two execution cases and the petitioner paid Rs. 750/- in cash to the decree holder who also granted a receipt for it, and it was settled that if the balance of the money be paid within one month then the decree holder would not proceed with the execution. A compromise to that affect was effected in presence of witnesses  The petitioner  it is alleged could not pay the balance of Rs. 250/- in time. The decree holder again proceeded with execution of both the cases for the entire decretal amount without adjusting Rs. 750/- paid by the petitioner. Thereafter the petitioner filed an application under section 47 C. P. C. alleging the aforesaid talk of compromise and the -payment of Rs. 750/- and a Misc. Case No. 53 of 1967 as stated above was started which was ultimately fixed for hearing on 24.6.67 but due to some illness the petitioner could not attend the court on that date and the case was dismissed for default. The petitioner then filed the present application on 20. 7. 67 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the said Misc. Case which was opposed by a decree holder opposite party.

3. The learned Munsif who heard this application was of the view that the petitioner could seek his remedy in the appellate court by preferring an appeal against the order of dismissal for default, but has not chosen to do so, the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not lie. He, therefore, rejected the application.

3. Mr. Haradhan Sarker, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner judgment-debtor has contended that the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity in rejecting the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that the order of dismissal for default was appealable. In this connection the learned Advocate has submitted that the definition of decree under section 2, sub-section (2) C.P.C. although includes "determination of any question under section 47" does not include "any order of dismissal for default" and, as, such, no appeal lies against the order of dismissal for default of his application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in that view of the matter, in the facts and circumstances of the case the Court should not have thrown out his application as not being maintainable but ought to have considered it on merits. In support of his argument, the learned Advocate has cited 7 D.L.R. 231 (Division Bench); 8 D.L.147 (Division Bench); A.I.R. 1961 Rajasthan 59 and I.L.R. 17 All 106 (P. C.) On the other hand, supporting the order of the learned Munsif, Mr. Abu Taher Chowdhury the learned Advocate for the opposite party has referred to A.I.R. 1930 Lah. 20; A.I.R.1937 Oudh 337 and 29 I.C. 395.

4. In 7 D.L.R. 231, Mr. Tabibar Rahman Talukder Vs Sudhir Numer Saba Chowdhury the question for determination was whether an order dismissing an objection that the value stated in the sale proclamation was too low and that it was not properly drawn up and published is open to appeal as an order under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

It was observed:

"It is not every order passed by an executing court that comes under section 47 of Code and is appealable under section 2 thereof".

5. In this ruling the following observation made by Sulaiman, J. in Muhammad Zakaria Vs. Kishan Narain (92 I.C. 644) was quoted With approval:

"Section 47 C. P. C, must be read with section 2 of the Code and the effect of reading both the sections together is not to make every order passed by the Execution Court appealable but only such orders arc appealable as determine the rights of the parties to the execution with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in suit and ultimately it was held that the order dismissing the objection did not come under section 47 C. P. C. and was not open to appeal. This ruling is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case.

5. In 8 D.L.R. 147, Benoyendra Nath Roy Choudury and others Vs. Jaday Chandra Roy Choudury, the judgment debtor appellants filed a Misc. Case under section 47 C. P. C. objecting to the executing of decree supported by respondent on the ground, inter alia, that it was barred under section 69 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and that no notice under Order 21 rule 66 C. P. C. for determination of the valuation of the mortgage property was served. The Misc. Case came up for hearing but as neither party took any step it was dismissed for default. This was restored on an application under section 151 C. P. C. and a date was fixed for peremptory hearing and on that date again the appellants did not take any step, although the decree holder was present. The Misc. case was again dismissed for default and on the same day again an application for setting aside the dismissal for default was filed which was subsequently rejected after hearing both the parties. Thereafter the appellants-judgment-debtor filed another application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the same ground as stated in the earlier application under section 47 C. P. C. which was rejected by the court against which the appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. It was observed by the Division Bench of the High Court as follows:

"It is true that Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to execution proceedings, but that will not improve the appellants position in the least. The appellants did not file any application under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the order of dismissal. They by two successive petitions under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure appealed to the executing Court to set aside the order of dismissal in the exercise of its inherent power but both the petitions were rejected. It is true that no appeal lies against an order under section 151 but the appellants were quite competent to move this Court in revision. They however, did not avail themselves of the provisions of section 115 but preferred to file a fresh application under section 47. To a superficial observer the second application may appear to be an impregnable citadel but to us it seems to be more vulnerable, the principle of constructive res-judicata being applicable to it with greater force. it is true that the order of dismissal for default had not the effect of a decree and as such was not appealable.. "

6. Although in this case the question whether an application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure dismissed for default was not at issue but from the observation quoted above it appears that their lordships were of the view that such order of dismissal for default have not the effect of a decree and as such was not appealable and lend support to the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. In A.I.R. 1961 Rajasthan 59, Jethmal & ors Vs Mst. Sakina it was observed:

"It may be that a proceeding under section 47 may under certain circumstances, be treated as a suit and vice versa but that in my opinion docs not make any vital difference to the conclusion at which I have arrived above. A proceeding under section 47 until it is converted into a suit is not a suit and continues to be an application and that being so the provision of Order IX cannot be held applicable to it even with the aid of section 141, C. P. C. As already pointed out above Section 141 has no application to proceedings in execution which, to my mind clearly includes an application under section 47 in view of the observations of the Privy Council in I.L.R. 17 All. 106 (P. C.)" (Page 62, para 13)

7. It may be mentioned that in this case no application under section 141 C. P. C. was filed for restoration but a suit under Order 21 rule 63 of the Code of Civil Procedure was filed by the wife of the judgment-debtor when the application against execution was dismissed for default In I.L.R. 17 All. J 06 same case in 22 Indian Appeal 44 (P.C.) Thakur Prasad Vs Fakirullah, it was held by their lordships or the Privy Council:

"It is not suggested that section 373 of the Civil Procedure Code would of its own force apply to execution proceedings. The suggestion is that it is applied by force of section 647 (section 41 of the present Code). But the whole of Chapter XIX of the Code, consisting or 121 sections, is devoted to the procedure in executions and it would be surprising if the framers of the Code had intended to apply another procedure, mostly unsuitable, by saying in general terms that the procedure for suit should be followed as far as applicable. Their lordships think that the proceedings spoken of in section 647 include original matters in the nature of suits such as proceedings in probates, guardianship, and so forth, and do not include executions. That is the view taken by the High Court of Calcutta, after consideration of the Allahabad decisions, in the case of Banko Bebary Gangoadbya Vs. Nil Madhab Chuttopadhya, I.L.R. 18 Calcutta 635."

8.  In A.I.R. 1930 Lah. 20, in the case of Hari Singh Vs. Balagi Mal & sons and another wherein execution case was dismissed for default was restored under section 151 C.P.C. On appeal it was upheld by the High Court on the principle that when the Court is competent to dismiss an application for execution for default, the power to restore that application must also exist In 1937 Oudh 337, (Division Bench), Ram Harakh Vs L. Manwary Lal it has been held:

"The definition of the term 'decree' given in section 2 sub-section (2) C.P.C., includes the determination of any question within section 47, but does not include any order of dismissal for default. Thus, there can be no doubt that if the judgment-debtors objections had been decided the order passed on them under section 47 would have amounted to a decree, and any subsequent application raising the same objections would have been barred by the principle of res-judicata it seems to us that when orders of dismissal for default were generally excluded from the definition of  decree the underlying intention was that such orders of dismissal were to be set aside under Order 9 rule 9 just as much in a case under section 47 as in the case of a regular Suit. The language of section 141 C.P.C. is also sufficiently wide to cover the case of the application under sect ion 47. The main reasons which have led to the exclusion of execution proceedings from the purview of section 141 are that the law as laid down In the Civil Procedure Code as well as in the Limitation Act contemplates successive applications for execution of a decree and that such applications are proceedings. In suits, Neither of these reasons is applicable to an application under section 47, Civil Procedure Code. In fact, on the contrary tile combined in act of section 2(2) and 47 is that an application under section 47, stands on the footing of a suit, and the determination of such an application is tantamount to a decree".

9. In 29 Indian Cases 395 in the case of Diljammihha Bibi Vs. Hemanta Kumar Roy and others, it has been held:

"An application for setting aside a sale under section 47 and Order XXI, rule 90 is not an application for execution. It is a miscellaneous proceeding in the nature of an original proceeding in which the auction purchaser is the principal interested party. I do not think that a proceeding of this kind IS excluded from the purview of section 141. I think, therefore, that Order IX, rule 9 is applicable to cases of this kind."

10. From the Privy Council case reported m I.L.R. 17 All. 106 (supra) it is clear that proceedings spoken of in section 141 include original matters in the nature of suits and do not include execution. Section 141 C.P.C. runs as follows:

"The procedure provided in this Code in regard to suits shall be valid, as far as it can be made applicable in all proceedings In any Court of Civil jurisdiction".

11.The corresponding section of the former Code, namely, section 647 of the Code of 1877 as it originally stood and on which their lordships of the Privy Council made the observation as stated above ran as follows :

"The procedure herein prescribed shall be followed as far as it Could be made applicable, In all proceedings In any court of civil jurisdiction other than the suits and appeals".

12. In interpreting this section different views are taken by different High Courts as to whether proceedings in execution were "'proceedings other than Sluts or appeals" to which this section could be applied. In order to save this conflict of views at rest the Legislature by Act. VI of 1892, added an explanation to the section as follows : "Explanation- This section (section 647) does not apply to applications for execution of the decree which are proceedings in suits."

13. The attention of their lords lips of Privy Council was called to that amendment introduced by Act VI of 1892 and their lordships  noted the fact that the amendment appears to have been made ill order to avoid the disturbance of practice caused by  the  Allahabad High Court, rulings and having regard to the controversies which have arisen and the difference of opinion between various High Courts their lordships "thought it right to state their opinion that the Act VI of 1892 does nothing more than express the true meaning of Civil Procedure Code."

14. After the decision of the Privy Council, it may be noted the explanation and the words other than suits and appeals" were thus rendered superfluous and unnecessary and have accordingly been omitted from the present Section, namely, 141.

<u>15. It is, therefore, evident that Order lX, rule 9 cannot be said to apply to an execution application which is dismissed for default and far less it would apply to an objection arising out of an execution application and thereafter dismissed for default. The case reported in 8 D.L.R. 147, as stated earlier, has also expressed the opinion that such order of dismissal for default had not the effect of a decree and, as such, is not appealable. Definition of decree under section 2 of sub-section (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure does not include "any order of dismissal for default". It is thus evident that there was no remedy by way of appeal left open to the judgment debtor, dismissing his application under section 47 C.P.C. for default. In these circumstances, his application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the order of dismissal for default cannot be thrown out in limine as not, maintainable and should have been considered on merits.</u>

16. The Rule is, therefore, made absolute. The order of the learned Munsif is set aside and I direct that the application under section 151 be re-heard and decided on merits. In the facts and circumstances of the case, I make no order as to costs.

Let the records of this case be sent down as early as possible and the case be heard expeditiously.

End.

Nurullah, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record — For Respondent No. 5. 
Ex Parte—Respondent. No. 1.
Not represented—Respondent Nos. 2-4 & 6-27.

VS.

case_source: (From judgment and order dated 5th April, 1995 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in FA No. 255 of 1991 (Dhaka) with Civil Revision No. 281 to 285 of 1988 respectively)
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ : Plaintiff-Appellants of Civil Appeal No. 48 of 1995 filed Other Suit No. 168 of 1985 against the defendant-respondents in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong for a declaration of title to recovery of khas possession in some part and also for confirmation of possession in the rest of the suit land. Defendant-respondent No. 1 Sreemati Shaibalini Ghosh filed SCC suits against the appellants for their eviction as tenants from the suit land originally in the First Court of Munsif, Chittagong which on transfer to the First Court of Subordinate Judge were registered as SCC Suit Nos. 13-17 of 1988.

2. Plaintiff-appellants in their suit alleged, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Amar Krishna Chowdhury and others. On 26-3-1936 they let out the suit property to one Protul Kumar Sen by a registered Bharanama for 9(nine) years at a monthly rental of Taka 8.00 ie, Taka 96.00 per year. It was, provided in the agreement that the landlords would take back the possession of the suit property after the expiry of the stipulated period of 9 years but in case of continuing possession by the tenant beyond 9 years the tenant would pay rent at the rate of Taka 20.00 per month. Subsequently one Sadananda Ghose was inducted into possession by the said Protul Kumar Sen as a bharatia and since then Sadananda Ghose had been paying rent for the suit premises to Amar Krishna Chowdhury and his co-sharers, namely, Benode Behari and others. Plaintiffs case further is that, Sadananda Ghose during his lifetime inducted plaintiff Nos. 1, 3, 4 and 5 and the predecessor of plaintiff No. 6, Parul Bala including defendant Nos. 6-21 in the suit property without the permission of the landlords Benode Behari and others as sub-tenants and that when the landlords raised objection Sadananda Ghose informed them that those persons were his own people and he had not sub-let the premises. After the death of Sadananda Ghose his heirs did not pay rent to Benode Behari and others and when the landlords intended to file suit for ejectment against the plaintiffs and others, the plaintiffs accepted Benode Behari and others as their landlords. Thereafter Benode Behari and others proposed to transfer the suit property as in schedule 1 to the plaintiffs which was subsequently purchased by them, namely, the plaintiffs, by registered kabala on 10-11-1984. Plaintiffs No. 1-7 became owners in possession of schedule 1 & 2 properties by further purchase on 2-12-84. Defendants No. 6-21 are in possession of schedule-3 as sub-tenants of Sadananda Chose. These defendants were asked to deliver possession (of schedule 3 land) who, however, denied the plaintiffs title whereupon the plaintiffs served notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, terminating the tenancy of the defendants in respect of the said premises and asking them to vacate the same. Upon these averments the plaintiffs filed the suit.

3. Defendants contested the suit by filing a written statement contending; inter alia, that PK Sen & Sons transferred the suit property to Sadananda Chose and his brothers by an agreement for sale dated 10-2-52 and possession was delivered to them. Since then they have been in possession under the name and style of PK Sen & Sons for more than 12 years adversely and to the knowledge of all. Defendants also alleged that the plaintiffs were inducted as tenants in the suit premises by Sadananda Chose during his life time and they regularly paid rent to him. Sreemati Shaibalini Chose (defendant No. 1) got the suit property from her husband Sadananda Chose on the basis of a ''Will'' which was probated in Probate Case No. 183 of 1979. When the plaintiffs refused to pay rent to her she filed the aforesaid SCC suits for their eviction upon serving notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.

4. Other Suit No. 168 of 1985 of the plaintiffs and the SCC suits of the defendant were tried analogously and the learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and decree dated 31-8-1988 dismissed the suit of the plaintiffs and decreed the SCC suits of the defendants.

5. Being aggrieved by the said decrees the plaintiff-appellants took an appeal to the High Court Division against the decree passed in Other Suit No. 168 of 1985 which was registered as FA No. 255 of 1991 (Dhaka). They filed Civil Revision Nos. 281-285 of 1988 against the decrees passed against them in the SCC suits.

6. A Division Bench of the High Court Division, which heard the First Appeal and the revision cases together, by one judgment dated 5 April 1995, which has been impugned in all these appeals respectively, dismissed the appeal and discharged the Rules in the revision cases with costs.

7. Admittedly Sadananda Chose, husband of defendant No. 1 entered into possession of the suit premises on the basis of an agreement for sale with PK Sen & Sons Ext. 1(1). The induction of PK Sen by the landlords in the suit property under a registered Bharanama (Ext. 3) in the year 1936 is also admitted. The learned Subordinate Judge, inter alia, found that the predecessor of the defendant had been possessing the suit property adversely within the knowledge of all for more than 40 years and that the plaintiffs obtained some alleged deeds of title from the original owners who had already lost their title over the suit property by such adverse possession.

8. It appears that at the hearing of the appeal in the High Court Division a preliminary point was taken on behalf of the defendant-respondents as to the maintain-ability of the plaintiffs suit itself on the ground that since the plaintiffs were admittedly inducted as tenants by Sadananda Chose and subsequently they continued as such under his wife Sreemati Shaibalini Chose, they could not maintain their suit for declaration of title without first surrendering their possession to the defendant from whose predecessor they got possession in the suit property. Reliance was placed for this proposition on Hajee Abdus Sattar vs. Mahiuddin & ors 38 DLR (AD) 97.

9. The High Court Division agreed with the said contention of the defendant-respondents that the suit was not maintainable and therefore refused to enter into the question of merit of the case on the basis of which the plaintiff's suit was dismissed and the SCC suits were decreed by the trial Court with costs.

10. It was argued on behalf of the plaintiff-appellants in the High Court Division that the aforesaid decision 38 DLR (AD) 97 has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case as that was a decision in an SCC suit, whereas the present suit by the plaintiffs was one for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession (in 3rd Schedule) and the defendant's SCC suits for eviction of the plaintiffs were tried along with the title suit as a matter of convenience and therefore a decision on the merit as to the plaintiff's title cannot be deferred until surrendering possession as in the cited case. It was also argued that the plaintiffs had purchased paramount title in the suit property from the original landlords and Sadananda Ghose had not acquired or could not acquire any valid title to the property either through Ext. 3 or Ext.1 (1).

11. The High Court Division observed that the principle laid down in Hajee Abdus Sattar's case applied more in the present case because PW 1 who deposed for the plaintiffs admitted that they were inducted into possession by Sadananda Ghose after the liberation of Bangladesh and they paid rent to Shaibalini Ghose after the death of Sadananda till August, 1984 and got receipts. The High Court Division also observed that the plaintiffs had filed their title suit after the filing of at least three SCC suits by Shaibalini Chose denying her title and claiming their own title in the suit land therefore "we hold that in view of the decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 97 the plaintiffs cannot maintain their suit as it appears to us that this is simply a counter-blast to the proceedings initiated by Shaibalini Ghose against the admitted tenants."

12. As to the SCC suits the High Court Division found that the defendants of those suits (appellants in these appeals) were defaulters in making payment of rents and, as such, they were liable to be evicted from the premises as mentioned in those suits.

13. At the hearing of the leave petitions, Mr. SR Pal, learned Advocate for the appellants, submitted that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the suit was not maintainable on the principle of 38 DLR (AD) 97 because in this case the learned Subordinate Judge was considering not only the SCC suits of the defendant but also the title suit of the plaintiffs and the main point that arose on the pleadings of the parties for decision was whether the contesting defendants had acquired title to the suit land by adverse possession and, as such, no question of surrendering/quitting the premises by the plaintiffs arose.

<u>14. At the hearing of the appeals, however, Mr. Pal shifted the thrust of his submission and made an attractive argument on the basis of the pleading of the plaintiff-appellants raising a mixed question of law and fact which was neither raised nor considered at any stage heretofore. The argument is that the plaintiffs while in possession of the suit land were threatened with eviction through Court by the landlord Benode Behari Chowdhury and others and the plaintiffs attorned to them and thus they suffered, what is called eviction by title paramount and, as such, the relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiffs and the heirs of Sadanada Ghose ceased. The question of surrender before seeking declaration of title therefore does not arise. Mr Pal argued that the Chowdhurys, the original landlords, remained the paramount title-holders because both PK Son and Sadananda Ghosh were lessees in relation to the original landlords. For the purpose of invoking the principle of eviction by title paramount one has to prove that he has been evicted by a third person and that the third person has a paramount title, superior to the title of his alleged lessor. It is not necessary that the person claiming paramount title must in fact evict the person occupying the premises but a threat of eviction only is sufficient to constitute such eviction in the eye of law if the person sought to be evicted attorn to the claimant because the claimant gets in to possession through the lessee who becomes his tenant. Mr. Pal referred to Hallsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition, Volume 23, paragraph 1213 and the case of Amritalal vs. Uttam Lal, AIR 1939 Calcutta 216 for illustrating the principle of eviction and title paramount. It is true that in the eye of law actual eviction is not necessary and a mere threat of eviction is sufficient to constitute eviction by title paramount if the person sought to be evicted attorn to the claimant of paramount title.</u>

<u>15. The question for consideration in this case is whether the plaintiffs have been able to prove that they suffered eviction in the lands of the paramount title-holders, namely, Benode Behari Chowdhury and others as pleaded by them in paragraph 4 of their plaint. It has already been noticed that this plea of eviction by title paramount was argued neither in the trial Court nor in the High Court Division. We have gone through the evidence of PWs 1-5 and found absolutely nothing therein to support the plaintiff's case in the plaint that the original landlords had threatened to evict them from the suit land whereupon they attorned to the said landlords or paid rent to them except that they purchased the suit land when the landlords being in need of money offered to sell it to the plaintiffs. There being no evidence at all in support of the plaintiffs case of attornment to the original landlords the principle of eviction under title paramount which has been sought to be invoked by Mr Pal, although appeared to be attractive, cannot be applied or taken advantage of in the facts and circumstances of the present case. On the other hand, the High Court Division found that it is admitted by the plaintiffs that they were inducted into the suit land by Sadananda Ghosh and they paid rent to him and after his death paid rent to Shaibalini Chose, his wife, until August 1984. The High Court Division has rightly found that the plaintiffs cannot dispute the title of Sadananda Ghosh and his heirs under section 116 of the Evidence Act and in order to claim title to themselves they must surrender the possession of the suit premises in terms of the decision in the case of Haji Abdus Sattar referred to above.</u>

16. Mr. Pal made no other submission. In view of the discussion made above we find no way but to dismiss these appeals.

In the result, therefore, the appeals are dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated July 23, 1999 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2118 of 1993)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This appeal by the plaintiff by leave is against the judgment and order dated July 23, 1999 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2118 of 1993 making the Rule absolute upon reversing the judgment and decree dated October 28, 1992 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Pirojpur, in Title Appeal No. 106 of 1986 decreeing the suit upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated August 31, 1986 of the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Bhandaria Upazila, Pirojpur, in Title Suit No. 29 of 1985 dismissing the suit wherein declaration was sought to the effect that the order dated February 5, 1985 of the Land Appeal Board in Appeal Case No. 98 of 1984 was illegal, void and not binding on the plaintiff.

2. Facts in the background of which the suit was filed, in short, are that Kamini Sundari Devi as owner of the land in suit on receiving Taka 700 out of total consideration of Taka 1,000 executed a bainapatra on 16th Magh, 1376 BS in favour of the plaintiff that on the date of execution of the bainapatra Kamini Sundari Devi delivered possession of the land to the plaintiff; that subsequent to the agreement for sale with the plaintiff Kamini Sundari Devi sold the land to defendant No. 1 by a Kabala dated March 12, 1970. The plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 161 of 1970 seeking specific performance of contract for sale of land against Kamini Sundari Devi and others. The said suit was decreed in terms of compromise effected between the parties and the defendant No. 1 (of the instant suit) upon receiving Taka 1,500 executed and registered a kabala on July 28, 1972 in favour of the plaintiff and made over possession to him. Later on the defendant No. 1 by forging signature of the scribe created an Ekrarnama showing the plaintiff as the first party and the defendant No. 1 as the 2nd party and on the basis thereof filed Miscellaneous Case No. 262 of 1982 under section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, in the Office of the Upazila Revenue Officer. Bhandaria and that upon suppressing the notice of the said Miscellaneous Case and creating evidence as regard appearance of the plaintiff in the said Miscellaneous case obtained an order on 21-10-1982 for conveyance of the land in suit. The plaintiff having had come to know about the said order of the Upazila Revenue Officer filed an application on January 2, 1983 in the Office of the Upazila Revenue Officer and thereupon the Upazila Revenue Officer directed the plaintiff  to file appeal against his order in the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Pirojpur and the plaintiff filed an appeal, being No. 91 of 1982, in the Office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, (ADC) (Revenue), Pirojpur and the same was dismissed by the ADC. Then the plaintiff filed appeal No. 279 of 1983 in the office of the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Khulna, who allowed the appeal upon setting aside the order of the ADC and the Upazila Revenue Officer. The defendant No. 1 then filed appeal No. 98 of 1984 before the Board of Land Administration and the Board set aside the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Khulna and restored the order of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Pirojpur and the Upazila Revenue Officer, Bhandaria, Pirojpur.

3. The plaintiff filed the suit contending primarily that at no point of time between him and the defendant No. 1 there was any agreement for reconveyance of the land and that he never executed any Ekrarnama to that effect in favour of defendant No. 1 and that scribe of the plaintiff's kabala, whereby defendant No. 1 in the light of the compromise decree in Suit No. 161 of 1970 transferred the land to the plaintiff, had never wrote the Ekrarnama, as claimed by the defendant No. 1, between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 for reconveyance of the land which was the subject matter of hereinabove mentioned Title Suit.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 1 stating, inter alia, that plaintiff executed Ekrarnama to re-convey the land and that Land Appeal Board is quite competent to make order of redemption and that Civil Court has no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the Land Administration Board.

5. The trial Court on the basis of the materials on record dismissed the suit on the finding that the Ekrarnama is a genuine document and that the suit so filed is not maintainable as in the light of the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (as amended by the President's Order Nos. 88 of 1972, 132 of 1972 and 24 of 1973) the Land Administration Board is competent to pass the order challenged in the suit.

6. The plaintiff went on appeal before the court of District Judge, Pirojpur. The appellate Court allowed the appeal and upon setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court decreed the suit on the findings that although the Ekrarnama is a genuine document yet, as the Ekrarnama is not a registered one, as such, on the basis of the same defendant No. 1 under the law cannot go for enforcement of the right of redemption and, as such, the order passed by the Land Administration Board was not legal. The defendant No. 1 as against the judgment and decree of the appellate Court moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained Rule in the aforementioned Civil Revision. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute upon observing that the question of genuineness of the Ekrarnama is a question of fact and that appellate Court having had found the Ekrarnama as genuine committed error in setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and thereupon decreeing the suit when the order of the Land Administration Board has not been found malafide, that an agreement for re-conveyance is not required to be registered and, as such, appellate Court was in error in setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

7. Leave was granted to consider the contention of the appellant that finding of the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Khulna Division as regard the Ekrarnama and the finding of the Civil Court as to the Ekrarnama being not uniform rather contradictory the High Court Division was in error in affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court as to the genuineness of the Ekrarnama without taking into consideration the fact that Ekrarnama was not examined by a Hand Writing Expert and that trial Court arrived at the finding as to the genuineness of the Ekrarnama without paying any heed to the caution given by the superior Court regarding giving decision on the genuineness of a document by making comparison of signatures upon resorting to the provision of section 73 of the Evidence Act, that defendant No. 1 executed and registered the kabala on July 28, 1972 in favour of the plaintiff-appellant on the basis of compromise decree in Title Suit No. 161 of 1970, but the learned Judge of the High Court Division wrongly reversed the judgment of the lower appellate Court without ascertaining the terms of the said compromise decree which was most vital evidence to ascertain the genuineness or otherwise of the Ekrarnama that High Court Division was wrong in setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court on the ground of concurrent findings of the courts below ignoring material evidence on record, particularly the evidence of the scribe of kabala dated July 28, 1972 who categorically denied the assertion of writing of the Ekrarnama by his assistant and that he also denied his signature appearing in the Ekrarnama.

8. The question for consideration in the appeal is how far in the background of the case of the respective parties and the evidence led from the side of the plaintiff, particularly the evidence of PW 2 scribe of the deed by which defendant No. 1 in the light of the compromise decree in the Title Suit No. 161 of 1970 transferred the land in the instant suit to the plaintiff, the courts were correct on comparison of the signature of the plaintiff in arriving at the finding as to the genuineness of the Ekrarnama on the basis whereof the defendant No. 1 went to the office of Upazila Revenue Officer for redemption of the land which he transferred to the plaintiff in the light of and in terms of the decree in the suit for specific performance of contract for sale of the land against the defendant respondent No.1 and another and was allowed by the Upazila Revenue Officer and that affirmed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Revenue, Perojpur but set aside by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Khulna and ultimately, the Land Administration Board set aside the order of the Additional Divisional Commissioner and thereupon restored the order of the Additional. Deputy Commissioner, Revenue and the Upazila Revenue Officer.

9. The plaintiff has filed the suit seeking declaration that the order of the Land Administration Board was illegal and void. The trial Court as well as appellate Court upon resorting to the provision of section 73 of the Evidence Act compared the signature of the plaintiff appearing in the Ekrarnama and held that the Ekrarnama was genuine although, PW 2 whose signature appeared in the ekrarnama denied the same.

10. The learned Counsel for the appellant has submitted that in view of the evidence of PW 2 categorically denying his signature in the Ekrarnama the courts is trial Court and the appellate Court, were in serious error in holding the Ekrarnama as genuine in disregard of the view of the superior courts as to making of decision in a situation, as in the instant case, as regard the genuineness or otherwise of a document upon resorting to the provision of section 73 of the Evidence Act. In this connection the learned Counsel for the appellant has referred to the case of Kessarbai vs Jethabhai Jivan reported in AIR 1928 PC 277 wherein it has been held " it is unsatisfactory and dangerous in any event to stake a decision in such a case as this on the correct determination of the genuineness of a signature by mere comparison with admitted signatures, especially without the aid in evidence of microscopic enlargements or any expert advice." In the aforesaid case in the background of contention as to genuineness of endorsement and writing in some documents the appellate Court to arrive at the decision in respect of the subject matter of the suit made comparison of the endorsement and writing in the contentious documents with the admitted writing and signature of the parties to the document and arrived at the finding as to the genuineness of the document and in the said state of the matter the Privy Council had held so. From the Bar the case of Pratik Bandhu Roy and others vs Alok Bandhu Roy and others reported in 49 DLR 241, has also been referred and in the said case the High Court Division has held that rejection of a document on comparison of signature by naked eye without an opinion of expert is not a correct approach in making decision as to genuineness or otherwise of the said document. The learned Counsel for the appellant has placed the evidence of PW 2 whose signature appears in the Ekrarnama, and he has denied the said signature as of not his and that also denied suggestion that he wrote the Ekrarnama and that stated said Ekrarnama was also not written by his assistant. It was the specific case of the defendant that PW 2, scribe of the deed by which defendant transferred the land to the plaintiff got the Ekrarnama written by his assistant and thereafter put his signature in the Ekrarnama as the scribe. In the background of the facts of the case the probability of execution of the Ekrarnama by the plaintiff appears to be something queer. In the state of the matter as are in the instant suit and in the background of the case of the respective parties as well as the evidence on record, particularly the evidence of PW 2, High Court Division was in error in setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. The High Court Division, the appellate Court and the trial Court upon resorting to an 'unsatisfactory and dangerous' procedure erred in staking their decision upon forming opinion as to the genuineness of the Ekrarnama.

11. The learned Counsel for the respondent has submitted that High Court Division was quite correct in setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court since the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court concurrently held the Ekrarnama as genuine. It was also submitted from respondent's side since no declaration has been sought as to title and that as no relief has been sought as regard the Ekrarnama the suit so framed is not maintainable.

<u>12. It has already been observed by us that the trial Court as well as the appellate Court upon resorting to 'unsatisfactory and dangerous' mode or procedure staked their decision as to the genuineness of the Ekrarnama. In the background of the facts of the case and the evidence on record said aspect of the case was not noticed by the High Court Division and consequent thereupon was in error in setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. The other contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent that no relief was sought seeking declaration of title and that against the Ekrarnama is not well founded in law since the suit has been filed against the order by which plaintiff's title to the land in suit was clouded and that no specific relief the plaintiff was required to seek against the Ekrarnama since the decree sought for against the order of the Land Administration Board would remove the cloud created by the order impugned and thereupon the Ekrarnama relating to plaintiffs land would have no bearing upon the land of the plaintiff.</u>

<u>13. Resorting to the 'unsatisfactory and dangerous' mode of comparison of the contentious signature or writing with the admitted writing or signature and thereby arriving at the 'notional view', 'seems to be', 'appears to be', may be assumed to' or 'perceiving' or 'guessing probability' of being similar to the admitted writing or signature without the aid in evidence of microscopic enlargement and any expert advice and then stacking judgment thereon is not only risky but unsafe too and consequent thereupon there is serious chancy of error in the final decision. So, to avoid the risk of falling into error as to genuineness of writing, signature etc. upon resorting to 'unsatisfactory and dangerous' mode or procedure of examining the contentious signature, writing, etc by the Court through comparison the best course, in our opinion, is to avoid said 'unsatisfactory and dangerous' procedure and the desired course should be to go for microscopic enlargement and expert advice since the science of examination of signature, writing, etc for determination of similarity through microscopic enlargement has advanced enough and has reached to the stage of accuracy and certainty as well as expertise skill is also available.</u>

14. In case of contentious writing, signature, etc, though provision of section 73 of Evidence Act permits the court to compare the contentious signature with the admitted signature, the safe and best course, in our view, for the court would be to avoid the practice of comparing the writing or signature, etc and should not stake its judgment on the opinion formed or view taken upon resorting to risky or, in other words, 'unsatisfactory and dangerous' procedure.

15. In the background of the discussions made here over we find substance in this appeal and the appeal is allowed.

16. The judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and the judgment and decree of the appellate Court is restored.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated May 23, 2001 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3381 of 1997)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This petition for leave to appeal by the plaintiff-petitioners in against the judgments and order dated May 23, 2001 of a single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3381 of 1997 discharging the Rule which was obtained against the judgment and decree dated May 29, 1997, of the 2nd Court of Additional District Judge, Barisal in Title Appeal No. 289 of 1990 (heard along with Title Appeal No. 156 of 1996) reversing the judgment and decree dated September 30, 1990 of the 1st Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Barisal in Title Suit No. 103 of 1990 (previously numbered 390 of 1982) decreeing the suit against defendant Nos. 1, 2, 4, 14 and 15 on compromise and against the defendant Nos. 17 and 18 on contest. The suit was for Specific Performance of Contract for sale of land.

2. In respect of the same land, that is, land that was the subject matter of Title Suit No. 103 of 1990 another suit being Title Suit No. 253 of 1990 seeking specific performance of contract for sale of land was filed by the defendant No. 17 of Title Suit No. 103 of 1990. In this suit i.e. in Title Suit No. 253 of 1990, plaintiff of Title Suit No. 103 was the defendant No. 17. The Title Suit No. 253 of 1990 was heard by the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Barisal and the same was decreed on 24-7-1996.

3. As against the decree in Title Suit No. 103 of 1990 defendant of the said suit i.e. plaintiff of Title Suit No. 253 of 1990, filed the appeal before the Court of District Judge, Barisal being Title Appeal No. 289 of 1990.

4. The defendant No. 17 of Title Suit No. 253 of 1990 filed appeal, being Title Appeal No. 156 of 1996 against the judgment and decree in the said suit.

5. Title Suit No. 103 of 1990 was filed stating, inter alia, that 0.55 acre of land belonged to Amir Ali Khan and he entered into an agreement for sale with the plaintiff on May 16, 1970 for a consideration of Taka 7,001. The seller on execution of an agreement for sale received Taka 5,001 and that before execution of the kabala seller Amir Ali Khan died. The heirs of Amir Ali Khan claimed balance of the consideration money and that plaintiff paid Taka 1,000 on March 1, 1983 and that in spite of repeated request the heirs of Amir Ali Khan (defendant Nos. 1-15), as did not execute kabala, the plaintiff was constrained to file the suit.

6. The suit was contested by defendant No. 17 (plaintiff in Title Suit No. 253 of 1990). The case of this defendant was that land in question belonged to Jitendra Nath and Anisuzzaman and that their land having been put to auction in a certificate case he purchased the same and took delivery of possession and that later on he sold 18 decimals of land to the defendant Nos. 18 and 19 and they are in possession of the said land by constructing but and digging pond. The defendant No. 18 filed written statement supporting the case of defendant No. 17.

7. Case of the plaintiffs in Title Suit No. 253 of 1990, suit for Specific Performance of Contract as well as for a decree for perpetual injunction, is that Amir Ali Khan entered into an agreement for sale of the land in suit with the plaintiffs on August 16, 1978 for a consideration of Taka 8,000 and received an amount of Taka 1,000 as earnest money. Amir Ali Khan died in the month of February, 1979 leaving heirs who are defendants in the suit. It is the case of the plaintiffs that they requested the heirs of Amir Ali Khan to execute the deed on receiving the balance of consideration money but they refused. It is also the case of the plaintiff No. 1 that he has sold 18 decimals of land to the plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3. Plaintiff No. 1 claimed the land on the basis of auction purchase.

8. The suit was contested by the defendant No. 17 (plaintiff of Title Suit No. 103 of 1990) by filing written statement making averments which were made in support of the relief claimed in Title Suit No. 103 of 1990.

9. The Title Appeals i.e. Title Appeal No. 289 of 1990 and Title Appeal No. 156 of 1996, were heard together and the Appellate Court allowed Title Appeal No. 289 of 1990 and consequent thereupon set aside the judgment and decree of the 1st Court of Additional Assistant Judge, Barisal in Title Suit No. 103 of 1990 and dismissed the suit. By the same judgment i.e. judgment and decree dated May 29, 1997, the appellate Court allowed the Title Appeal No. 156 of 1996 and consequent thereupon set aside the judgment and decree of the court of Senior Assistant Judge in Title Suit No. 253 of 1990 dismissing the suit as against the defendant No. 17 i.e. plaintiff of Title Suit No. 103 of 1990.

10. As against the judgment and decree of the 2nd Court of Additional District Judge in the aforesaid 2 appeals the plaintiff of the respective suit filed Civil Revision Nos. 3381 of 1997 and 2649 of 1998 respectively.

11. The appellate Court dismissed the Title Suit No. 103 of 1990 on the finding that plaintiff failed to establish his case of entering into an agreement with Amir All Khan for purchase of the land in suit and that also failed to establish that the said bainapatra was burned. The appellate Court in Appeal No. 289 of 1990 arrived at the finding that the money receipt and the solenama were created collusively.

12. As regards the subject matter of Title Suit No. 253 of 1990 the appellate Court on scrutiny of the evidence arrived at the finding that the plaintiffs of the said suit failed to prove the agreement for sale and thereupon allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. The High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record arrived at the finding that the appellate Court in dismissing the suit upon reversing the judgment and decree of the Courts of first instance committed no illegality.

<u>13. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division was in error in concurring with the finding arrived at by the court of appeal below that plaintiff of Title Suit No. 103 of 1990 failed to establish his case of entering into an agreement for sale of the land by Amir Ali Khan and that in concurring with the finding that the solenama and the money receipt were the product of collusion of the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 of the said suit. This submission of the learned Counsel merits no consideration since he failed to point out that the finding arrived at as to the case of the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 103 of 1990 relating to agreement for sale said to have been entered into by Amir Ali Khan is not based on evidence or that has been made on misleading or non consideration of the evidence and other materials on record.</u>

14. Since no infirmity of any kind in the judgment of the High Court Division has been pointed out, we find no substance in the petition.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Asrarul Ilossain with Syed Sakhwat Ali ------ For petitioner. 
Shafique Ahmed with A.F.M. Mesbahuddin ------ For the opposite party.
parties:
Sonali Bank  ------ Petitioner
VS.
Mahbubul Amin & others  ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J : In this Rule the defendant judgment-debtor has challenged order Nos. 9 and 10 dated 3.6.87 and 17.6.87 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No. 1, Dhaka in Money Execution Case No. 791 of 1986. 

2. The plaintiff/decree-holder filed a Money Suit against the defendant Bank and others for recovery of an amount of Tk. 97,750/-. The suit was decreed in the following terms: 

"That the suit be decreed on contest against the defendants 1-3 with costs and ex-parte against the rest without costs. The plaintiff do get Tk. 97,750/- with interest @ 15% per annum till realisation." 

3. The petitioner filed an application in the said Money Suit stating that the plaintiff has not filed any Execution Case against the defendants but the defendants pray for directing the Court to deposit Taka 1,07,095/- through challan for satisfaction of the decree. The trial Court by Order No. 64 dated 13.11.86 allowed the prayer and directed the judgment-debtor to deposit the amount through challan and the defendant petitioner deposited the amount on 15.11.86 by challan No. 6241. By Order No. 66 dated 23.12.86 the Court permitted the plaintiff to draw the amount and the money was withdrawn by the plaintiff. Thereafter the decree-holder filed the Execution case for recovery of Tk. 76,361.25 as interest @ 15% for the period from the institution of the suit till realisation. 

4. Main contention of the petitioner is that reading of the decree shows that the interest is to be paid from the date of decree and not from the date of institution of the suit and hence the trial Court acted wrongly in proceeding with Execution Case. The impugned orders show that the Execution Court is-sued order of attachment in pursuance of the decree and refused to stay the execution of the decree as prayed for by the petitioner. 

5. A counter affidavit has been filed by the opposite party No. 1 stating that the plaintiff filed the suit and prayed for a decree of an ascertained amount of sum namely 97,750/- against the defendant Bank along with cost and interest pendente life till realisation of the decrial amount @ 15% per annum. Ac-cording to the opposite party the Court has decreed the suit in terms of the prayer and as such the petitioner has wrongly calculated the interest from the date of the decree which in fact will be calculated from the date of the filing of the suit till realisation. In the counter affidavit it has also been stated that the defendant No. 1 Bank has already deposited the balance amount of interest of Tk. 76,361.25 paisa from the date of filing of the suit vide pay order No. 505373 dated 5.7.87 and the said amount is lying be-fore the Executing Court. It has also been stated that there is no certificate of full satisfaction of the decree by the Executing Court. 

6. The short point involved in this Rule is whether the interest as awarded by the trial Court is to be calculated from the date of decree or from the date of institution of the suit.

7. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner firstly submits that as per section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure no interest has been specifically granted from the date of filing of suit and as such execution of the interest pending litigation is illegal. Secondly, he argues that a certificate of satisfaction of the decree having been granted, the execution case is liable to be dismissed and the same cannot be re-opened and proceeded in law. 

8. Mr. Shafique Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite party No. I submits that the decree has been passed in the present case as per the relief claimed from the date of filing of the suit till realisation and there being no ambiguity in the decree as such the learned Advocate for the petitioner wrongly interpreted that the interest has been refused from the date of filing of the suit. 

9. A reference to section 34 C.P.C. shows that it is the discretion of the Court to grant interest and the Court may grant 3 kinds of interest istly court cant grant interest from the date of the suit to the date of the decree. The award of interest under this section after the date of filling of the suit is entirely a matter of discretion of Court. This purely is a matter of statutory power. In a decree for the payment of money, the Court may pass an order of interest at such rate as the Court deems reasonable to be paid on the principal sum adjudged, from the date of the suit to the date of the decree. In the present case the relief that was sought for, is one of interest pendente the till realisation of the decretal amount @ 15% per annum. The trial court decreed the suit awarding the interest @ 15% per annum till realisation. Normally in such suit when the claim is pending litigation the court al-lows such interest unless of course on the contrary a very sufficient cause for not awarding interest is made out. Mr. Hossain's main contention is that the decree has not specifically mentioned that the interest is to be paid from the date of the filing of suit and that is why it should be read as awarded from the date of the decree. This is not a case where the decree is totally silent with regard to the interest but interest has been awarded in the suit with 15% per annum till realisation. Thus it is difficult for us to hold that the interest has been refused from the date of filing of the suit. The other two kinds of interest which the Court may grant in a case under section 34 C.P.C. are interest for the period prior to the institution of the suit. This is, of course, a matter of substantive law and is outside the purview of the section and next the Court can award interest for the period after passing of the decree till the payment of sum due. Section 34(2) of the Code of course speaks of further interest on such aggregate sum from the date of decree, to the date of payment or other earlier date. Thus it appears to us that as regards interest from the date of the suit however the position is different and the matter is covered by Section 34 Which gives complete discretion to the court to sward pendente lite interest. In the present case the trial court had adjudged the principal sum and has ordered for payment of interest 15% per annum till realisation. Mr. Hossain has submitted four decisions for our consideration. Firstly, he cited a case reported in 1940 (Madras), 29. That was a case, where decree is silent with respect to the payment of further interest from the date of the decree to the date of payment and the decree follows the Judgment, the Court must be deemed to have refused it. 

In that reported decision nothing was stated in the Judgment with regard to the payment of further interest after the date of the decree. That was a case under Sub-Section (2) of Section 34. In that decision it was observed like this: 

"Section 34(I) provides that where and in so far as a decree is for the payment of money the Court may, award further interest, but sub-sec. (2) expressly states that where a decree is silent with respect to the payment of further interest from the date of the decree to the date of payment or other earlier date, the Court shall be deemed to have refused such interest, and a separate suit therefore shall not lie." 

Thus this case is not of much help in the present case. A.I.R. 1937 (Madras) 511 is a case where "Once a decree-holder has admitted payment by Judgment-debtor he cannot be allowed to execute his decree for same amount over again." 

The reported decision is case of constructive res Judicata. A.I.R. 1931 (Madras) 650 is a case where it has been held that the Executing Court can-not allow interest when decree is silent as to interest. 

10. Thus this case is also not of any help to us in deciding the present case. Another case cited is 3 B.C.R. 1983 (HCD) 339. That was a case with regard to payment of further interest-on the aggregate sum from the date of decree to the date of payment and in that reported decision the decree being silent, Court held that interest is deemed to have been refused. Thus the four decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner are not very relevant in the facts of the present case. 

11. The learned Advocate for the Opposite Party also cited the case of M/S. M.M. Ispahani Vs. Sonali Bank and Ors. reported in 1985 D.L.R. (A.D.)l. The learned Advocate submits that in that reported decision a decree was passed in the following terms a decree for Tk. 6,31,10,307.13 with interest thereon at the rate of 12% per annum till realisation." The learned Judges of the Appellate Division at paragraph 8 observed as follows: 

"As to the rate of interest from the date of the filing of the suit to the date of judgment, the High Court Division held that as the award of interest fell within the discretion of the Court which was duly exercised by it, no interference was called for. The order of interest at the rate of 12% during the pendency of the suit and until realisation did not suffer from any illegality." 

12. In that reported decision their Lordships of the Appellate Division on a different consideration reduced the quantum of interest. In the present case' interest having been awarded there is fie) scope for holding that the interest has been refused from the filing of the suit. 
	
13. From Order No. 1 it appears that the execution case was started on 23.12.86. Before starting of the execution case the defendant filed an application on 13.11.86 before the trial Court in the money suit for putting the detrital amount suo moto as per decree on his own calculation. So in reality the execution case has not started as per provision of Order 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure and before starting of the execution case the money was deposited. Thus factually it cannot be said that the executing Court has granted the certificate of satisfaction in the execution case at all. In the present case the judgment was passed on 26.8.86 and the decree was drawn on 4.9.86 and the petitioner filed an application on 13.11.86 for deposit of money in the suit itself according to his own calculation. Thus both the points of the learned Advocate for the petitioner fail. 

14. In the result, this Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The stay order granted by this Court staying the Execution Case No. 791 of 1986 is vacated. The Execution Case will proceed in accordance with law. 

15. The records be sent down at once. 

End.
