case_source: (From the judgment and order dated May 17, 1994 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No.8035 of 1991).
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: This is a plaintiffs appeal by leave and arises out of judgment and order dated 17 May, 1994 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division discharging the Rule in Civil Revision No. 8035 of 1991.

2. The plaintiffs instituted OC Suit No. 116 of 1985 in the court of the Subordinate Judge, Jamalpur for a declaration that the decree dated 9-1-84 passed in OC suit No.271 of 1982 of the said court was fraudulent, void inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The first defendant (respondent No. 1) filed written statement and on 27-7-89 which was fixed for peremptory hearing prayed for an adjournment which was rejected. The learned Subordinate Judge then passed an ex parte decree on the same date ie 27-7-89, the relevant portion of which reads as follows: "

“জামালপুর সাব জজ আাদালতের ২৭১/৮২ অন্য প্রকার মোকদ্দমার ইং ৯/১/৮৪ তারিখের ডিক্রি রদ রহিত ও বাদীর উপর প্রযোজ্য নয় ঘোষিত হয়।

স্বা/-কৃষ্ণ দেবনাথ।

3. The defendants went on appeal, OC Appeal No. 63 of 1989 and the learned District Judge, Jamalpur heard the same.

4. The learned District Judge observed in his judgment that the plaintiffs did not pray for setting aside the decree in OC Suit No. 271 of 1982 in which they were not parties to the suit. But the learned Subordinate Judge passed a decree setting aside the aforesaid decree, although no ad valorem court fee was paid for by the plaintiffs either. The learned District Judge further observed that there was a distinction between a declaratory decree and a decree setting aside certain document, in the former case a fixed court-fee is payable on the plaint and in the latter ad-valorem Court-fee is required to be paid by the plaintiff, and that the learned Subordinate Judge was not clear in her conception as to the said distinction. So saying the judgment and decree of the trial Court were set aside "being conceptually erroneous and wrong" and the appeal was allowed by judgment and decree dated 25-4-91.

5. The plaintiffs took a revision to the High Court Division as aforesaid against the appellate judgment and decree and, as already noticed the Rule was discharged by the impugned judgment and order upholding the view taken by the learned District Judge in appeal.

6. Leave was granted to consider whether the aforesaid view was legal and proper and the suit was liable to be dismissed as a whole.

<u>7. Admittedly the plaintiffs were not parties to OC Suit No. 271 of 1982 and the decree passed in that suit was impugned by them in their suit, OC Suit No. 116 of 1985, praying for a decree that the ex parte decree dated 9-1-84 passed in OC Suit No. 271 of 1982 was fraudulent, void, inoperative and not binding upon them. It appears from the decree as quoted above that the learned Subordinate Judge passed a decree declaring that the impugned decree was not binding upon the plaintiffs as prayed for and further set aside the impugned decree. The learned District Judge and the learned Judge of the High Court Division took the view that the decree could not be set aside because the plaintiffs neither prayed for the same nor paid ad-valorem court-fee as required for the relief under the law.</u>

8. It has not been found either by the learned District Judge or the High Court Division that there was any illegality in the decree being passed in the ex parte manner but the decree itself was objected to on the ground that without payment of ad-valorem court fee the relief for setting aside the decree could not be granted. Neither of the Court, however, noticed that the suit was also decreed in the declaratory form as prayed for by the plaintiffs that the decree in OC Suit No. 271 of 1982 was not binding upon them. No exception could be taken to that part of the decree and the further decree setting aside the decree in OC Suit No. 271 of 1982 only could have been set aside.

9. The learned Advocate-on-Record for the appellants submits that the decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge was severable and insofar as it relates to the declaratory part, it ought to have been upheld or in the alternative the plaintiffs should have been given an opportunity to pay the ad-valorem court-fee if they wanted to have the benefit of the other part of the decree also even though it was not necessary for them, but the learned District Judge and the High Court Division failed to do either occasioning an apparent failure of justice.

10. This appeal is not opposed by the respondents.

<u>11. We find substance in the contention raised on behalf of the appellants. There was no reason to set aside the decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in its entirety inasmuch as no exception could be taken as far as the declaratory part is concerned. As for the setting aside part of the decree the Court could always allow the plaintiffs an opportunity to pay the ad valorem court-fee (vide section 149 CPC) if they desired to have the benefit of that part of the decree also. Even if the setting aside part was not there, the plaintiffs relief would be complete with the declaratory part only inasmuch as they were not parties to the suit in which the impugned decree was passed.</u>

<u>12. In view of the discussion above, we hold that the impugned judgment and order are not sustainable in law. The declaratory part of the decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is restored and the other part, namely, setting aside of the decree will also be restored provided the plaintiffs deposit ad-valorem court-fee in the trial Court for the said relief within 3 (three) months from date.</u>

The appeal is allowed in the above terms without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: The petitioners seek leave to appeal against the impugned judgment and order discharging the Rule against the order dated 15-12-1988 refusing rejection of plaint of Title Suit No. 110 of 1985.

2. Mr. JN Deb, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the High Court Division while finding the suit to be maintainable did not appreciate the fluctuating and uncertain body of persons like villagers cannot maintain a suit for declaration of title in a specific parcel of land by jote right and adverse possession which is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

3. The suit was filed in a representative character for declaration of jote right and title by adverse possession in the suit land measuring 12.99 acres of land stating, inter alia, that villagers have been holding the land in jote right for over 100 years under Chowdhury Mirasdars and making use thereof by catching fish and growing Boro paddy and also acquired title by adverse possession. Hazi Rifat Ullah and Hazi Arjad Ali and others, on behalf of the villagers and with their money, purchased some share in the permanently settled tanks attracting the suit land; that the suit land was originally a beel and the plaintiffs was holding the same on payment of rent at first to the mirasdars and then to the Government; that the beel was silted up long before 1360 BS and the plaintiffs were growing Boro crops, but the same was recorded in SA survey as Beel in Khatian of the Government which they learnt on 20-5-1978 for the first time.

4. The petitioner contested the suit stating, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to them and they have been in possession thereof by growing Boro and fodder grass and by grazing their cattle since time immemorial; that the Chowdhury Mirasdars filed Title Suit No. 221 of 1940 in the 3rd Court of Munif, Habigonj, for recovery of khas possession which on trial was dismissed on 24-8-1940; as against which they preferred Title Appeal No. 398 bf 1940 which after contested hearing was also dismissed on 7-1-1941 and their Second Appeal also failed and the contesting defendants continued in possession and enjoyment as before; that the raised land on 3 sides of the suit land belonged to them and that plaintiff/respondents have had no interest ever in the suit land; but they for making wrongful gain filed the suit on allegation false to their own knowledge.

<u>5. The suit has been filed for declaration of jote right and title to the suit land by adverse possession in a representative character asserting possession therein and there is no provision in law either under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act or any other law including Evidence Act specifically providing any bar in filing the suit of the nature for which the plaint of the suit is liable to be rejected. From the reading of the averments of the plaint it self we find that no cogent reason to interfere with the impugned order.</u>

The petition is dismissed.

End.

Sadrul Amin Budhu (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Asaduzzaman and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Aziz J: This Revisional application has been directed against the Judgment and order dated 20-10-97 passed by Mr Md Anwarul Hoque, District Judge, Rajshahi, in Miscellaneous Case No. 98 of 1997 rejecting the application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure wherein a Rule was issued upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the aforesaid order should not be set aside and or pass such other or further orders as this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The petitioner, one of the defendants in Other Suit No. 107 of 1992 subsequently re-numbered as Other Suit No. 71 of 1997 now pending before the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi, filed this application under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. His case, in short, is that, the opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 as plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid Other Suit No. 107 of 1992 renumbered as Other Suit Suit No. 71 of 1997 for declaration of title with recovery of Khas possession against the petitioner who is the defendant No. 1 in the said suit and others. The case of the plaintiff opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 is, in short, that, the suit property belongs to their predecessors and the plaintiffs opposite parties 1 to 3 were in peaceful possession of the same and the same has been recorded correctly in their names in SA Khatian and RS Khatian measuring 2562 decimals in SA dag No. 240 and RS Dag No. 461. Their names were recorded correctly in the SA Khatian and they were owning and possessing the same as their ejmali properties. But this defendant petitioner is trespasser in the suit land who took possession of the same on 10-6-92 in absence of the plaintiffs. This has resulted in filing the Other Suit No. 107 of 1992 with a prayer for declaration of title with recovery of khas possession.

3. The defendant-petitioner contested the suit by filing written statement denying the averments made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that he himself is a co-sharer in respect of the suit land being an heir of one admitted predecessor named Setaruddin Sarker, whose name was also recorded in SA Khatian. The petitioner filed a partition suit being Other Suit No. 165 of 1995 for separate saham of the suit properties together with other properties against the plaintiffs-opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 and others before the First Court of the Subordinate Judge, Rajshahi. When this Other Suit No. 71 of 1997 became ripe for disposal, then the petitioner filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, for staying of all further proceedings of the suit until the disposal of the partition suit being Other Suit No. 165 of 1995. But the petition was rejected by the learned Court. Thereafter the petitioner filed an application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Miscellaneous Case No. 98 of 1997 before the learned District Judge, Rajshahi for withdrawal and transferring of either of the aforesaid suits from one court to another court for analogous trial for convenience of the parties and of justice. The learned District Judge having rejected the application on hearing by the aforesaid impugned judgment and order dated 20-10-97, the petitioner obtained this Rule against the same.

4. We have perused the plaints of both the suits enclosed by the petitioner with this revisional application and the impugned Judgment and order, etc. and heard the learned Advocates of both the parties.

5. Mr AB Roy Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the learned District Judge has rejected the application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure illegally and without applying his judicial mind and has thereby erred in law occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that the learned District Judge thoroughly misconceived the facts of the case and the law and failed to appreciate that the parties and the subject matter of both the suits are the same and identical and, as such, the impugned Judgment and order has resulted into occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that the impugned order is not maintainable in law inasmuch as it has been passed without applying the judicial mind in the respective cases of the parties and the court having failed to exercise his jurisdiction under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

6. Mr Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, submits that, the learned District Judge has rightly passed the impugned judgment and order rejecting the application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further submits that the application made by the petitioner for analogous hearing of the suits by either of the Courts is misconceived and not tenable under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as such, the application has rightly been rejected by the learned District Judge who has very wide and ample power to do so. Mr Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties Aziz has however admitted that the parties and the subject matter of the suit properties are the same.

<u>7. We have examined the impugned judgment and order and found that the learned District Judge rejected the application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the finding that the suit matter and the properties of both the suits are completely-different. It appears from reading by us of the respective plaints of the suits enclosed with its revisional application that, the learned District Judge has not gone through those plaints at all correctly. We find from the plaints that the parties of both the suits are same along with others and the subject matter, that is, the properties involved in both the suits, are also the same together with some other ejmali land or both the parties. It is true that, under the provision of section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the learned District Judge has wide and ample discretion to either allow or reject the application but that must be exercised judiciously and for reasons of common convenience of the litigating parties. A Division Bench of this Court has taken the similar view in a case between Abdul Jalil vs Abdul Kader, reported in 36 DLR 306, The said view has been followed in many cases by this Honble Court including in the case by a Single Bench between Tambia Khatun vs Abdur Rouf Sowdagar, reported in 13 BLD 248= 46 DLR 521. On our careful reading of the impugned order and in view of the aforesaid principle of law as laid down by this Court, we find that the impugned order suffers from non-application of judicial mind and it is liable to be set aside.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned Judgment and order dated 20-10-97 passed by the learned District Judge, Rajshahi, is hereby set aside. The partition suit bearing other Suit No. 165 of 1995 is hereby withdrawn from the Court of Subordinate Judge, First Court, Rajshahi, and is transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Rajshahi for disposal. The learned Court will decide whether the suits would be heard analogously or simultaneously in the facts and circumstances of each case at his own discretion. The Court is, however, directed to dispose of both the suits expeditiously.

The order of stay granted earlier is hereby vacated. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

Vs.
Abdul Shahid & others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the order dated 13-8-82 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Execution Case. No. 67 of 1985.

2. Short facts relevant for the purpose of this Rule are that opposite party Nos. 2-3 as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 108 of 1982 before the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka against the predecessor-in-interest of the petitioner and others praying for a specific saham in the suit property according to their shares.

3. The suit was contested by defendant No. 5 Abdus Salam, the predacessor-in-interest of the petitioner, defendant No. 7 and defendant Nos. 14-16 by filing written statements denying the material allegations of the plaint contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs have no title and possession in the suit property and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge by his impugned judgment dated 10-7-65 was pleased to decree the suit in the preliminary form. Thereafter opposite party No 1, who was defendant No. 7 in the suit, filed on 20-7-67 an application praying for appointment of an Advocate Commissioner for effecting partition of the suit property in terms of the preliminary decree and the learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 16-8-67 was pleased to allow the said prayer and directed the decree holder to deposit the requisite commission fees. The learned Subordinate Judge was eventually pleased to accept the Advocate Commissioner''s Report on 3-5-84, although the judgment-debors raised objection against the said report. The preliminary decree was subsequently made final on 3-5-84.

5. On 6-8-1986 the petitioners filed an application for staying all further proceeding of Execution Case No. 67 of 1985 alleging, inter alia, that the predecessor-in-interest defendant No. 5 Abdus Salam had died on 3-3-84 ie about two months before passing of the final decree on 3-5-1984 and, as such, the said final decree is a nullity in the eye of law and consequently the petitioners prayed for setting aside the final decree as being passed against a dead man in defendant No. 5 Abdus Salam and prayed for staying all further proceeding of the Execution Case in question. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned order dated 13-8-86 rejected the petitioners'' prayer holding that although defendant No. 5 died on 3-3-84 and the final decree was passed on 3-5-84 the decree in question cannot be treated as a nullity in view of the provision of Order 22 rule 4(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

6. Mr Abdul Hamid Chowdhury, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge seriously erred in law in passing the impugned order on an erroneous view of law regarding the provision of Order 22 rule 4(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Order 22 rule 4(4) CPC reads as follows:

"(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-rule (3), the plaintiff shall not be required to substitute and shall be exempt from the necessity of substituting the legal representatives of any such defendant who has failed to file a written statement or who having filed it, has failed to appear and contest the suit at the hearing and judgment may, in such a case, be pronounced against the deceased defendant notwithstanding the death of such defendant and shall have the same force and effect as if it had been pronounced before the death took place".

<u>7. There is no dispute to the fact that deceased defendant No. 5 Abdus Salam filed written statement in the suit and contested the suit by adducing evidence and he was allotted a saham for 1.31 acre of land. There is also no dispute to the fact that deceased defendant No. 5 Abdus Salam, one of the judgment-debtors, died on 3-3-84 before the passing of the final decree on 3-5-84. It is thus manifestly evident that the final decree was passed against deceased defendant No. 5 Abdus Salam without bringing his legal representatives on record by way of necessary substitution. It is true, the rights of the contending parties in a suit for partition are determined in the preliminary decree and the final decree is just a follow-up of the preliminary decree in effecting partition of the suit properties by metes and bounds keeping in view the existing possession of the parties as far as practicable. The final decree is, in fact, a continuation of the preliminary decree in course of which the parties are put to actual physical possession of the suit properties according to sahams allotted to them. So, if the final decree is completed in the absence of a party who was allotted a specific saham it is likely that his vital interest go unrepresented and he is adversely affected thereby. Since, in the instant case, a definite saham measaring 1.31 acre of land was allotted to deceased-defendant No. 5 Abdus Salam he had and after his death, his legal representatives have a right to get possession in their allotted saham with reference to the existing possession of the parties but unless they were brought on record their interests can be said to be properly safeguarded by the action of the Advocate-Commissioner, against whose report written objection had already been filed. Since evidently the final decree was passed against deceased defendant No. 5 Abdus Salam on 3-5-84 ie after two month of his death without bringing his legal representatives on record by way of substitution, it is to be held that vital interests of the petitioners have been adversely affected in effecting the final decree in their absence.</u>

8. In the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, I find that the learned Subordinate Judge misread and mis-appreciated the provision of Order 22 rule 4(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and fell in error in passing the impugned order. The impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge does not appear to be either legal or fair and the same has occasioned failure of justice. For the reason stated above, I find that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in passing the impugned order on an errroneous view of law regarding the provision of Order 22 rule 4(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

9. In the result, the impugned order dated 13-8-86 is set aside and the Rule is made absolute. The learned Subordinate Judge is directed to proceed with the execution case in question in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made in the body of this judgment. There will be no order as to costs. Since this is a very old case it is desirable that the case should be disposed of as expeditiously as possible, preferably within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of this order. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is vacated.

Let a copy of the order be sent to the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka at once.

End.

caseno: Civil Rule No.294 (FM) of 1996. (FMAT No.518 of 1996)
lawyer:
Mainul Hosein with Azizul Haque, Mozammel Huq and Humayun Kabir Bulbul, Advocates — For the Petitioner. 
Rafique-ul-Huq with Md. Sharful Islam Khan and Ahsanul Karim, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties 1 and 3. 
Md. Aminul Hoque with Md. Abdul Jabbar, Advocates — For the Opposite Party No.2.
parties:
PKS Ltd  ----- Petitioner
vs.
IFIC Bank Ltd. and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md. Sirajul Islam J: This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner was issued calling upon the defendant-respondent-opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 to show cause as to why they should not be restrained from Getting refund of the disputed amount of Taka 1,48,00,000/- from the petitioner till disposal of FMAT No. 518 of 1996 pending in this court or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The appellant-petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 117 of 1996 in the court of Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for a declaration that the demand note of the defendant No. 1 issued to the State Bank of India, Overseas Branch Calcutta calling for refund of US Dollar 3,52,000 equivalent to Taka 1,48,00,000 (approx) vide telex No. 01/C/IMPORT/3065/96 dated 20-6-1996 is illegal, inoperative, malafide and not binding on the plaintiff. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the plaintiff is a reputed company dealing with export of Rice incorporated in India under the Indian Companies Act with its office at the address given in the plaint in Calcutta, India. The defendant No. 2 contacted that plaintiff over telephone on 13/14th December, 1995 requesting him for shipment of 1000 metric tons of rice from India @ US Dollar 235 per Metric Ton. The defendant No. 2 being known to the plaintiff as importer of rice from India since long agreed to the request for export of the said quantity of rice at the aforesaid rate and sent proforma Invoice No. PKS/MT/1073/95-96 dated 16-12-95 and accordingly the importer-defendant No. 2 opened L/C against the said Proforma Invoice vide L/C No. JFJCB/ACU/0001/96 dated 1-1-96 for US Dollar 1,17,500.00 only. After getting confirmation about opening of the L/C by the defendant No. 2, the plaintiff-company made shipment of 1000 Metric Tons of rice by Trucks through Sona Masjid Land Custom Station on Bangladesh border and Mohadipur Land Custom station on the Indian border. After receipt of this consignment of rice the defendant No. 2 through IFIC Bank Ltd. (defendant No.1) requested the plaintiff for sending another consignment of 1000 Metric Tons of rice in the similar way by amending the L/C on 18-1-1996. The plaintiff accordingly sent the consignment through the same route. The defendant No. 2 again requested the plaintiff for sending another consignment of 500 Metric Tons of rice by amending the L/C for 2nd time by Telex dated 6th February, 1996. The plaintiff accordingly sent the same. The defendant No. 2 after receipt of the same again requested the plaintiff for sending another consignment of 1475 Metric Tons of rice by amending the L/C through defendant No. 1 by Telex dated 10-3-1996. In this process the defendant No. 2 received a total consignment 3975 metric tons of rice from the plaintiff to talling the credit value of US Dollar 9,35,125.00. All the above mentioned consignments were sent by the plaintiff after getting clearance from the Indian Customs Authority and the plaintiff company got payment at the first phase US Dollar 4,70,000.00, the value of 2000 Metric Tons of rice. The plaintiff company thereafter received payments of the disputed 1500 metric tons of rice valued at US dollar 3,52,500.00. That the plaintiff being a company of International repute is always diligent about high-rate performance and that after taking the rice tested by Indian Atomic Research Centre, Calcutta properly and correctly, sent the consignments received by defendant No. 2 and payments were accordingly made. Thus after full payment was made the transaction became complete but the defendant No. 1 thereafter raised some objections pointing out some discrepancies like non-receipt of certified invoice from the Sona Masjid Land Custom Station of Bangladesh and on such pleas the defendants 1 and 2 started demanding refund of the price of the disputed rice of 1500 Metric Tons amounting to US Dollar 3,52,000.00 (Taka 1,48,00,000 in Bangladeshi Taka) The defendant No. 2 by an unfair collusion with defendant No. 1 and Bangladesh Custom Authority started demanding the price of last 3 consignments of 500 metric tons each of rice on various illegal pleas through the defendant Bank of the importer. The defendant No. 1, the importer's bank (IFIC Bank) asked its agent, the State Bank of India, Overseas Branch, Calcutta to get refund of money from proforma defendant No. 7, the Union Bank of India and accordingly the defendant No. 1 continued to insist on demanding the refund of money from its agent, the State Bank of India, who in turn is demanding refund from plaintiff's banks United Bank of India. This demand for refund of money already paid to the exporter-plaintiff is illegal and malafide, hence the plaintiff filed the Suit No. 117 of 1996 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for declaration as aforesaid.

3. After filing of the suit the plaintiff filed an application under Order 39 rule 1 CPC for temporary injunction restraining the defendant respondent opposite party No. 1 from getting refund of the money. The defendant Nos. 1 and 3 appeared and contested the plaintiff's application for temporary injunction by filing a joint written objection denying the plaintiff's case stating inter alia that the plaintiff received payment of the amount of money of the disputed 1500 metric tons of rice hastily on some illegal and discrepant papers and documents and, as such, the defendants are entitled to get the refund of the money received by illegal means through discrepant papers. After hearing both the parties and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction vide his judgment and order dated 26-1-96.

4. Being aggrieved by this rejection order dated 26-9-1996 the plaintiff as an appellant has preferred FMAT No. 518 of 1996 in this court. After admission of this appeal as FMA the plaintiff appellant PKS Ltd as petitioner has filed a separate application praying for injunction for restraining the defendant respondent-opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 from insisting on getting refund of the disputed amount of money, whereupon the present Rule was issued.

5. Only question in this Rule appears to be a question for decision whether the plaintiff appellant petitioner is entitled to get any temporary injunction as prayed for pending disposal of the appeal.

6. Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff appellant-petitioner, has submitted that the importer defendant No. 2 duly received the goods sent by the disputed consignments and then being satisfied its bank defendant No. 1 duly made the payment to the seller company through defendants agent bank, State Bank of India at Calcutta, and thus the transaction for payment and receipt with the plaintiff and defendant No. 2 is a completed transaction and, as such, the defendants have no right to demand the refund of the disputed amount already paid to the plaintiff petitioner. Mr. Mainul Hosein further submitted that this is not a case of L/C and so the buyer-defendant No.2 cannot interfere with the payment already made and that it is a bank to bank transaction but that the defendants with a malafide intention started demanding the closed transacted money and, as such, the demand of refund of money already paid is an illegal demand made by defendant No. 1 to the plaintiff and his agent Union Bank of India through defendants Bank State Bank of India and that if the refund is taken by the defendant No. 1 during the pendency of the suit, the plaintiff shall suffer irreparable loss and, as such, the plaintiff is entitled to get a temporary injunction as prayed for.

7. Mr. Rafique-Ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 has raised a preliminary objection that the declaration as prayed for by the petitioner is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as the letter of credit is not a property as contemplated in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that a suit for declaration of title can only be filed by a plaintiff to protect his proprietary right or a legal character but that a letter of credit does not confer any legal right as to property or legal character and, as such, the suit is not maintainable in this form. He further submits that the State Bank of India, the defendant's agent bank is the reimbursing bank but that bank has not been made a party in the suit from whom the demand is allegedly being made by the defendant's issuing bank, IFIC Bank of Bangladesh and in that view of the matter also the plaintiff is not entitled to get any relief of injunction as prayed for. He further submits that defendant No. 1 the IFIC Bank is asking for the refund of the disputed money from its own Bank, the State Bank of India in Calcutta and not from the plaintiff nor from its bank and, as such, the plaintiff's suit itself will not be maintainable as framed and so temporary injunction cannot be granted as prayed for.

8. The contentions as put forward by the learned Advocate of the defendant-respondent appears to be touching upon merit of the suit. While dealing with a matter of temporary injunction, we propose not to enter into the merit of the suit at this stage.

9. We are primarily to see whether the plaintiff has got any prima facie case for temporary injunction as prayed for.

10. The first requirement for the purpose of granting a temporary injunction is to see whether the plaintiff appellant has been able to make out a good prima facie case for getting any temporary injunction.

11. In this connection Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate for the defendant opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 referred to Articles 13 and 14A of the ICC Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits, 1993, Revised publication No. 500 (hereinafter referred to as UCPDC) and that L/C is a transaction between bank to bank and that this mechanism of L/C is of different level which must be allowed to be honoured free from interference from any court, otherwise trust in international commerce shall be irreparably damaged and as such the plaintiff is not entitled to get any temporary injunction on an international Trade Transaction between bank to bank. In support of this contention Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq referred to a decision in the case of Tarapore and Co. Madras vs. Tractore Export, Moscow and another reported in AIR 1970 (SC) page 89 wherein it has been held by the Supreme Court of India as under:

"An irrevocable letter of credit has a defiant implication. It is a mechanism of great importance in international trade. Any interference with that mechanism is bound to have serious repercussions on the international trade. Except under very exceptional circumstances, the courts should not interfere with that mechanism".

12. The learned Advocate referred to another decision in the case of United Commercial Bank vs. Bank of India and others reported in AIR 1981 (SC) 1426. A similar observation has been made therein that:

"The courts usually refrain from granting injunction to restrain the performance of the contractual obligations arising out of letter of credit or a bank guarantee between one bank and another. If such temporary injunctions were to be granted in a transaction between a banker and a banker, restraining a bank from recalling the amount due when payment is made under reserve to another bank or in terms of the letter of guarantee or credit executed by it, the whole banking system in the country would fail. It is only in exceptional cases that the courts will interfere with the machinery of irrevocable obligations assumed by bank. They are the life-blood of international commerce. The machinery and commitment of banks are on a different level. They must be allowed to be honoured, free from interference by the courts. Otherwise, trust in international commerce would be irreparably damaged".

13. In another decision in the case of Janata Bank vs. Ahmedia Garments reported in 40 DLR 72 it has been similarly observed as under:

"A letter of credit has an autonomy of its own and its need be negotiated or paid without reference to the very contract out of which the credit arose. The L/C is independent and never qualified by the contract of sale or by any under-lying transaction or dispute between the parties and as a matter of fact this established and known principle of international commercial transaction and Bank system has been spelt out in the Uniform Custom and Practice for documentary credit, which has been made a part of the instant L/C".

14. In the case of Uttara Bank vs. Macneill and Kilburn Ltd and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 298 (1981) and BLD (AD) 231, their Lordships of the Appellate Division have quoted from Halsbury's Laws of England as under:

"An irrevocable letter of credit has a definite implication. It is a mechanism of great importance in international trade. Any interference with that mechanism is bound to have serious repercussions on the international trade of this country. Except under very exceptional circumstances, the courts should not interfere with that mechanism.

Their Lordships further observed applying these principles that the least that can be said is that the decisions show that the courts are very reluctant to interfere with commercial transactions which have been entered into by the parties in business transaction. The decision shows that court will not interfere, by granting injunction, in discharging the contractual obligations.

15. The instant case before us is a case of Commercial Trade transaction on the basis of contractual relation and the transaction in dispute before us is a transaction between bank to bank. In the light of the above observations, we are of opinion that this transaction does not call for any interference in the form of temporary or ad-interim injunction as prayed for.

16. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned advocate submits that the payment was fraudulently obtained by the plaintiff bank on some discrepant papers and that the payment was obtained before verifying the papers submitted to the defendant issuing bank. He submits that defendant's issuing IFIC bank received the documents on 13-4-96 and on the same day the Indian Bank was informed about the discrepancies of the document on 13-4-96 but the bank of India made the payment earlier on 4-4-1996. Mr. Rafique-Ul-Huq referred to Articles 13 (b) of the UCPDC and submits that seven (7) days time is allowed for verification of papers but before this allowable time, payment was made by the Indian bank and therefore, the issuing bank is entitled to get the refund of money as because the payment was made on discrepant papers before verification of the same and in violation of the international principle of payment. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq drew our attention to a copy of the concerned L/C to show that the documentary credit has been made subject to the Uniform Custom and Practice for documentary credit 1993 Publication No. 500. He referred to a particular condition of the agreement of the L/C wherein it has been stated that the negotiating bank will send a telex to the opening bank at least 3 days prior to the reimbursement claim regarding the payment. Mr. Huq submits that in violation of this condition, the negotiating bank has made the payment on 4-4-1996 only one day after sending the documents on 3-4-1996.

<u>17. It appears from the copy of the plaint that the plaintiff has prayed for injunction for restraining the defendant respondent opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 from insisting on getting refund of the disputed amount of money as mentioned in the schedule of the plaint. But it has not been stated from whom the refund of money was demanded by defendant Nos. 1 and 3 and the non-mentioning of the persons or bank from whom the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 will be restrained from demanding money, makes the whole prayer for temporary injunction to be vague, unspecified and unintelligible for the purpose of granting an equitable relief of temporary injunction.</u>

18. In this respect Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, submits that this is a new case of this nature and that in spite of some defects in the prayer for temporary injunction, the broad fact remains that the defendant has been insisting on demanding refund from their bank. It is the principle of law that whatever may be the nature of a case, the prayer for an injunction must be made clearly and specifically as to whom to be restrained from making the payment as because the plaintiff must come with clean hand to seek an equitable relief of temporary injunction. There is no such clear or specific prayer in this matter.

19. It may be mentioned here that although the show cause notices of the Rule was not issued upon defendant opposite party No. 2, yet Mr. Aminul Hoque, the learned Advocate, entered appearance on behalf of the respondent-opposite party No. 2 by filing power and a counter affidavit and has submitted that all payments were made illegally on discrepant papers and, as such, bank has the right to demand back the illegally paid money and hence in conformity with the international banking transaction, there cannot be any temporary injunction creating a dislocation in the normal course of international banking transactions.

20. Considering all the above facts and circumstances, we find that the plaintiff has got no prima facie case for any temporary injunction.

21. The next question to be decided for the purpose of granting a temporary injunction is whether the plaintiff in the absence of any temporary injunction will suffer irreparable loss. In the instant case we find that the whole case relates to payment or non-payment of money. Plaintiffs case is a case of payment already made and hence the refund of such paid-money cannot be asked for. The defendant's case is that the payment has been illegally obtained by the plaintiff through some discrepant papers in violation of terms of L/C and, international commercial transaction and, as such, the defendant is legally entitled to get back the money. So it appears that the whole subject matter centers round payment and refund of money. If the refund of money is made and subsequently it is found that papers were not discrepant then the question of plaintiff's loss shall arise and that loss will be a money loss which can be safely compensated by paying back money. So the question of irreparable loss is not present in the instant case and, as such, the plaintiff does not appear to have a case for temporary injunction on the ground of irreparable loss.

22. The next question is to see whether the balance of convenience and inconvenience lies in favour of the plaintiff for the purpose of getting temporary injunction as prayed for. It has been held by their Lordships in the case of United Commercial Bank vs. Bank of India and others reported in AIR 1981 (SC) 1426 that:

"A payment" under reserve" is understood in banking transactions to mean that the recipient of money may not deem it as his own but must be prepared to return it on demand. The balance of convenience clearly lies in allowing the normal banking transactions to go forward. Furthermore, the plaintiffs have failed to establish that they would be put to an irreparable loss unless an interim injunction was granted".

<u>23. From the principle as laid down above, it appears that the banking transactions should be allowed to go forward without any hindrance of any sort. Mr. Mainul Hossein submits that the payment in the transaction under consideration in this case was not made under any reserve. But the fact remains that the defendant's clear case is that the payments were made before receipt of papers and documents by the Bank (IFIC) and before getting any opportunity for verification of discrepancies therein. Therefore, the alleged demand has been made by one bank to another bank, making it also a normal banking transaction. Thus it appears that in such case of normal banking transaction the balance of convenience and inconvenience does not lie in favour of the plaintiff for getting any temporary injunction. In the facts and circumstances, we find that balance of convenience and inconvenience for the purpose of equitable relief of temporary injunction heavily lies against the plaintiff.</u>

24. In consideration of all the above facts, circumstances and the principles of law, we find that the plaintiff is not entitled to get any temporary injunction in the manner as prayed for. It may be noted here that any of our observations made above will not go to prejudice any of the parties hereof in the disposal of the pending First Miscellaneous Appeal and the suit on merit.

In view of all the facts and reasons stated above, the prayer for temporary injunction is rejected and the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 16.7.1975 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 119 of 1993).
full_judgment:
Md. Ismailuddin Sarker J : One Fakir Ahmed and Angia Khatun, petitioner No. 6 instituted a suit for partition being Title Suit No. 150 of 1964 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Comilla Sadar, against petitioner Nos. 1-5 and others and the suit was decreed in preliminary form on 13-6-1967. After the preliminary decree an Advocate Commissioner was appointed to effect partition of the suit property who submitted a report, according to which the final decree was passed on 10-11-1967; but the said final decree was set aside by the learned Assistant Judge on 26-1-1988 by exercising his inherent jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Thereafter another Advocate Commissioner was appointed by the learned Assistant Judge on 16-4-1992 for effecting partition of the suit property in accordance with the preliminary decree and the Advocate Commissioner submitted his report on 29-11-1992 along with field book, map, etc. On receipt of the report of the Advocate Commissioner the Assistant Judge fixed 13.1.1992 for filing any objection against the Commissioner's report but since no objection has been filed by any party, the Commissioner's report was accepted by the learned Assistant Judge on 16-1-1993 and accordingly, final decree was passed on 19.1.1993 and the final decree was sealed and signed on 21-1-1993. Thereafter Title. Execution Case No. 1 of 1993 was filed by some of the parties in the proceeding for getting possession of their land allotted in their saham. Thereafter on 24.1.1993 defendants 8 (ka) and 8 (Cha) filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for cancellation of the Advocate Commissioner's report, after setting aside the final decree on the ground that the sahams were not allotted according to the preliminary decree and the learned Assistant Judge after hearing the parties rejected the Advocate Commissioner's report by his order dated 22-2-1993 in exercise of his jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and thereby set aside the final decree.

2. The respondents thereafter moved the High Court Division in revision and obtained the Rule and the learned Judge of the High Court Division after hearing the parties made the Rule absolute by the impugned judgment and order dated 16-7-1995.

<u>3. It is contended by Mr. Md. Awlad Ali, learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners, that the learned Judge of the High Court Division has committed an error of law in not holding that the Advocate Commissioner's report was not in accordance with the preliminary decree and he has rendered the final decree ineffective and that the trial Court was right in setting aside the final decree in exercise of its power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. There is no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners, inasmuch as other remedies such as an appeal is provided by the Code of Civil Procedure; and when there is specific provision for appeal the Court cannot exercise its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This is not a case of clerical mistake which can be corrected by the trial Court under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. As such, the learned Judge of the High Court Division rightly held that the learned Assistant Judge has committed an illegality in interfering with the final decree under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

4. The petition is, therefore, dismissed.

End.
